Barabak: Is this purple state about to go blue? Nevada's GOP governor faces an anti-Trump backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Is this purple state about to go blue? Nevada’s GOP governor faces an anti-Trump backlash
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Joe Lombardo is no MAGA warrior, but his Democratic opponent has tied him to the president at every opportunity.
- Lombardo hopes Nevada voters will judge him on his performance, not Trump’s.
LAS VEGAS — Five days after settling back into the White House, President Trump embarked on a political victory lap that took him to a rally in downtown Las Vegas.
Joined by Nevada’s Republican governor, Joe Lombardo, Trump told boisterous supporters that, as a first order of business, he’d directed every member of his Cabinet “to marshal all powers at their disposal to defeat inflation and bring down the cost of daily life.”
That hasn’t happened — not even close — and that failure is one big reason that Nevada’s governor is fighting for his political life.
Democrats, still smarting from their loss four years ago, have made Lombardo their No. 1 gubernatorial target this election season. Republicans are battling to keep their top-of-the-ticket foothold in a state that will, once more, stand at the center of the presidential campaign.
With just over a week to go — and with more than 335,000 ballots already cast — the contest could go either way.
Nevada Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo is running for reelection against Atty. Gen. Aaron Ford. Part of Lombardo’s strategy comes from a well-thumbed playbook, tying the Democrat to Newsom and California.
After a career in law enforcement and eight years as sheriff of Clark County — home to Las Vegas — Lombardo made the leap to governor in 2022 in a pandemic-fueled backlash against Democratic incumbent Steve Sisolak.
Reserved by nature and a political civilian most of his life, Lombardo has spent the last four years focused on the basics — crime, education, job growth, economic development — and largely steered clear of the country’s incendiary culture wars.
Unlike other Republican lawmakers, Lombardo has also shied away from the provocations and flamboyant pugilism of the MAGA movement.
Still, Trump hangs like an anvil around Lombardo’s neck — a fact his Democratic opponent, Aaron Ford, exploits at every turn.
Appearing last week at a gas station two miles off the Las Vegas Strip, Ford cited record-high fuel prices — and the knock-on effects they’ve had on tourism, groceries and online shopping — and said Nevadans were suffering for no other reason than Trump’s “war of choice” against Iran.
“And where,” Ford asked rhetorically, as traffic whooshed past, “is our current governor? As usual, he’s at Trump’s feet, serving as his doormat.”
Ford, who’s bidding to become Nevada’s first Black governor, has one of those up-by-the-bootstraps biographies that campaign consultants see as spun gold.
He grew up in Dallas in a family that struggled to stay above water and, as a single father in his early 20s, relied on Medicaid and food stamps to get by. He worked as a waiter and a teacher to pay for law school and a Ph.D. in education before moving to Nevada in 2007. After six years in the state Senate, Ford was elected in 2018 to the first of two terms as the state’s attorney general.
Like Democratic candidates everywhere, Ford has made affordability a key component of his campaign.
Barabak: This Las Vegas Republican had high hopes for Trump. But a ‘Trump slump’ made life worse
Aaron Mahan, who’s spent decades as a server on and off the Strip, says inflation and Trump’s pugnacious immigration and foreign policies have chased tourists away. He’s feeling it in his wallet.
Standing on the sidewalk outside a Circle K — where regular was going for $5.35 a gallon — Ford squatted to sign a blown-up copy of a “letter” to Trump demanding a $2,000 “pain-at-the-pump” rebate for every Nevada household. A line was provided, obligingly but obviously unnecessarily, for Lombardo’s signature.
Four years ago, Ford noted, when gas was around $4.68 a gallon, his Republican rival wrote on social media that hard-pressed Nevadans needed “leadership that ensures our families and businesses are protected from these disastrous policies.”
“But once he got in office,” Ford said, Lombardo “stopped fighting for us in Nevada and he started working for Trump full time.”
A few hours later, at a country-themed nightclub in northwest Las Vegas, the governor took to the stage to extol his performance these last four years.
Small-business creation and job growth are up, he told a crowd of supporters gathered on the dance floor. Teachers are better paid and more people are working in Nevada than ever before. “Kicking butt,” he said, referring to either himself, Nevada or both; it wasn’t clear which. “Kicking butt.”
Also, Lombardo added, Nevada’s crime rate has fallen for both violent and property crimes — “without any help from the attorney general.”
The words “Donald” and “Trump” never passed the governor’s lips.
Lombardo has had a somewhat mixed relationship with the president.
He kept his distance during the 2024 campaign and has occasionally, selectively, taken issue with the administration since Trump returned to office. The governor, for instance, spoke out against cuts to Medicaid as well as the shuttering of wind and solar projects in Nevada.
.
But Lombardo didn’t help himself in the least when Trump came to town in August for another rally, this one at the Red Rock Casino. He heaped praise on the president and defended, of all things, the care and feeding of Trump’s plutocratic pals.
“Quite often when the press and the media runs him down, they think about, you know, he’s taking care of his billionaire friends,” Lombardo said. “Those billionaire friends provide jobs. Unless you take care of them, those jobs are absent.”
Naturally, the moment showed up in a campaign ad, showing the grinning governor alongside a smirking Trump and ending with the tagline: “Joe Lombardo. For Trump, Not Nevada.”
The contest in Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District should be a shoo-in for Republicans. But a problematic candidate, inflation and Trump’s unpopularity give Democrats not far-fetched hopes for a massive upset.
For his part, the governor has portrayed Ford as feckless and borderline corrupt.
He’s seized on the attorney general’s abundant out-of-state travel — for official business, Ford says — to portray him as a high-flier beholden to the special interests that financed his jaunts.
Lombardo has also accused Ford of being weak on crime, citing, in particular, the case of a Nevada inmate convicted of manslaughter in the killing of a pregnant woman. Ford placed the inmate’s bid for clemency on the agenda of the state pardons board — an example, Lombardo claims, of the way Ford treats criminals.
The Democrat said he was merely following procedure and would have opposed the clemency request had he not missed the board’s meeting due to an unspecified family emergency.
With a big financial advantage and the benefit of a highly practiced campaign team, Lombardo has kept the race close despite the rough political climate. But to a considerable degree, his fate is beyond anything that Lombardo can control. The key question is how big the Democratic wave is on Nov. 3 and how strong the Trump undertow.
Those forces of red and blue — more than anything either candidate says or does — will determine the winner in this most purple of states.

As vote nears, Trump's AI gamble fuels economic uncertainty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25

As vote nears, Trump’s AI gamble fuels economic uncertainty
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Trump is vowing to expand a ‘golden age’ of prosperity through the end of his presidency.
- Economists warn that Trump has overseen fiscal policy that would give the federal government fewer tools than it has had in the past to respond to a crisis.
WASHINGTON — In September, just weeks before Americans were set to vote in this year’s midterm elections, a sudden panic over the dangers posed by artificial intelligence caught the White House off guard. A whistleblower had gained viral attention warning the technology could soon pose an existential threat.
President Trump was quick to dismiss concerns, evoking urgency in the U.S. race to achieve global dominance in superintelligence. He rejected calls to negotiate guardrails on the most advanced AI models with China’s leader, Xi Jinping, weeks later, during a prime opportunity to do so in Washington.
Privately, the president expressed concern that public hysteria over AI could jolt markets that have become excessively concentrated in AI-related stocks. He had already seen fresh polling that showed widespread bipartisan opposition to the boom in construction of AI data centers, a push by Trump that has cannibalized chips and energy from other sectors of the economy, driving up costs.
Now, on the campaign trail in the final days before the vote, Trump is vowing to expand a “golden age” of prosperity through the end of his presidency. But experts say his policies on AI have set the U.S. economy up for a period of tremendous risk over the next two years.
Some of the world’s leading financiers are sounding increasingly alarmed about an AI bubble. Ray Dalio, founder of Bridgewater Associates, has warned that AI stocks have become detached from financial fundamentals, pushing markets to precarious highs. Ken Griffin, the world’s richest hedge fund owner, said last week that AI is “almost certainly” fueling a market bubble that could be on the verge of a burst.
Trump’s push to end the war that has raged since 2022 comes as midterm elections could give Democrats control of Congress, expanding their oversight powers.
Economists warn that Trump has overseen fiscal policy that would give the federal government fewer tools than it has had in the past to respond to a crisis.
“Trump could easily run into a financial crisis before his term is up,” said Kenneth Rogoff, an economist at Harvard. “It is entirely plausible to have a 30% — or more — drop in the stock market, and in the context of an economy so dependent on AI, this in turn could easily lead to a recession and widespread financial distress.”
Spending on data center infrastructure last winter and spring accounted for nearly all U.S. economic growth, according to independent analyses. Without it, growth would have slowed to a mere fraction of a percentage point, leaving the economy nearly stagnant and flirting with recession.
The Nasdaq 100 has about 70% of its index weight in companies that depend on AI, from semiconductor manufacturers and Big Tech giants to cloud platforms and software providers. Anthropic, one of the top AI industry leaders, plans an initial public offering next month, while its chief rival, OpenAI, expects to go public next year.
“Because government finances are already strained, with the national debt on a patently unsustainable trajectory, there is no guarantee of a sharp drop in long-term borrowing rates for the government,” Rogoff continued. “So the options for bailing out the financial sector, or fighting recession, could be much more constrained than during the global financial crisis.”
While doubling down on the promise of an untested, frontier technology, Trump’s other economic policies may be hobbling its growth. Tariffs have raised the costs of imported chips, servers, networking equipment, metals and electrical components, and visa restrictions have tied the hands of industry leaders trying to secure the world’s best talent. Runaway federal deficits have driven long-term bond interest rates, adding pressure on AI firms already strapped with debt.
Servaas Storm, an economist closely following the AI sector at the Delft University of Technology, said the industry is already facing severe financial headwinds that could precipitate a panic.
Prices for energy, chips and minerals are driving up the cost of doing business, while early AI adopters such as Microsoft, Meta and Walmart are scaling back its use as employees spend too much time correcting errors, cleaning up low-quality output and addressing security lapses.
Slower adoption could further complicate the search for revenue, particularly for companies already struggling to monetize the technology. For now, hyperscalers are shouldering the cost of financing frontier AI labs that, as Storm put it, “do not have a credible path to profitability.”
“There is indeed an AI bubble in the stock market and in data center construction, which could pop rather soon, as rising debt loads and elevated interest rates could prove too much to sustain it,” Storm said. “That moment is not imminent, but it is approaching — and it will very likely happen before the end of Trump’s presidency.”
Alarm mounted throughout the summer as researchers at leading AI labs found the pace of development far outstripping their expectations.
An economy already under duress from Trump’s other economic policies — from tariffs and tax cuts to the Iran war — could precipitate further pain, said Darrell Duffie, a finance professor at the Stanford Graduate School of Business.
Leading AI companies are already running “day-after” drills in anticipation of an AI-related crisis within the next year, according to Axios.
Americans head into election day deeply pessimistic about the economy, with 77% rating it fair or poor, according to a Fox News poll. A separate CNBC survey found that just 34% approve of Trump’s handling of the economy, while 35% of Republicans disapprove — a record high within his own party.
Inflation has fallen sharply from its 9% peak in 2022, during a pandemic-era surge, reaching 2.9% by the end of Biden’s presidency. Under Trump, it has climbed once again to 3.7%, driven by rising energy, transportation and housing costs — among the top concerns for voters entering next month’s vote.
Persistent inflation has forced the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates elevated, squeezing borrowers. And those rates — paired with high government spending and concerns over mounting deficits — have pressured the bond market, pushing 10-year Treasury yields to levels not seen since the early 2000s.
“Financial crises, by their nature, are virtually impossible to predict,” Duffie said, asked whether he shared concerns of a potential AI bubble.
“If we know we are going to be in a crisis soon,” he added, “markets advance the crisis to now.”

Qatar official calls for peace and security to boost trade, investment
Speaking at the World Investment Forum in Doha, state minister says peace and security are essential for trade and investment prosperity.
Qatar’s Minister of State for Foreign Trade Affairs Ahmad bin Mohammed al-Sayed has called for greater international cooperation and economic stability, warning that trade and investment cannot flourish without peace and security.
Speaking at the United Nations-led World Investment Forum in Doha on Sunday, al-Sayed said geopolitical upheaval and growing economic fragmentation were threatening global investment prospects.
“The global economy is undergoing changes. There are geopolitical changes. These are all issues that redefine the landscape of global investment,” he said.
“We believe that investment in the future is related to investment in peace and security,” the minister added.
“Trade will prosper, and long-term investment will create its potential only with a safe and stable environment.”
Organised by the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the World Investment Forum brings together heads of state, policymakers, CEOs and investors to discuss global investment, opportunities, challenges and sustainable development.
Al-Sayed’s remarks come as several conflicts continue to rage around the world, and with growing fears of an escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran in the coming weeks.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments, has been disrupted since the US and Israel launched the war on February 28. Iran responded by effectively blocking the strait and attacking targets across the region.
Prior to the war, one-fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas flowed through the strait.
In the past week, escalating attacks on shipping in the strait and uncertainty over diplomatic efforts to end the nearly eight-month war have led to a surge in oil prices, putting further pressure on the global economy.
On Thursday, oil prices climbed about 4 percent to a five-month high, with Brent futures crossing $113.17 a barrel.
‘Further cooperation, less isolation’
Al-Sayed stressed the need for predictable international rules and stronger economic partnerships at a time of heightened uncertainty.
“In our world, which is facing further uncertainty and economic fragmentation, our message stays clear. It is a call for further cooperation and less isolation, further cooperation and less division,” he said.
Iranian strikes on Qatar’s Ras Laffan industrial complex in March damaged facilities, with repairs expected to take several years.
The minister outlined Qatar’s efforts to strengthen supply chains, diversify economic partnerships and “open new markets for our exports”.
He said Qatar attracted 373 foreign direct investment projects in 2025, a 50 percent increase from the previous year, generating more than 15,000 jobs.
Qatar has also unveiled infrastructure projects worth $38.5bn over the next five years, alongside an anticipated $22.5bn in private sector investment in hospitality and real estate, al-Sayed added.

Jordan church attack survivor says her cousin died before her eyes
HAMOUD, Jordan, Oct 25 - When gunmen began opening fire on a church in Jordan, Sahar al-Halsa hid behind a pillar as she heard the shooting and people screamed in panic during a funeral service for her cousin's daughter.
When she rushed outside in the chaos, she said she spotted the assailants and another cousin lying on the ground wounded.
"I went to him and said: 'Assem, Assem, my darling, answer me'," she said.
She said he opened his eyes to look at her, but then "he was gone".
Friday's attack on the Greek Orthodox place of worship in Karak governorate, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital Amman, prompted King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against Islamist militant groups, to order security forces to respond with an "iron fist" to what authorities described as extremist terrorism.
PRIEST SENDS MESSAGE OF LOVE AND PEACE
Nine people died in the shooting that witnesses said lasted for several minutes. Their funeral service is expected on Sunday. Forty people were wounded in the rare attack on minority Christians.
Speaking from her home, from where the red dome of St George's church is visible, al-Halsa concluded that God must have saved her.
"My life starts now, because I was going to die," she said, speaking beside her husband Ziad al-Halsa. A statue of Jesus on a cross was displayed on a shelf.
Authorities have said they are still searching for the attackers, adding it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan.
There has been no immediate claim of responsibility.
Sahar's husband Ziad said he ran the short distance to the church after he heard the gunfire, describing the overwhelming sense of relief when he realised Sahar, who he described as "the love of his life", was safe.
"To my cousins, may God have mercy on them," he said.
Such attacks are highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities there say they have foiled several Islamist plots in recent years.
Speaking ahead of the funerals, priest Yuhanna Hamati said:
"Our message from this church, from this place where this horrific crime was committed, is a message of love, peace, and reassurance. A message that we send to the whole world." REUTERS

Leaked emails show AfD co-leader’s U-turn on ‘explosive’ nationalist colleague
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:47:30 UTC
18:47:30 KST

Alice Weidel and Björn Höcke react to exit poll results at the Alternative for Germany's headquarters in Berlin on Feb. 23, 2025. | Pool photo by Soren Stache via Getty Images
BERLIN — As she was climbing the ranks of far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) a decade ago, Alice Weidel privately denounced one of her party’s most influential figures for using racist arguments and Nazi-era language, and sought to have him expelled.
Years later, she praised his leadership, said a bid to ban him from the party was “exaggerated” and that he was suitable for a federal cabinet position.
That striking reversal emerges from a massive leak of internal AfD communications, including emails in which Weidel condemned Björn Höcke, the party’s leader in the eastern state of Thuringia, and warned that extremists were driving away mainstream conservative voters.
Advertisement
The revelations come from more than 420,000 emails and roughly 48,000 documents released by hackers this week, providing a rare glimpse inside Germany’s largest far-right party. An anonymous spokesperson for the hackers told Die Zeit the attack was not “politically” motivated “in the sense that [they] support another party,” but that they published the allegedly stolen material to promote “transparency and public accountability.”
The AfD confirmed the breach, saying hackers had attacked a hosting provider in late September. It condemned the leak as “an attack on the German party system and therefore on democracy itself.”
WELT, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, examined emails from one of Weidel’s accounts between 2015 and 2017, when she was a relatively junior figure in the party’s leadership.
Asked by WELT to explain the contrast between her warnings at the time and her present position, Weidel declined to comment through a spokesperson.
A spokesperson for Höcke did not respond to a request for comment sent by POLITICO on Saturday.
‘Deeply problematic’
The messages seen by WELT show a politician deeply alarmed by the growing influence of Höcke, who championed an ethnically defined German nationalism drawing on ideas associated with the Nazi era.
Advertisement
In October 2015, Weidel warned colleagues that the party’s proximity to Pegida, an anti-Islam street movement, and the neo-Nazi National Democratic Party (now known as The Homeland) was alienating the conservative voters it needed to attract.
“In the west we are losing the mainstream conservative electorate completely through our proximity to Pegida, and to the NPD in the east,” she wrote.
Weidel also strongly pushed back on a speech from Höcke that same year, where he contrasted a “life-affirming African expansionary type” with a “self-negating European placeholder type,”
“This is deeply problematic, because the reasoning here is racial. It is fundamentally wrong,” she wrote to the AfD’s federal executive board. “And please, spare me the usual ‘that’s-not-how-it-was-meant.’ I can’t hear it any more.”
In another message, she warned that extremists were deliberately blurring the boundary between the AfD and neo-Nazi politics, driving mainstream conservatives away “in horror.”
She also feared that Höcke’s rhetoric could bring the party under scrutiny by Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, its domestic intelligence service monitoring threats to the constitutional order.
Advertisement
“Höcke’s statements alone, and the use of the term Volksgemeinschaft” — the Nazi-era concept of an ethnic national community — “are enough to land the AfD in that report,” she wrote, referring to the intelligence service’s annual assessment. “Some in our party seem in a hurry to drive the AfD, deliberately or not, into oblivion.”
In May 2025, the agency classified the AfD as a “confirmed right-wing extremist organisation”, citing, among other things, an exclusionary concept of the German nation. The classification, which grants authorities broader surveillance powers, was provisionally suspended by a court in Cologne last February.
‘Wake up, for once’
The leak also features emails about a speech Höcke gave in January 2017 to the AfD’s youth wing, attacking Germany’s culture of Holocaust remembrance.
Höcke described Berlin’s Holocaust memorial as a “memorial of shame,” criticized the country’s efforts to confront its Nazi past and demanded a “180-degree turn in the politics of memory.”
Weidel herself brought a motion to expel him from the AfD.
The motion, obtained by WELT, accused Höcke of using “vocabulary from Adolf Hitler” and endorsing the “Führerprinzip” — the Nazi doctrine of absolute leadership authority. It described him as displaying an “affinity in essence with National Socialism.”
Advertisement
In an internal message, Weidel urged colleagues to recognize the implications of Höcke’s language. “Wake up, for once,” she wrote, warning of the “explosive force of the double meanings” in his speech.
As Weidel prepared to seek the party’s nomination as lead candidate for the 2017 federal election, the leaked correspondence shows that she blocked the recording of her own motion against Höcke in the minutes of a party leadership meeting, arguing that further controversy would damage the party.
Höcke subsequently acknowledged that his speech had been a mistake and asked the leadership to withdraw the move against him.
Weidel publicly welcomed his letter as a “positive signal” and called for an end to the infighting.
Within weeks, she had secured her nomination as the AfD’s lead candidate. Asked whether she would campaign alongside Höcke, she replied: “Yes, of course. We are two parts of one party.”
Indeed, the emails suggest that Weidel’s private misgivings had not entirely disappeared. In May 2017, she condemned an AfD election poster featuring a pregnant woman and the slogan “‘New Germans?’ We’ll make our own” as “an NPD poster,” in a reference to the neo-Nazi party.
Advertisement
Today, Weidel no longer publicly criticizes Höcke. She has praised his leadership in Thuringia and even suggested him for a federal cabinet position.
“We get along very well and we got to know each other over the years,” she told BILD in a 2025 interview. When she was asked whether Höcke was suitable for a federal cabinet position, she simply replied: “Yes.”
When asked in February 2025 about the 2017 expulsion proceedings against him that were backed by Weidel, Höcke called it “old news.”
“We got to know each other and came to appreciate each other. Alice Weidel was the right lead candidate and did a top job,” Höcke told WELT at the time.
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, The Telegraph, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

Over 50,000 killed in Europe over summer due to worst heat wave on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:44:20 UTC
18:44:20 KST

Over 50,000 people were killed this past summer in Europe due to a brutal heat wave, marking it as the deadliest the continent has ever faced, CNN reported on Friday.
The report cited a new analysis published in two peer-reviewed papers in the journal Nature Health that attributed over half of the deaths to climate change driven by fossil fuel pollution.
According to the journal, temperatures reached levels 2.9 degrees Celsius above the 1991-2020 average, with some areas seeing periodic temperatures over 12 degrees Celsius above the average.
The findings come as world leaders are set to attend annual United Nations climate talks in Turkey, according to CNN, with a UN report earlier last week warning that the planet has missed its chance to limit the effect of global warming to an increase of 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.
The Nature Health report concluded that the 2026 summer season was "likely to have been the most dangerously hot summer that Europe has experienced to date," with southern and western Europe being worst affected.
UK, other generally cooler European regions experienced record heat, CNN reports
CNN noted that the United Kingdom and other European regions known for cooler climates also suffered from thousands of heat-related deaths.
Nature Health evaluated 854 European cities in 30 countries, comparing recorded temperatures with those estimated after removing climate change from the equation. Scientists then used the relationship between high temperatures and daily deaths to model the likely number of heat-related deaths between June and August through peer-reviewed research.
According to the report, over 800 people between the ages of 20 and 44 were killed by the heat wave, though the highest rates were among those 85 and older.
An estimated total of 50,391 people died over the summer, with the analysis noting the death toll as being substantially higher than the 2022 and 2003 summer heat waves in Europe, as well as the highest in 26 years.
The journal also found that fossil fuel pollution-driven climate change accounts for about two-thirds of modern heat-related deaths, compared with around 40% earlier this century.
"I think we can be quite confident in stating that the summer of 2026 is likely to have been the worst on record for heat-related mortality across much of Europe," Clair Barnes, an author on the reports and an extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial College London, told CNN. "We’re well off-track to limit the worst consequences of climate change, and governments need to realize that without faster action and coordination, things will only get worse."
"Until we kick the fossil fuel habit, we will continue to see increasingly hot and dangerous summers," she added. "These numbers are a stark reminder that our hotter, more extreme summers are having an increasingly severe impact on public health. Behind these statistics are real people whose lives were lost and real families who grieve for them."
Extreme heat a 'silent killer,' Warwick University associate professor says
Warwick University health and environment associate professor Raquel Nunes told CNN the findings are "growing evidence of how deadly extreme heat can be, despite being described as a ‘silent killer’ due to its impacts not always being immediately visible."
Nunes, who CNN noted was not involved in the research, added that the high death toll amongst those under 65, numbering in the thousands, was particularly alarming.
European Mortality Monitoring Network (EuroMOMO) chief physician Lasse Vestergaard acknowledged that the Nature Health findings largely matched the network's, but advised CNN that the results must be treated with caution "as they involve several uncertainties and assumptions."
The Environment and Climate Change portal is produced in cooperation with the Goldman Sonnenfeldt School of Sustainability and Climate Change at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. The Jerusalem Post maintains all editorial decisions related to the content.

The IDF is making an effort to characterize Friday's incident in Hebron as an encounter between combat troops and two terrorists, rather than a terrorist attack, in an attempt to avoid professional criticism over the advance preparations of the Judea Regional Brigade, operating under the 98th Division.
At the same time, however, the military says the troops' response prevented a larger attack. At the time of writing, the assessment is that the attack was carried out by a Hamas cell that received assistance from the organization's headquarters in Turkey.
This was not the work of a lone attacker, but rather an organized terrorist network that received assistance from additional operatives in obtaining a handgun, an M4 rifle, ammunition, and training. The terrorists studied the terrain, conducted reconnaissance, and developed operational plans that enabled them to hold off IDF forces for more than 20 minutes. During that time, the military was unable to deploy an attack drone or an aerial surveillance system to eliminate them.
Nevertheless, the IDF has noted that the bravery of the soldiers must be acknowledged. The regional defense officer, who found himself caught up in the incident, and the deputy battalion commander actively engaged the terrorists and killed them.
There is no doubt that this terrorist network operated under the noses of IDF and Shin Bet intelligence officials, despite a general warning that Hamas intended to carry out attacks in the area ahead of the elections scheduled for this coming Tuesday.
Shin Bet, IDF arrest suspects for possible knowledge, support of terror attack
Over the past 24 hours, IDF and Shin Bet forces have arrested several Palestinians suspected of assisting the terrorists, or at least knowing that they were preparing to carry out an attack.
The suspects were transferred to the Shin Bet for questioning, and further arrests are expected.
IDF Central Command chief Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth emphasized that the military acted as a protective barrier, shielding the civilian population from terrorism, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz spoke of offensive operations.
At a time when tensions in the West Bank are escalating, and the IDF has deployed an additional divisional headquarters, the 98th Division, to improve command and control capabilities in violent hotspots and areas facing an immediate terrorist threat, the question must be asked: What has the IDF actually done so far?
IDF demolishes illegal structures in Hebron
The IDF demolished illegal structures in the Hebron area earlier in the morning, demolitions that had already been planned and were unrelated to the terrorist attack. Troops searched 200 buildings in Hebron without finding weapons, ammunition, or terrorist infrastructure. According to the defense minister, approximately 2,000 residents were evacuated.
It is clear that these residents will return to their homes shortly and that the evacuation was intended to protect them from potential clashes while IDF forces searched the area.
A new and effective approach is needed to address terrorist hotspots in a city such as Hebron, which presents different challenges from the refugee camps in Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nablus. Such an approach is necessary not only to prevent copycat attacks and attacks inspired by this incident, but also to dismantle organized terrorist networks.
The terrorists came from a very large clan in Hebron, one of whose members was released as part of the Gilad Schalit prisoner exchange deal. The threat of further terrorist attacks continues to loom.

North Korea Expands Missiles and Drones With Russian Help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

North Korea has advanced its ballistic missile systems and established mass production lines for strike drones with technical and operational assistance from Russia, The New York Times reported.
Moscow is transferring military technologies, telemetry feedback, and operational expertise to Pyongyang in exchange for North Korean ammunition, labor, and combat troops deployed in support of Russia’s war effort in Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In early October, North Korea conducted a test launch of a tactical ballistic missile that Pyongyang claimed is capable of delivering a nuclear warhead.
South Korean and Japanese defense tracking systems recorded the munition traveling approximately 700 kilometers (435 miles), whereas state media in Pyongyang asserted the missile achieved an operational flight range of 1,000 kilometers (621 miles).
Departing from routine diplomatic protocols that traditionally limit Seoul to brief statements of condemnation following Northern missile tests, South Korea conducted its first operational test of a domestically developed hypersonic ballistic missile five days later.
The test launch was observed in person by South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, reflecting growing institutional concern in Seoul regarding Pyongyang’s accelerated technological timeline.
Russian combat feedback, accuracy, and mass drone assembly
Western intelligence and defense analysts observe that Pyongyang is leveraging Russian operational data detailing how North Korean weapons perform in real combat environments against modern Western-supplied air defense systems.
Russian Drone Hits Vinnytsia Apartment Block, 6 Injured
Defense analyst Anton Ponomarenko noted that telemetry and performance feedback provided by the Russian military have enabled North Korean engineers to refine the guidance accuracy and terminal maneuverability of tactical ballistic missiles, increasing the conventional and nuclear strike risk posed to South Korea.
Concurrently, Moscow has assisted Pyongyang in establishing domestic industrial manufacturing lines for loitering munitions and strike drones.
Pyongyang has adapted lessons from the armed conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, where cost-effective unmanned platforms have repeatedly saturated and depleted advanced, high-cost air defense networks.
During North Korean military drills conducted last month, an integrated swarm of unmanned aerial vehicles conducted synchronized saturation strikes against an island target while cruise and ballistic missiles launched simultaneous strikes from multiple vectors.
Defense specialists emphasize that countering coordinated drone-swarm and missile saturation tactics could compel South Korea and its regional allies to overhaul integrated air and missile defense postures at substantial financial cost.
Expanding military alliance and troop deployments
The reciprocal technology transfers underscore the deepening military axis between Moscow and Pyongyang following the signing of a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Pyongyang in June 2024, which codified a mutual defense clause.
In a birthday dispatch addressed to Putin on Oct. 7, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un reaffirmed “invariable support” for Moscow, characterizing Russia’s war in Ukraine as a “sacred war of justice” and pledging to expand bilateral strategic alignment.
The partnership encompasses significant conventional transfers and frontline force commitments. North Korea has supplied artillery munitions and ballistic missiles to the Russian military while deploying an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 military personnel to Russian, including roughly 10,000 combat infantry and 1,000 military engineers deployed in the Kursk region.
According to casualty assessments compiled by South Korea’s National Intelligence Service (NIS), approximately 6,000 North Korean soldiers deployed in support of Russian operations have been killed or wounded in combat, reinforcing Pyongyang’s reliance on Russian technological reciprocity to compensate for troop and material losses.

Russia Transferred Over $80 Million in Submarine Technology to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:39:38 UTC
18:39:38 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Transferred Over $80 Million in Submarine Technology to China
Russia supplied China with more than $80 million worth of submarine-related technology and technical documentation, helping Beijing develop its conventional submarine fleet through cooperation that continued after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to an October 22 report titled A Marriage of Convenience? by the Washington-based research organization C4ADS, Russia’s Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering conducted 12 shipments to Chinese military procurement agencies and China Shipbuilding and Offshore International Co. (CSOI) between August 2015 and April 2023.
The transfers, valued at more than $80 million, reportedly involved conceptual designs for non-nuclear submarines, testing documentation, and technologies intended to improve underwater stealth.
Two shipments in October 2019 and January 2020 included documents related to submarine testing, particularly cavitation—a phenomenon that generates underwater noise and can make submarines easier to detect.
A maritime security expert consulted by C4ADS assessed that the documentation indicated Russian assistance in evaluating Chinese submarine noise-reduction technologies.
The cooperation also operated in the opposite direction. Between December 2019 and September 2022, CSOI supplied Rubin with submarine testing equipment, including instruments and control-panel components used to evaluate onboard information and control systems.
Documents accompanying a September 2022 shipment also referenced a joint design and manufacturing contract, indicating that technical cooperation continued after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Rubin, a subsidiary of Russia’s state-owned United Shipbuilding Corporation, is subject to sanctions imposed by the United States, European Union, and Japan.
China’s conventional submarine fleet has historically relied on Soviet and Russian technology, although Beijing has since developed its own designs. The C4ADS findings indicate that Russian expertise continued to support Chinese submarine development, particularly in acoustic stealth and underwater systems.
Earlier, an October 19 report revealed that Chinese companies had supplied Russia with industrial equipment, engine components, and navigation technology, helping expand production of Shahed-type attack drones at the Alabuga facility to a reported capacity of more than 3,000 per month.

At the bottom of the ocean, scientists discovered a mysterious grave with a unique ecosystem
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:37:04 EET
18:37:04 KST

At the bottom of the ocean, scientists discovered a mysterious grave with a unique ecosystem
Kyiv • UNN
Norwegian researchers discovered the remains of a toothed whale at a depth of 2,777 meters. An ecosystem with potentially new species had formed around them.
Norwegian researchers discovered the remains of a whale at a depth of nearly 2.8 kilometers, around which an unusual ecosystem had formed. The findings included the marine mammal’s bones and teeth, as well as deep-sea organisms, some of which may belong to species previously unknown to science. ScienceAlert reports this, according to UNN.
Details
During an expedition by the Norwegian seabed research program MAREANO, scientists discovered an unusual site on the Arctic Mid-Ocean Ridge. The discovery was made on April 23, 2026, using the Ægir6000 remotely operated underwater vehicle. At a depth of 2,777 meters, the researchers noticed a cluster of tubular formations that differed sharply from the surrounding seafloor. At first, the scientists called the find a "strange site," but further research showed that the remains of a large marine animal were hidden beneath a layer of sedimentary rock. When the underwater vehicle began collecting soil samples, a dense black cloud rose in the water. Later, among the samples brought up, the researchers found fragments of bones and several whale teeth.
Experts from the Norwegian Institute of Marine Research established that the remains belonged to a member of the toothed whales. At the same time, it has not yet been possible to determine the animal’s exact species, the cause of its death, or how long it had been on the seafloor.
Scientists were most intrigued by the ecosystem that had formed around the remains. The researchers found polychaete worms, mollusks, crustaceans, sea spiders, and other invertebrates. Particular attention was drawn to worms of the genera Notomastus and Anobothrus. Some of the organisms discovered may turn out to represent species not yet described by science, but additional research is needed to confirm this.
Scientists explain that this phenomenon is known as a whale fall. After the death of a large marine mammal, its body sinks to the seafloor, where it gradually becomes a source of nutrients for numerous organisms. Initially, deep-sea scavengers consume the soft tissues. Later, the organic remains enrich the bottom sediments, while bacteria that break down compounds inside the bones create conditions for other organisms to survive. Such ecosystems can persist for decades. According to the researchers, the discovery is important for understanding biodiversity in the ocean depths. Similar sites can serve as unique centers of life and contribute to the dispersal of deep-sea species.
At the same time, scientists warn that the industrial extraction of minerals from the seafloor poses a potential threat to such ecosystems. Because whale remains are often hidden beneath sedimentary rock, they may be destroyed before scientists have an opportunity to study them.
As a reminder
In May 2019, in Wales, United Kingdom, after a hurricane, the water receded from the sea, revealing a sunken forest that had been buried under water and sand for more than 4,500 years.

Thousands march across Italy as protests bring isolated clashes with police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:32:06 UTC
18:32:06 KST

Demonstrations took place in Italy on Saturday over the rising cost of living. No serious clashes were reported, with nine people arrested nationwide.
Thousands of people took to the streets on Saturday across Italy's main cities to protest over a range of issues, including the rising cost of living, Giorgia Meloni's government and the wars in the Middle East.
The protests were mostly peaceful, although some moments of tension were reported towards the evening in Turin, Florence, Bologna and Rome.
After last weekend's violence, the government enacted a significant new security operation, with police officers and soldiers patrolling city centres.
In Milan, 500 soldiers were also deployed in response to attacks on shops last Saturday.
In Florence, as in Turin, Milan and Rome, protesters did not organise a single main march, but instead small groups gathered in different parts of the city and later joined up. They repeatedly tried to reach the city centres but were blocked by security forces.
Protesters enter the Colosseum
In Rome, tensions flared when a small group of protesters broke away from the main march on Via Cavour and headed for the Colosseum.
There, they managed to enter the Flavian Amphitheatre, chanting slogans and holding up placards. The authorities later escorted them out of the historical site as the march continued through the streets of the city.
Later on, a young demonstrator also stood in front of a police water cannon truck, which continued for a couple of metres before the young man almost ended up beneath it. Officers then forcefully dragged him away, videos circulating on social media show.
In Florence, tensions also spiked when demonstrators tried to cross the Santa Trìnita bridge, but officers maintained the security cordon and used batons as protesters pushed to break through the barrier.
In Bologna, a march was prevented from continuing towards Via Marconi and Via Reno, with bottles and other objects hurled at security forces, who responded with a water cannon and tear gas.
One person was taken to hospital after being struck by police officers.
In Milan, the situation was calmer on Saturday; at least three marches joined together and moved through the streets around the city centre. There were verbal clashes between protesters and some far-right activists.
Nine arrests made
By the end of the day, nine people had been arrested and 87 were reported to the authorities, according to the Department of Public Security. A further 371 people were taken to police stations for checks, including 110 minors and 69 foreign nationals.
In Milan, 30-year-old Youssef Siher was also detained and placed under investigation on suspicion of aggravated incitement to commit a crime. He is alleged to have been behind the "17 October Movement," a group through which thousands of people are said to have shared information about taking part in last weekend's protests.
Meloni praises security operation
In a post on social media on Saturday evening, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni praised those involved in the efforts to manage the demonstrations.
"The right to demonstrate must always be guaranteed, just as the right of citizens to live in their cities in safety," Meloni said.
"Safety must be guaranteed for everyone. For those who want to protest peacefully, for those who work and for those who want to live in their city without fear. Without leaving room for those who seek only confrontation and violence," she added.

Terrorists in the West Bank: Settler violence and the excusing hand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:31:56 UTC
18:31:56 KST

The persistent violence from Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied territories of the West Bank has become such common fare it risks becoming banal. Unfortunately, it takes events such as those befalling veteran photojournalist Heidi Levine of The Washington Post and European diplomats to return the attention to something that is not only grotesque but programmatic.
On 16th October, while covering the annual olive harvest in the West Bank Levine, fellow journalists and a group of Palestinians became the ripe targets of Israeli settlers. The auguries of violence were already present: over the course of 24 days since the season commenced, 125 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters had been reported. After an initial gathering at a hilltop in the proximity of Abu Falah, the numbers of the assailants ominously swelled. They approached the group menacingly, burning olive trees on route. Then came tear gas and shots. A Palestinian was wounded in the leg.
Levine, in her description, was forced to the ground. “They just kept kicking me and hitting me with sticks, and it just kept going on and on. And then I actually thought, okay, maybe I’ll just play dead and pretend I’m dead, and they’ll stop and they’ll leave me alone.” The decision failed to yield the desired result.
Her camera bag, lenses, pouch filled with her US passport, credit cards, documents and relevant items were seized. She was hauled to her feet.
Eventually, a group of Palestinian men intervened to stand “in front of me to protect us, me and my rescuers from being attacked again.” Without that involvement, the group “would have been in the same situation as me.” In that encounter, Levine suffered a broken rib, a broken vertebra and a severe finger injury needing surgery.
In a separate attack on 17th October, French, Belgian and Polish diplomats and dignitaries of the Catholic Church found themselves targets at the mostly Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
The window of a car from the Belgian consulate was smashed. Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was beaten
The response from the Israeli government was, as to be expected, guarded, qualified and, in the end, light on the egregious conduct of the assailants. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar merely called the attacks on the European officials the cavalier work of “Israeli rioters”, blaming those who had organised the convoy for not coordinating “with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors’ security.” Presumably, irresponsible Palestinian olive pickers do not coordinate with the IDF sufficiently to prevent settler attacks they invite upon themselves for simply being there.
A new sanctions regime: Targeting Israel’s West Bank settlements
An official statement from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office suggested that “serious questions” remained unanswered regarding the attack on Levine, a neat way of suggesting that non-settler accounts were to be treated as mendacious, self-interested and ultimately, unreliable. “Reports indicate some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths.” Those Arabs, those leftists, in a struggle against unblemished Israeli youth. The violence that ensued had a certain equivalence – so the PM’s office seemed to imply. “Footage shows masked individuals on both sides hurling objects, amid reports of fireworks fired at Jewish youths.”
As for Levine, was she to be trusted? After all, “footage appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual.” Not so, rebutted Levine.
The attackers “only stood me up because they couldn’t manage to get everything off my shoulders to rob me, including ripping off my gold necklace that my daughter gave me for my birthday.”
The statement went on to reveal the whole rationale of such parrying responses. “We will not allow disputed incidents to be exploited to demonize the hundreds of thousands of law-abiding Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria.” Hard to be law abiding if one’s entire presence is premised on illegal occupation.
Stung into modest, cosmetic action, the Israeli authorities detained ten suspects regarding the two attacks on 19th October. On 21st October, nine of them were ordered by a Jerusalem court to be released to house arrest. “In the vast majority of attacks against Palestinians, no arrests are made at all,” explained Yonatan Kanonich, head of research at the Israeli rights outfit Yesh Din. “In cases that receive media coverage … the police arrest several settlers and release most of them shortly afterward.” Assaf Gonen of the legal aid organisation Honenu, bluntly claimed that such arrests were only “for show” with the intention of satisfying “media pressure and foreign interests.”
Interest has now shifted to the latest spate of bloodletting, with the 23rd October shooting deaths of two IDF soldiers at a checkpoint in Hebron giving Netanyahu the pretext to dig in, condemn and authorise acts of collective punishment. The IDF describes its avenging operation as “focused and limited to the area from which the terrorists operated”, which suggest that the area in question is likely to be flattened. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich is unreserved in justifying the demolition orders against “illegal structures” to “create deterrence and exact a price for the serious attack”.
Dreams about Gaza: Israel’s ethnic cleansing proposals
The PM has an election to win, and the security and military forces have become his electioneering playthings. As for the terrorising settlers, Netanyahu only has warm words of praise. They were “heroic” emissaries of Israel’s broader project of settlement. “You are standing in the breach. You are a role model for the people of Israel, you are role model for the State of Israel. We are going to destroy the terror infrastructures, and we are going to build the settlement infrastructures.”
Levine acknowledges the asymmetrical interest shown for Palestinian residents relative to the tenacious, gluttonous coverage given notable foreign visitors who have suffered injury at the hands of the same assailants. “What hurts me most is I can now really understand what others have gone through, what Palestinian women, children, men have gone through,” she reflected in an 22nd October interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper.
“I’m an American, I work for The Washington Post, my story is getting a lot of attention around the world, everyone wants to talk to me – but I can’t imagine what it’s like for all the victims that have gone through the same ordeal and are living with the threat of this violence on a daily basis.”
The response from Democratic Congresswoman Rosa DeLauro from Connecticut to the attack had the good sense to note that the Palestinian “farmers in the grove had no flak jackets and no helmets. They had no major American newspaper behind them. If the settlers will do this to an American journalist on camera, in broad daylight, imagine what Palestinian families face when no one is watching.” Heroic deeds, according to Netanyahu, with more to come.

World leaders congratulate Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Republic Day
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has received congratulatory messages from heads of foreign states and leaders of international organizations on the occasion of Kazakhstan’s national holiday, Republic Day, Qazinform News Agency cites the Akorda press service.
In his message, Russian President Vladimir Putin highlighted Kazakhstan’s achievements in the economic and social spheres, noting the country’s significant and constructive role in international affairs and its well-deserved standing on the world stage.
“Relations between Russia and Kazakhstan are successfully developing in the spirit of strategic partnership and alliance. I am confident that we will continue to consistently strengthen mutually beneficial Russian-Kazakh ties across all areas, for the benefit of our friendly peoples and in the interests of enhancing security and stability across the Eurasian region,” Vladimir Putin wrote.
President of the People’s Republic of China Xi Jinping noted that Kazakhstan is consistently implementing large-scale political reforms, maintaining social stability, sustaining steady economic growth, improving the well-being of its population, and strengthening its regional and international standing.
“I attach particular importance to the development of Kazakh-Chinese relations. I stand ready to continue our joint efforts to further deepen bilateral cooperation and make it more substantive for the benefit of the peoples of our two countries,” Xi Jinping stated.
Earlier, U.S. President Donald Trump sent a congratulatory message to our Head of State.
“I am grateful for the Enhanced Strategic Partnership between our nations and I look forward to continuing the great relationship that you and I have built during both of my Presidencies. I am proud to join in celebrating this important milestone,” Donald Trump emphasized.
President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev expressed satisfaction that, in recent years, through the joint efforts of the two leaders, the strategic partnership and alliance between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, founded on the principles of good-neighborliness and close friendship, have continued to grow stronger.
President of Kyrgyzstan Sadyr Japarov noted that the adoption of the Declaration of State Sovereignty on October 25, 1990, paved the way for the emergence of an independent Kazakhstan, reflecting the country’s commitment to its historical heritage and the people’s firm determination to shape their nation’s future independently.
President of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon spoke highly of the relations of friendship and cooperation with Kazakhstan, rooted in historical traditions and the principles of mutual respect and trust.
In his congratulatory message, President of Turkmenistan Serdar Berdimuhamedov emphasized that, over the years of sovereign development, Kazakhstan has made significant progress in strengthening its statehood, improving the well-being of its people and enhancing its standing on the international stage.
President of Türkiye Recep Tayyip Erdoğan expressed confidence that the special relations between the two countries, rooted in deep historical and cultural ties, would continue to develop in the spirit of an enhanced strategic partnership for the benefit of both peoples.
“The sixth meeting of the High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council between Kazakhstan and Türkiye, held in Astana on May 14, 2026, followed by the informal summit of the Organization of Turkic States in Turkistan, served as clear evidence of the strength of our strategic partnership,” Recep Tayyip Erdoğan emphasized.
President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev noted that Azerbaijan, as a brotherly nation, sincerely rejoices in Kazakhstan’s significant successes and achievements.

I highly appreciate your recent visit to Azerbaijan to participate in the seventh CICA Summit,” Ilham Aliyev wrote.

President of the Republic of Korea Lee Jae Myung expressed confidence that, drawing on its rich traditions of statehood, social stability and national unity, Kazakhstan would continue confidently along the path of progress and prosperity.

Israeli forces turn Hebron homes into military posts amid lockdown
Evictions, raids and outpost expansion continue across the occupied West Bank amid heightened tensions.
Israeli forces have turned Palestinian homes in the city of Hebron into barracks and observation posts after forcing residents to leave, as a military operation in the southern occupied West Bank continues, the Palestinian news agency Wafa has reported.
They took over homes in the Khallat Manna and Dahiyat al-Zaytoun areas of southern Hebron to use them as barracks, and forced residents from homes in other neighbourhoods to use the properties as observation posts, Wafa said, citing sources.
The Israeli military has imposed a lockdown in Hebron and conducted hundreds of raids since two armed Palestinian men allegedly carried out an attack on an Israeli army reserve base on Friday, killing two soldiers. The two suspects were also killed.
The evictions follow the forced displacement of hundreds of families amid extensive raids, road closures and tight restrictions on movement.
According to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society, Israeli forces have detained at least 47 Palestinians across Hebron since Friday, while forcibly displacing 293 families, comprising about 2,200 people.
Among those displaced from Hebron are 127 infants, 81 pregnant women and 26 people with disabilities, the NGO told Al Jazeera. The displaced also include 134 Palestinians with chronic illnesses and 265 elderly people over the age of 60.
Israeli troops also conducted hundreds of field interrogations, subjecting Palestinians to detention and abuse, the group said.
New settler outposts
Meanwhile, Israeli settlers began establishing two new outposts on Palestinian-owned land in the town of Yatta, south of Hebron, Wafa reported.
Activist Osama Makhamra told Wafa that settlers began setting up an outpost in the Khallet al-Fara area, west of Yatta, where they pitched a tent, brought in bulldozers and excavation machinery, and started levelling and digging the land in preparation for construction.
He added that another outpost was established in the Yatta desert area, on Palestinian-owned land between the villages of az-Zuweidin and Umm Qussa, where settlers pitched several tents and began installing infrastructure, including water and electricity networks.
Near Bethlehem, Israeli forces continued to close roads and entrances across the governorate for the third consecutive day on Sunday, affecting several towns and villages, Wafa reported.
On Saturday, Israeli forces shut down dirt roads leading to Tuqu to block access, firing tear gas canisters and stun grenades towards Palestinian vehicles travelling along rough alternative routes near the town.
The latest attacks and closures come days before Israel’s general elections and as tensions remain high across the occupied Palestinian territory, where settlers, backed by the military, have carried out a wave of pogroms targeting olive harvesters.

Infant dies of mpox in Pakistan's Sindh
China

18:26:54 KST

ISLAMABAD, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- A 53-day-old infant died of mpox in Pakistan's southern Sindh province on Saturday, raising the death toll from the disease in the province to 12 this year, health officials said.
The infant, a resident of Karachi's Malir district, was transferred to the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital and Research Center (SIDH&RC) after developing symptoms following a circumcision procedure at a private hospital, the facility's medical superintendent, Abdul Wahid Rajput, told local media.
Rajput confirmed that mpox was the cause of death.
The Sindh Healthcare Commission (SHCC) has sealed Ibn-e-Hassan Hospital in Malir, where the procedure was performed, after an investigation found inadequate infection prevention and control measures, poor hygiene and unqualified staff, according to an official statement.
The commission said the infant contracted the virus through contaminated scissors used during the procedure. Laboratory testing confirmed the infection.
Separately, the Sindh health department reported two more mpox cases on Friday, bringing the provincial tally to 98. Authorities have stepped up surveillance, contact tracing and infection-control measures to curb the spread of the virus.
Mpox can spread through close physical contact with infected people and contaminated items. Symptoms include fever, body aches, swollen lymph nodes and skin rashes or blisters. ■

KATHMANDU, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Nepal earned 5.93 billion Nepalese rupees from electricity exports to India in the third month of fiscal year 2026/27, which began in mid-July, the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) said on Sunday.
Revenue from electricity exports in the month increased by 962 million rupees compared with the same month last year, according to data from the state-owned power utility. Nepal earned 4.96 billion rupees from electricity exports to India during the same period last year.
The NEA reported an increase in export earnings despite damage to several hydropower projects caused by the devastating floods of Aug. 26, which forced some plants authorized to export electricity to suspend generation.
Nepal had suspended electricity exports to Bangladesh following the floods, but shipments resumed on Friday, according to the NEA. The country has been authorized to export up to 40MW of electricity as per the tripartite agreement between Nepal, India and Bangladesh.
During the first three months of the current fiscal year, from mid-July to mid-October, Nepal recorded electricity export transactions worth a total of 16.15 billion rupees.
The Aug. 26 floods severely damaged seven operational hydropower plants, three of which had received approval to export electricity. A total of 12 hydropower projects, including operational plants and those under construction, were damaged by the floods, according to the Nepal Development Update released by the World Bank earlier this month. SYDNEY, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) - Western Sydney International Airport officially launched passenger operations on Sunday, with Jetstar flight JQ362 departing for the Gold Coast as the airport's first commercial passenger flight.
The fully booked inaugural flight opened for check-in at 8 a.m. local time and took off around 11:20 a.m., Xinhua reporters learned at the airport.
Jetstar flight JQ363 from the Gold Coast landed at the new airport at around 3:10 p.m. The day's schedule also included Jetstar flight JQ375 to Melbourne.
"I'm so excited to see this airport. I just want to be part of history," Francis, a passenger on the inaugural flight, told Xinhua.
Francis, who lives in Strathfield in Sydney's west, said he took a train to St Marys before transferring to a bus to reach the airport, with the journey taking about one hour and 20 minutes.
Although the airport is not yet directly connected to the rail network, Francis said its round-the-clock operations would be particularly convenient for frequent travelers and that he would consider using the airport again.
Western Sydney International Airport CEO Simon Hickey told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) that the opening marked a significant milestone and a generational change for Australia's aviation industry.
Hickey said the airport had been designed with future growth in mind, with annual passenger traffic expected to approach 10 million by the early to mid-2030s.
Located about 45 km west of central Sydney, the airport began cargo operations in July after seven years of construction.
Unlike Sydney's existing Kingsford Smith Airport, which is subject to a night-time curfew, the new airport can operate 24 hours a day.
Under the announced flight plans, the airport will serve domestic destinations including the Gold Coast, Melbourne and Brisbane. Its first international passenger service, connecting Western Sydney with Auckland, New Zealand, is scheduled to begin on Monday, with more international routes planned for the future. ■

Arab Israeli voters are essential to Israel’s democratic future - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:26:04 UTC
18:26:04 KST

I remember it well. In the 2015 Knesset elections, I came out of the voting booth in my kibbutz in the Galilee, Hanaton, and read on the news: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of the State of Israel (yes, then too), announced to the public: “The Arabs are flocking to the voting booths! Go out and vote!”
I was stunned and horrified. I had moved to Israel 20 years before, from the US. Back then, 10 years ago, before President Donald Trump’s rise to power, I could not imagine a US president saying something like, “The blacks are flocking to the voting booths! Go out and vote!” Even if a president was thinking that, he would not have dared to say it back in 2015. Maybe before then or after then, but not then.
What shocked me was that the prime minister, who is supposed to be the prime minister of all citizens of the state, would blatantly and unabashedly address one portion of the state and pit them against another, as if Arab Israelis were not citizens, too.
Moreover, it was clear that the country’s prime minister was upset they were exercising their democratic right to vote! I was truly shocked.
Since then, I have been participating in a state-wide group (with smaller groups across the country) that does voter encouragement work in Arab Israeli towns and cities before national elections. We are not affiliated with a specific party, nor do we encourage people to vote for one.
The idea is to encourage people to exercise their democratic right to vote – especially in Arab Israeli society, where the voting percentages in the national elections are so low.
In the 2022 Knesset elections, only 52% of Arab Israelis came out to vote. I admit that I feel extremely invested in defeating this government. I find our current coalition terrifyingly dangerous on many levels. And yes, if the Arab population comes out en masse to vote, that will help democratically remove this government from power.
But my involvement in this work began before this particular election, and it is only one example of my activism to create a shared society among Arab and Jewish Israelis in this country. In the Galilee, where the population is 50-50 Arab-Jewish, this is our way of life. Despite Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and MK Zvi Sukkot’s campaigns to create conflict among us, we live in peace, and often even friendship.
My children went to a Hand in Hand bilingual Arab-Jewish school, and I am heavily involved in my local chapter of the grassroots Arab-Jewish movement Standing Together, as well as in an interfaith group of spiritual leaders in the Galilee called Spirit of the Galilee. (To my delight, both groups are starting a youth program this year.)
Life in the Galilee could (and should) be much more integrated, and there is a lot of work to be done. But the work should be done in the direction of building more connections and bridges, not breaking those that have already been built and pitting our communities against each other.
I see in the news gangs of Jewish youth attacking Arab bus drivers in Jerusalem and Beit Shemesh, and it shatters my heart. Or adults – police officers – beating up Arab security guard Qais Haddad outside Teddy Stadium a year ago.
I wept when I read of a gang of Jewish youth in my area, in Haifa’s bayside suburbs, who beat up high school senior Khalil Sabach from Shefa-Amr, an Arab town I frequent, only 15 minutes from my home.
I went with a group from Tag Meir to visit him. What a lovely and impressive young man he is. He told us this incident did not break his spirit or his belief in Arab-Jewish partnership and let me hug him.
Government failure on crime in Arab Israeli society
Since this government came into power, the homicide rate from organized crime in Arab Israeli society has skyrocketed. It was bad before, but at least the previous government, the Yair Lapid-Naftali Bennett “Government of Change,” had a plan in place to combat this crisis – and it was working!
In fact, Yoav Segalovitz, who is running alongside MK Mansour Abbas in the Ra’am party, was instrumental in applying this plan. He worked under Omer Bar Lev, the public security minister at the time.
When Itamar Ben-Gvir took over this position (and its title was changed to national security minister), he stopped the program, and the problem has intensified to the point that there is on average about one person killed every day in Arab (and mixed) cities and towns.
This is intolerable, and if not stopped, the next generation of Arab Israelis who can manage to leave will do so – which is, of course, Ben-Gvir’s goal. That, and to have them kill one another.
This goal of ethnic cleansing in the Galilee, just like Smotrich and Sukkot are doing, mimicking the flags at the entrances of Jewish settlements in the West Bank, trying to scare away Arab residents by recruiting Jewish youth to hang swarms of Israeli flags at the entrances to Jewish villages and along main roads in areas heavily populated by Arab Israelis – is meant to intimidate them and send the message: We are the landlords here!
I know because this happened in my own village of Hanaton, where youth hung two long rows of Israeli flags all along the road leading up to our front gate. And I see it in other areas – including the area around Karmiel, where a group of young men were planted on Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund land bordering on agricultural land of residents of the Muslim town of Majd el-Kurum, to intimidate farmers from the town going to work their land.
The Jewish youth were supposed to be shepherding, to keep the weeds under control; yet, they had no sheep. I know because I went there to protest until KKL-JNF said they would move them to a nearby location and make sure they do have sheep and are actually shepherding. Let’s see if they keep to their word.
Arab Israeli society has suffered terribly since October 7, when they, too, suffered. Thirty-four Arab Israelis (mostly, but not only, Bedouin) were killed on October 7, and more after (as soldiers and as victims of missiles from Gaza, Iran, the Houthis, and Hezbollah). There were also nine taken hostage to Gaza.
Hamas tried on October 7 to incite Arab Israelis to rise up against Israel from within, but they did not. Instead, they helped clean out shelters, treat the wounded in hospitals, collect supplies for and house the displaced, like the rest of us. They proved their loyalty to the state.
And when some did speak out against the war in Gaza – which is their democratic right – they were arrested, humiliated, and released with no charges (because there was no legal case against them). This was done to intimidate, silence, and frighten a big section of the population into either leaving or becoming passive citizens.
But we must not let the government get away with this. I understand why so many Arab Israelis are despairing. But when I go out into the streets of Nazareth, Shefa-Amr, Kafr Manda, Bir al-Maksur, and other Arab towns and cities around my kibbutz, I urge them not to give up hope, not to squander their democratic right to influence the direction of our shared country.
Being loyal but passive citizens is not enough. In order to put the country back on track, Arab Israelis must overcome their fear, anger, and depression, and come out and vote. If not out of a love for the country (although some do love the country, despite their complicated relationship with it), then out of self-interest – for the sake of their futures and the futures of their children and grandchildren.
Some can leave, but not all. And some will choose not to, even if they can. Like my own children. In the end, there will always be Arabs (some who identify as Palestinian and some who don’t) and Jews living in this country. I personally prefer it that way.
But even those who don’t, like most in the current coalition, must wake up to that reality and understand that for life here to be tolerable – let alone thriving, which is, ideally, what anyone sane wants – we must work to make it good for us all.
Organized crime, bigotry, never-ending war, Jewish terror in the West Bank – these are not our fate. If we get rid of this government, we could salvage our chances of living together here in peace and harmony.
Therefore, we all – proud Jewish Zionist Israelis included – must encourage this part of the population – full citizens of the Jewish State of Israel – to exercise not only their lawful right to vote but their lawful right to sit in the Knesset, be in the governing coalition, and serve as government ministers. And we must accept them with open arms when they “flock” to do so.
This is the only viable, sustainable, and livable future for this country.
