Arab world hopes for an Israel without Netanyahu, but doubts it will change - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:25:35 UTC
18:25:35 KST

The Arab media are following Israel’s upcoming elections with considerable interest, recognizing that their outcome could have significant implications for Israel’s regional policies and its approach toward the Palestinians.
One striking feature of Arab media coverage is the in-depth familiarity many Arab commentators display with Israel’s political system, including the differences between and within its political parties – a level of understanding that is not always matched by Israeli coverage of politics in Arab countries.
The term “Arab media” encompasses a broad and diverse range of outlets, including satellite television networks, print and online newspapers, and social media platforms across numerous countries in the region and beyond. It is therefore difficult to present a comprehensive and reliable picture of the various voices and perspectives expressed within this vast media landscape.
But, at the risk of oversimplification, Arab discourse on the Israeli elections can be divided into two main trends.
The pessimistic view: a prominent perspective within this camp regards Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu not as the problem itself but rather as a manifestation of deeper trends within Israeli society and politics, which have shifted sharply to the Right since October 7 and embraced a hardline security doctrine.
Accordingly, even if Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot becomes prime minister, the change would primarily be reflected in a different tone, improved relations with Washington, and greater diplomatic pragmatism, rather than any fundamental shift in policy toward the Palestinians. This perspective is particularly prominent in the coverage of Qatar’s Al Jazeera network, although it is also reflected in other Arab media outlets.
For example, Jordanian journalist Osama al-Sharif published an article on a Saudi website with a title that speaks for itself: “Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Lapid: Three Names, One Anti-Palestinian Policy.”
In his view, the elections offer no genuine alternative for Palestinians or the wider Arab world, since all the leading candidates share similar security-oriented positions and offer no new approach to resolving the Palestinian question.
Although Israel’s endless wars have failed to bury the Palestinian cause, he argued, there is little reason to expect any meaningful change in Israeli policy toward it. This assessment is shared by numerous Palestinian observers and journalists.
Supporters of this view emphasize the historical processes and sociological transformations that have reshaped Jewish Israeli society, both ideologically and politically, creating formidable obstacles to any significant change in Israeli policy following the elections.
From this perspective, the identity of the prime minister matters relatively little, since any government would be constrained by coalition politics and compelled to respond to an electorate that is predominantly right-wing.
Arab skepticism stems not only from assessments of the political balance of power within Israel but also from the deep scars left by the wars since October 7 – scars that will not necessarily disappear with a change of government.
The optimistic view: commentators representing this perspective believe that a new Israeli government could create fresh diplomatic opportunities for dialogue, potentially leading to an expansion of the Abraham Accords.
This approach can be found in several Gulf media outlets. Yet the optimism it expresses is cautious and conditional, and does not necessarily reflect the official positions of the governments concerned.
For example, Egyptian columnist Sobhi Shabana wrote in the Saudi newspaper Al Jazirah that Eisenkot’s election could open a window of opportunity for change. Unlike Netanyahu, who remains beholden to the far Right, Eisenkot views military force not as an end in itself but as a means of achieving political objectives.
In the same newspaper, columnist Ahmed Adam argued that a new Israeli government could make it easier for countries that have signed the Abraham Accords to expand their public relations with Israel, facilitate the resumption of high-level political dialogue between Israel and Egypt and Jordan, remove a major political and psychological obstacle to improving regional relations, and create conditions for renewed negotiations with Saudi Arabia – provided that the new government offers tangible progress on the Palestinian issue.
The tension between these two schools of thought is well illustrated by Omar Raddad, a Jordanian political and security analyst. On the one hand, he argued that various regional actors view the Israeli elections as an opportunity to reshape Israeli policy in ways that could open a new window for peace and normalization processes that have stalled because of the policies of the far Right.
On the other hand, he cautioned that the elections may merely replace political figures without altering the fundamental principles of Israeli policy, which remain rooted in security doctrines that have become more entrenched since October 7.
Beyond the question of whether a new government would change Israeli policy, Arab commentators are also examining who might bring such a government to power.
Role of Arab Israelis in the election
In this context, considerable attention has been devoted to the role of Arab citizens of Israel in the elections. Many observers suggest that a high voter turnout among Arab citizens could determine Netanyahu’s political fate, with particular attention focused on Mansour Abbas and his Ra’am party.
Yet alongside recognition of the Arab electorate’s potential political influence, there is considerable skepticism about the willingness of Jewish opposition parties to rely on Arab parties in forming the next government.
This creates a paradox: Arab citizens could play a decisive role in bringing about a change of government without necessarily becoming partners in shaping its policies.
Perhaps the most revealing finding emerging from Arab media discourse is the gap between hopes for a change of government in Israel and skepticism about whether such a change would produce a meaningful shift in Israeli policy.
For some commentators, a new government could open a window of opportunity for improving regional relations and perhaps even reviving the normalization process. Yet even the optimists do not anticipate a fundamental change in Israel’s approach toward the Palestinians.
In this sense, Arab discourse can largely be described as “pessoptimistic,” to borrow the term coined by Palestinian writer Emile Habibi: it combines hope for political change with pessimism about the prospects for strategic transformation. The Arab world, it seems, longs for an Israel without Netanyahu, but doubts that an Israel without Netanyahu would necessarily be a different Israel.
Prof. Elie Podeh teaches in the Department of Islamic and Middle Eastern Studies at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and is a board member of Mitvim – The Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies.

Israel braces for rainy Election Day, but can bad weather affect voter turnout?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:25:28 UTC
18:25:28 KST

Election day in Israel is expected to bring cooler temperatures and rain in southern and eastern Israel, raising the question: Will Dreary weather keep Israelis away from the polls?
The expected rain will intensify at midday, mainly in the south and east, with thunderstorms, gusty winds, and hail. Significant flash flooding is also possible in the Negev and Arava streambeds, and in the Dead Sea area.
Is there any real basis for this fear? The data show the answer is an unequivocal no.
Looking back, Israel has no proven link between rain and voter turnout. In fact, the all-time turnout record of 87% was set in the First Knesset elections in January 1949, on an especially stormy winter day. By contrast, the Second Knesset elections were held on an ordinary summer day in July 1951 and recorded just 75%, lower than any election held in the country until 2003.
The all-time low was recorded in the 2006 elections (the 17th Knesset), when only 63.5% of Israelis voted. That election was held on March 28, a spring day, but clouds and rain covered parts of the country. The media at the time rushed to blame the weather, but an in-depth review by the Israel Meteorological Service showed that rain has no real connection to voter participation; political and social factors drive it.
The paradox is simple: rain supposedly keeps people at home under the covers, while pleasant sunshine sends them to the beach, parks, and malls, supposed “enemies of the ballot box.” In practice, polling stations stay open for a full 15 hours, rain in Israel mostly falls in short bursts, and no outing lasts all day.
First Israeli election on schedule in three decades
Israel’s lawmakers actually considered the weather in advance. A 1959 amendment to Basic Law: The Knesset set the Hebrew month of Cheshvan as the fixed election date, and 2006 documents from the Knesset Constitution Committee explain that it is a comfortable month, falling right after the Tishrei holidays and before the peak of winter. The assumption was that mild weather would make it easy to get to the polls, and that early sunsets, especially in winter, like the switch that took effect this week, would send day-trippers from the beaches straight to the polling stations well before closing.
But political reality in Israel rarely goes by the book. Since 1988, every election has been moved up (though the November 2022 election was held in Cheshvan because the Knesset dissolved itself). If the election on Tuesday, October 27, goes ahead as planned, it will be the first time Israelis vote on the original date set by law in 38 years.
A statistical look at the 25 elections held since the state's founding, along with this week’s election for the 26th Knesset, shows an almost even seasonal spread: seven in winter, seven in summer, six in spring, and six in fall. Most elections, 14 of them, were in fact held in the “hard” seasons (winter and summer), and 12 in the “comfortable” ones (fall and spring).
The bottom line: turnout shows no real difference between summer and winter, partly because the July–August elections took place long before Israelis began flying abroad en masse for vacation.
But what about the rest of the world?
How weather impacts elections worldwide
An American study of 14 presidential elections found that roughly 25 mm (about an inch) of rain lowered turnout by about one percentage point. In the Netherlands (13 elections between 1971 and 2010), researchers found a similar result: pleasant sunshine encourages people to go out and vote. In Sweden, by contrast, researchers found no significant effect of rain.
Rather than settling on a single country, researchers at the University of Copenhagen combined data from 34 studies worldwide, published in the journal Electoral Studies.
The conclusion: every centimeter of rain lowers turnout by about 0.95%, with young people and undecided voters six times more sensitive to the weather than others. Even so, applying this to Israel is hard; here, Election Day is a public holiday, unlike in many countries where people vote on a regular workday.
An International IDEA institute report this past April, together with King’s College and Griffith University, found that between 2006 and 2025 at least 94 elections and referendums in 52 countries were disrupted by natural disasters (in 26 of those cases the vote was postponed; in 2024 alone, 23 elections in 18 countries were disrupted).
But don't worry, that study focuses on typhoons, hurricanes, massive wildfires, and devastating floods that paralyze infrastructure, events irrelevant to Israel's climate.
A local autumn shower may mean grabbing an umbrella on the way to the polls, but Israeli history shows it won't stop voters from having their say.

Dimona's former Netanyahu loyalists turn to Eisenkot as battle for final undecided voters heats up
Unknown

Former supporters of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the once Likud party hub of Dimona are campaigning for rival candidate Gadi Eisenkot in the days leading up to Tuesday's election.
The ballot is Israel's first since Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack that shook the country and plunged the region into turmoil, as Israel went to war on the terrorist group in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran.
The October 7 security breach saw Likud's popularity plummet. Opinion polls have predicted for months that Netanyahu's coalition will lose its majority. But his top rival, Yashar's Eisenkot, has no clear path to power either, and the race has become tighter as the election nears.
Dimona, where an Iranian missile wounded dozens in March, has become a political battleground.
"We must have change. Bibi has to go," said Yossi Assayag, 74, who says he has supported Likud most of his life. "Bibi has brought disaster to Israel."
Eisenkot's Yashar party targets Likud Loyalists
Assayag is part of a group of town residents trying to convince their community to vote for Eisenkot's party, which is neck and neck with Likud in the polls.
It's a tough task in Dimona, where half the voters in the 2022 election voted for Likud.
"I will never betray Likud," said Ruti Ohana, a pensioner, who says she has voted Likud ever since immigrating to Israel from North Africa more than 60 years ago. She said Netanyahu was a cut above his rivals, and that detractors unfairly blamed him for October 7.
Likud long ago formed a core voter base among Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent, known as Mizrahis, who felt neglected by the European-influenced Labor Party that dominated Israel for generations.
Labor has since dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightward, and around half a dozen other parties now court Likud voters, from the center to the far right. But the link to the party among its past supporters remains strong.
"Most people here vote for Likud just because that's how they were raised," said Oria Asaf, 25, a past Likud voter now backing Yashar. "The change will come when people start to think about their children's future rather than their parents' past."
The Dimona battle for wavering 'Likudniks'
While Netanyahu has a substantial base of supporters that can't be won over, the prize is undecided voters who "understand that we are in a state of crisis" and are open to persuasion, said Michal Elmalem Abu, elected as a member of the city council from Likud and now leading Eisenkot's Dimona campaign.
Some 13% of Israeli voters still haven't decided how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute.
Of those who voted for Likud in 2022, just 55% now say they will vote for the party again on Tuesday. Fifteen percent will support parties aligned against Netanyahu, including 8% for Yashar. Another 14% will vote for alternative right-wing parties, and 9% are undecided.
In places like Dimona, Eisenkot could take a chunk out of Likud's base, said Amotz Asa-El, a columnist for The Jerusalem Post and political scientist at the Hartman Institute.
A child of Moroccan immigrants who rose through the ranks to become military chief of staff, Eisenkot, 66, has a personal story of humble origins in the Mizrahi community that "appeals to a big swath of the Israeli electorate, particularly Likud's traditional electorate," Asa-El said.
In an electoral field crowded with ex-soldiers, his peerless security credentials are an asset. The loss of his son, killed in combat in Gaza in December 2023, resonates with voters.
At a town hall in Dimona in July, residents said they were excited about the prospect of a Mizrahi leader. Others approached him with hugs and tearful condolences for the loss of his son.
But a week later Netanyahu held his own event, demonstrating his powerful appeal in the hardscrabble Negev, where Likud governments have long boasted of bringing development funds.
"Look around you, look at your community, look at what was here then and what is here now, and ask yourselves which governments invested in this monumental effort. And I do this out of immense love," he said.
Lior Katzav, a Likud former mayor of Kiryat Malachi, another small-town stronghold, said party surveys show voters who had abandoned Likud are returning as the election nears.
But even some who sympathize with Netanyahu say it may be time for a change. Israel's youngest prime minister when he was first elected 30 years ago, he has since become its longest-serving, now 77, having governed for 18 years over six terms.
"It's time for him to go," said Dimona software engineer David Iskali. "He's done a lot for Israel, but it can't go on. I won't give my vote to someone almost 80 years old."

Taiwan pushes social media platforms to label deepfake and AI images
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:18:06 UTC
18:18:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Digital Affairs is urging social media platforms to make AI-generated images clearly identifiable, proposing a three-layer labeling system to help users distinguish authentic content.
The proposed system would combine voluntary disclosures by content creators, automated detection, and reporting channels for suspected violations. The ministry said the initiative aims to build a trustworthy digital environment and prioritize high-risk deepfakes that could mislead the public, per CNA.
Tsai Shou-chuan (蔡壽洤), director of MODA's Department of Digital Strategy, said the ministry has held meetings with Meta, Google, Line, and industry associations since the beginning of the year to discuss ways to improve labeling of AI-generated images.
The ministry is not currently requiring platforms to adopt a uniform labeling format but wants disclosures to be prominent and easy for users to notice, Tsai said.
He cited YouTube as an example, saying its existing disclosure that content was generated using AI appears beneath the video description and requires users to click “More” to see it. MODA wants the platform to display a more visible AI label below videos.
The first layer of the proposed system would require platforms to give creators a way to identify and disclose AI-generated images when uploading content.
The second would involve automated detection. AI-generated images may contain embedded or otherwise hidden provenance information that software can read even when it is not visible to users, Tsai said. MODA wants platforms to detect these signals and add labels when appropriate, including when uploaders have not disclosed the use of AI, he said.
Tsai acknowledged that both measures could have gaps. Users may deliberately remove or damage embedded identifiers, while platforms may struggle to detect every instance of AI-generated content because of the volume of material uploaded.
The third layer would establish channels for government notifications, public reports, and privacy-related complaints. Platforms would then assess individual cases involving potentially misleading, infringing, or otherwise prohibited content.
Where AI-generated images are connected to fraud or violations of others' rights, MODA would coordinate with platforms on appropriate responses, including adding labels or removing content, depending on the applicable regulations and circumstances, Tsai said.
Regarding implementation, Tsai said Google was making the fastest progress, while Meta was continuing technical adjustments. Line would initially focus on public-facing material, such as advertisements, because private one-on-one conversations and group messages raise privacy concerns, per CNA.
The initiative follows broader efforts to develop guidance for AI-generated content and deepfakes. In March, MODA said it would consult industry representatives, experts, and other stakeholders on AI governance to develop initial policy principles or a framework by the end of the year, per CNA.
In September, MODA fined Meta a combined NT$10 million (US$306,000) in two cases involving disclosure of AI-generated or deepfake images in advertisements and the handling of suspected scam advertisements. The cases underscore the challenges regulators face in ensuring platforms adequately disclose synthetic content and respond to harmful material.

A survey confirms interest in a direct train service between Switzerland and London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:17:37 UTC
18:17:37 KST

A survey confirms interest in a direct train service between Switzerland and London
The Swiss are overwhelmingly in favour of a direct train service to London. A survey confirms widespread support for this rail link, which is seen as essential for competing with air travel and reducing the impact on the climate.
The introduction of direct trains to the United Kingdom is generating considerable interest in Switzerland. A YouGov poll found that 58% of those surveyed are in favour, whilst only 8% are against. The survey, conducted amongst 1,048 people and published on Saturday, was commissioned by the organisations T&E, actif-trafiC and ATE.
Those surveyed favour flying because of its speed (79%). To encourage them to choose rail, lower fares (61%), direct connections (37%) and shorter journey times (37%) would be key factors.
The choice to travel by train is driven by its appeal (58%), its low environmental impact (55%) and the location of stations in city centres (45%). “By removing the stopover in Paris, the journey time between Geneva and London would be reduced from over seven hours to around five hours 30 minutes,” emphasised Victor Thévenet of the T&E association.
SBB has signed a memorandum of understanding with SNCF and Eurostar. Obstacles remain, and implementation is not expected until the 2030s.

Audi heads to US: Trump hopes to score at the polls with German carmaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:15:55 UTC
18:15:55 KST

Audi plans its first car plant of its own in the United States, investing billions in a new production site in the state of Georgia.
Audi is taking a major step into the American market: the premium manufacturer from Ingolstadt plans to invest around 4 billion US dollars in its first dedicated US car plant in the state of Georgia.
The announcement was made on Saturday, 24 October 2026, at an election campaign rally by US President Donald Trump in Perry, Georgia. Trump appeared alongside Döllner and stressed in his speech that his trade policy was encouraging companies to move production to the United States. The timing of the announcement is likely to play well in the battle for the midterm elections on 3 November.
Audi chief executive Gernot Döllner justified the investment in his address by pointing to the company’s long-term ambitions in the United States: the American market is one of the most important premium car markets worldwide, but Audi has not yet fully tapped its potential there.
Production scheduled to start in the early 2030s
The plans envisage an annual capacity of up to 200,000 vehicles and around 4,500 jobs. The plant is to be built at the Middle Georgia Megasite in Peach County, near the city of Macon. Georgia was chosen as the location, according to the state authorities, (source in German) partly because of its established supplier industry, transport links and available skilled workforce. The option of expanding the facility at a later date also played a role in the choice.
According to the company, preparatory work is due to begin in 2027, with series production to ramp up in the early 2030s. The government of Georgia is naming 2031 as the targeted start of full-scale production.
With around 4,500 planned jobs, the project would be a major industrial undertaking for the region. Additional positions would be created at suppliers, logistics firms and service providers.
Large SUVs for the American market
The new plant is primarily intended to build large, high-priced sport utility vehicles. Reuters, citing a US government official, reports that the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 models are planned. Audi itself speaks of particularly large and high-end SUVs that will be tailored to the needs of North American customers.
For Audi, the move is strategically significant, as until now the company has imported its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico. Local production would reduce dependence on international supply chains and exchange-rate fluctuations. At the same time, Audi would be manufacturing closer to its American customers and strengthening its competitive position against carmakers with their own US production, the company emphasised in an official statement.
Trump claims success for his tariff policy
Trump has imposed additional tariffs on the import of cars and car parts and has repeatedly called on foreign manufacturers to produce more in the United States. For companies such as Audi, this policy increases the cost of imports, making production on US soil economically more attractive. According to Reuters, Trump’s tariffs cost Audi around 1.2 billion euros last year.
However, it cannot be inferred from this alone that tariffs were the only factor behind the choice of location: Audi also points to the long-term expansion of its US business, access to the sales market, the existing infrastructure and the regional supplier base.
What does this mean for Germany?
The decision raises questions for the Volkswagen Group’s German sites. Additional production in the United States does not automatically mean job losses in Germany, but it does change the geographical distribution of future investment and increases the importance of North America.
Audi stresses that Germany and Europe will remain the industrial backbone of the company; the existing expertise in development, engineering and production is merely to be complemented by the new site.
According to public broadcaster Tagesschau, the IG Metall union broadly welcomes the stronger push into the US market, but at the same time is calling for binding long-term prospects for employees at German plants. The union also says that the final decision is still subject to approval by the responsible Volkswagen committees.
Georgia: an industrial hub with an automotive tradition
Georgia has long been a centre of the American car industry. South Korean carmaker Kia has been producing in West Point since 2009, while Hyundai, also from South Korea, has built a multi-billion-dollar plant for electrified vehicles near Savannah. In addition, the high-capacity ports of Savannah and Brunswick allow vehicles and components to be transported internationally.
For Trump, the investment would be another trump card in his strategy of bringing more industrial production back to the United States. For Audi, it marks a step closer to one of the world’s most important car markets.

‘Why would I leave?’: Middlesbrough pushes back against ‘hardest place to grow up’ label
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:00:58 UTC
18:00:58 KST

“It’s disappointing, it’s just another kicking,” said a youth worker after the town in which they work was labelled as the hardest place in which to be a child in England.
“It suggests our children are living unhappy lives,” said a teacher, who described her pupils as joyful.
A clearly riled Chris Cooke, the mayor of Middlesbrough, said: “We get told a lot by people outside this place what we are. We know what we are. There is another side.”
They were all reacting to a report published this week by the children’s commissioner, Rachel de Souza, titled The Childhood Lottery, in which she declared childhood to be in “a state of emergency”.
The report drew on a “landmark dataset” that “brings together 162 measures of children’s lives to build a comprehensive picture of the areas in England where it is the hardest to grow up”. The metrics included everything from child poverty to exclusion rates to poor air quality. And at the bottom was Middlesbrough.
The Guardian visited the town this week and spoke to children and professionals about growing up there. No one denied there were many challenges, but equally no one thought the label was helpful.
At a busy, buzzy youth club in the residential suburb of Coulby Newham, children aged 10 and up were making papier-mache Halloween decorations, cooking, playing table tennis and, outside on a strikingly mild October evening, getting ready to play dodge ball. “You’d think they were playing professionally,” said one volunteer.
Hannah*, 15, said her life was good but she knew it was not the same for others. “I love living in Middlesbrough. I love Albert Park and the Dorman Museum. I love going to the football. I love coming to youth club and making friends,” she said.
A boy looked confused when asked if it was hard being a child in Middlesbrough. “I’m going to be here the rest of my life,” he said. “Why would I leave?”
His friend let the side down by declaring: “I’m going to a hot country when I’m older … Hawaii. Or Zanzibar. Middlesbrough is too cold and scruffy.”
Wayne Mason, a former soldier who is chief executive of Linx Youth Project, which runs the club, said of the report: “We are disappointed. What it’s doing is attaching yet another label to Middlesbrough and its young people, and we already have many, many labels. It’s disappointing … all this negativity attached to the town.”
He and the project’s deputy, Eilís Sexton, were at the club but could not stay long as the local Rotary club was about to give them a much-needed and much-appreciated cheque.
Sexton was worried about the message the report sent out. “I’ve been thinking about young people who want to start their own families and how it’s going to make them feel, knowing that their child is going to have the ‘most difficult upbringing’ in the country? It is quite demoralising for them,” she said.
She was born and raised in the area and studied at Teesside University. “I did move out of Middlesbrough for six months and I hated it,” she said.
Neither of them disputed the statistics but they said there was another side. “Pride is the overriding thing that we see with the young people,” Mason said. “We know youngsters living in some of the most deprived areas of Middlesbrough, of which there are many, who don’t want to leave. They don’t want to leave because this is their home.
“We always talk about deprivation and poverty and crime, but we don’t talk about community.”
The report comes weeks after a collision on the A66 in which a car with five young people inside crashed into a police car carrying two police constables, killing the occupants of both vehicles.
Some subsequent media portrayals painted a picture of an urban dystopia where gangs were in charge, but residents said the reality was different.
It would have been hard for children to avoid media coverage about the deaths. Hannah said she had been past where it happened and burst into tears.
In Middlesbrough town centre there is a huge open square and the contemporary art gallery Mima, currently hosting the Turner prize. Next door is the town’s oppressive 1970s-built magistrates court building. Opposite is the grand Victorian town hall where Cooke, the elected Labour mayor, has his office.
When it comes to the subject of it being hard to grow up in Middlesbrough, Cooke is better equipped than most to talk about it. He grew up in a violent family. His father took his own life when he was a teenager, and his mother’s mental health spiralled. He said that as a young boy he felt he had to be in charge of everything because he was terrified of being separated from his sister.
Cooke had periods of not going to school and ended up in care. “I bounced around the system. People struggled to take me because I was quite difficult. I think that’s the polite version. What wouldn’t have helped me during any of that time is someone telling me that my life was difficult or that my life would get harder or that this place wouldn’t let me achieve the things I wanted to.”
He said he remembered applying for jobs as an apprentice and being told not to include his TS6 postcode for fear of being judged. He not only included it, he made it bigger, he said. “This is why I’m angry. I don’t need people characterising Middlesbrough when we already know the challenges.”
The fact that Cooke came out the other side was, he said, because of “beautiful” foster carers and other people around him. Middlesbrough is one of 16 councils in England that spend more than 80% of their core funding on social care. Cooke said he was passionate about spending on youth services, reeling off a list of initiatives that included a fund to ensure there were youth clubs in every Middlesbrough postcode.
A 15-minute walk from the town hall is Newport primary school, where the headteacher, Patricia Maxwell, showed the Guardian around. It has a particularly well-stocked, well-used library – Middlesbrough’s reading for pleasure stats are way over the national average.
Maxwell had read the commissioner’s report. “It wasn’t telling me anything anything I didn’t already know,” she said. “But also it wasn’t telling people about all the positives that our children grow up with in Middlesbrough.”
Stacey Carlisle, the school’s deputy head, agreed. “It just suggests that those children are living really quite unhappy lives, and that is not the case for our children,” she said. “They’re joyous and joyful, our children. Yes, there might be challenges at home for some, but it’s the same in affluent areas as well.”
Both teachers said they would not want to work anywhere but Middlesbrough. “We’d like to do more,” Maxwell said. “We want our children to reach their full potential and to thrive and flourish and become the doctors or whatever it is that they want to be in the future.
“But what we don’t want is them to feel labelled and told that they can’t go on and achieve those things. Just because you’re living in a challenging environment does not mean that that defines you.”
*Name has been changed

====================================================================================================

Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:00:57 UTC
18:00:57 KST

Insolvent businesses reacquired by their previous management in “pre-pack” administrations are much more likely to fail again and tend to repay far less to creditors, research for the Guardian suggests.
The study is the latest to raise questions about the practice of “phoenixism” – accounting’s controversial art of liquidating companies to allow directors to return with a new entity, free of debts.
The process tends to involve pre-pack administrations, where a supposed corporate rescue is agreed before commencing insolvency proceedings. These orchestrated deals often leave unsecured creditors nursing large losses. HM Revenue and Customs estimates that phoenixisms cost taxpayers hundreds of millions of pounds a year.
Cases have included owners extracting millions of pounds in dividends and loans from businesses they subsequently arrange to buy back from administrators.
The study was commissioned by the Guardian from Turnstone Intelligence, which used AI agents to read official documents relating to more than 1,700 administrations during 2019. The research company noted much poorer outcomes when a business’s assets were reacquired by “connected parties”, such as former directors and shareholders.
It found that 44% of pre-packs had resulted in a second insolvency by July 2026 when assets were bought by a connected party. Just 26% of pre-packs produced a subsequent insolvency when the acquirer was unconnected to the failed company.
Ben Sims, managing director of Turnstone Intelligence, said: “I was surprised how big the gap remains. These results support what many in the industry have long suspected and will feed the continuing debate as to whether saving these businesses is worth the impact on taxpayers and creditors.”
The data showed that connected parties appeared far more likely to be permitted to defer payments in pre-packs. A total of 198 out of 303 connected-party administrations – 65% – allowed former owners and directors to reacquire the assets via future instalments. For unconnected pre-packs, 28% of buyers used deferred payments.
Unsecured creditors, who typically include HMRC, received a return in only 23% of pre-packs involving a connected party deferring payments, with those deals paying out just 1.58p in the pound. When the buyer was unconnected, 36% of pre-pack administrations resulted in repayments to those creditors, at a rate of 7.86p in the pound.
“What was interesting to us was the sheer scale of losses,” Sims said. “You would hope these deals would provide better outcomes to creditors, but we see them getting almost nothing. Of course, the biggest loser is often the taxpayer.”
The findings appear to closely mirror results from two well-known reports in the field: research by the University of Wolverhampton for the government in 2014 (Graham review) and a European Union-funded 2018 study. Both pointed to poorer outcomes in connected pre-pack administrations. Those issues were compounded when the assets were reacquired by connected parties through deferred payments.
Riz Mokal, an honorary law professor at University College London who co-authored the EU study, said: “These are striking findings and are consistent with our earlier work. They reinforce a wider concern that connected-party pre-packs can allow non-viable ‘zombie’ businesses to shed their unsecured liabilities and continue trading, harming not only their creditors, including HMRC, but also competitors that continue to pay their way.”
The methodology used by the latest researchers was broadly consistent with the earlier, EU-funded study. They used AI agents to read filings submitted over the past seven years for administrations commenced in England and Wales in 2019 – which Turnstone said was “long enough for creditor returns to settle and buyer failures to show”.
The sweep of insolvency filings identified 544 pre-pack sales in 1,738 administrations during 2019, with the study’s numbers checked by other computer models and verified by humans.
Phoenixism is legal and its defenders say the practice can deliver better returns for creditors, with experienced directors sometimes better-placed than newcomers to salvage a failed company.
R3, an insolvency industry body, said the research looked only at cases that predated 2021 rules that “increased scrutiny of connected-party pre-pack sales and introduced additional safeguards and transparency requirements”. These included requiring independent evaluators to clear sales to connected parties.
Caroline Sumner, chief executive of R3, said: “A connected-party pre-pack administration sale is a legitimate and regulated insolvency process overseen by licensed insolvency practitioners and subject to extensive professional and statutory requirements. The duties of an administrator in a pre-pack administration sale are to achieve the best outcome for creditors of the company overall.
“It’s important to distinguish between phoenix activity and connected-party pre-pack administrations. Concerns about phoenixism generally relate to businesses seeking to avoid liabilities while continuing to trade through a new entity.”

We Linked 150 of Ikea’s $10 Speakers to Make a Wall of Sound
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

When Ikea launched its super-cheap $10 Bluetooth Kallsup speakers in April, aside from the rock-bottom price and bright, white/green/pink colors, the claim that really caught WIRED’s ear was that the Swedish furniture brand said it was possible to chain 100 of these 2.75-inch sonic cubes together, should you so wish.
Now, because it’s highly unlikely any one household will ever own more than a handful of mini Bluetooth speakers, this is one of those consumer-tech statements that rarely gets tested. So we asked the good folks at Älmhult in Ikea headquarters if they’d let us do just this. To our surprise, Ikea not only agreed, but it also upped the ante, saying it might be possible to link up to 150 without breaking the connection, so that’s exactly how many it sent us. “No one has ever tried this, though,” an Ikea spokesperson said. “We haven’t.”
That is how we ended up building a literal wall of sound at our London office, stacking 150 Kallsups carefully on top of one another to test how many would chain-play from a smartphone. Sadly, one casualty during shipping from Sweden—a single Kallsup—despite lighting up correctly and looking ready to chain, made an ominous rattling sound as if its innards weren’t entirely secure. Sure enough, it refused to play ball (or anything else), so we ended up with 149 speakers.
The chain process itself is simple. Once you have paired a single Kallsup with your music device—in our case, an iPhone 16 Pro—and it’s up and running, simply power on another cube while playing and hold down the Play button until a chime tells you it’s in “multi-speaker” mode. It should then immediately start playing whatever the Bluetooth-connected Kallsup is playing.
Thanks to this near-effortless chaining process, linking up all these Kallsups took much less time than we'd expected, about 30 minutes. We stopped at 100 to test how loud the “system” sounded at that stage before resuming the build and moving on to the maximum amount. As the music continued while we chained the speakers, it would be obvious when the collective refused to add more cubes. But this didn’t happen, and the plucky Kallsups joined forces without grumbling right up to the full 149.
It Might Get Loud
It’s tempting to preface the next few paragraphs with the phrase “for a $10 speaker,” because, despite Ikea’s vast buying power, experienced research and development team, and global presence, the ability to produce a tiny speaker that doesn’t sound absolutely horrible for less than a pint of half-decent craft beer is pretty incredible.
Each Kallsup has a single 1.8-inch, full-range driver powered by a 3-watt amplifier, with Bluetooth 5.3 support. No separate tweeter or woofer, just the one tiny driver.
On its own, the Kallsup speaker sounds fine. Yes, it lacks anything resembling the deep rumbling bass people talk about in audio reviews, but did we mention it’s a $10 speaker? It is a bit tinny, and you won’t want to push the volume very hard, but as a little desktop speaker, one by the side of the bed, or to throw in a suitcase, the Kallsup does the job. It doesn’t match the performance of one of our best Bluetooth speaker recommendations, but keep the cost in mind, and it’s hard to be disappointed.
Even at low background volumes, the Kallsups worked surprisingly well together, especially playing acoustic tracks. As we paired more speakers, the sound gradually grew nicely in scale. Nothing was overpowering or dominating, just the cumulative effect of all those tiny drivers moving small amounts of air.
With 149 individual 1.8-inch drivers, the combined surface area is roughly equivalent to one enormous 22-inch driver. Each Kallsup also has its own 3-watt amplifier, giving our wall a combined rated output of 447 watts. That doesn’t mean it behaves like a giant subwoofer or a conventional 447-watt speaker, but it explains why things got so loud.
But before we turned these up, if you will, to 149, we listened at 100, and when we pushed the volume, the collective Kallsups were seriously loud. But for the record, loud like a fire alarm, not a hi-fi system. With the wall complete, we worried the collective vibrations might send the whole thing crashing down. Disappointingly for the socials, it stayed resolute. Instead, we played Trans Lunar by Twin Dimensions (WIRED director of consumer tech and culture Mike Calore’s excellent band) and slowly increased the volume to maximum.
We almost wish we hadn’t. The noise was brain-numbingly loud as we blasted, somewhat appropriately, Richard Strauss’ Also Sprach Zarathustra. We couldn’t hear each other speak, and we could feel our internal organs vibrating. Any sense of fidelity disappeared, but—all power to the Kallsups—it worked. We’d successfully linked 149 Bluetooth speakers, though sadly we’re well short of the world record of 1,500 speakers set by Majority Audio in March 2026.
At more modest, realistic volumes, everything sounded considerably more composed, even if the music lacked levels of depth and detail. The overall lack of clarity could also be due to minor timing differences between the individual drivers.
At $1,490, a wall of Kallsups is quite an investment, and not one we’re recommending, but it is extremely impressive that we managed to sync and play music wirelessly through so many small, cheap speakers.
We also tested the wall alongside WIRED’s choice for best overall party speaker, the $500 LG Xboom Stage 501. Cranked up, both reached similarly ear-splitting, frankly uncomfortable volumes. But with two 5.25-inch woofers, two 2.5-inch full-range drivers, and clever digital signal processing, the LG delivered understandably fuller, deeper bass and a considerably more musical experience, as expected.
Powering Down
What’s remarkable about this experiment is that so little went wrong. Only one of the 150 speakers shipped didn’t work, clearly broken in transit. We managed to get all 149 sound cubes chained easily and quickly. And when we weren’t blasting the wall of sound at max volume, instead keeping levels moderate, the speakers sounded surprisingly competent as a collective.
However, there were hints of the Kallsup chaining capacity reaching its limit, as Ikea suspected. As we got beyond 100 units linked together, the incidence of failing to chain on the first try increased. Still, no speaker refused more than twice as we got toward the end of the build.
We also would have preferred indentations on the tops of the speakers, which would have given us a bit more confidence that the whole stack wasn’t going to collapse in a heap as volume ramped up (which it didn’t). Such a simple design feature would help whether you’re dealing with just a couple placed on top of each other, let alone 149—but this is splitting hairs.
Lastly, although this setup was impressively loud, no one in their right mind would do this in their own home. Ikea has been a good sport letting us try this out, but the ultimate, unsurprising lesson is: If you want high-quality audio, spend your money on a better speaker. As for the Kallsup? Simple to use, easy to chain, with approachable sound and clean design. You really can’t ask much more for $10.

Saudi man who bugged OpenAI office faces espionage charges – WSJ
The FBI is examining whether a former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging an executive meeting room intended to offer secrets to Saudi Arabia.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is weighing an economic espionage charge against a former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a restricted conference room, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday, citing a law-enforcement official.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was arrested on October 9 after OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, discovered an encrypted recorder behind a television in an executive meeting room at its San Francisco offices. He is currently charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications, an offense carrying up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
Investigators are now examining whether Alfozan stole information to offer to the Saudi government, even without having been recruited to do so, according to the WSJ. He is also reportedly being investigated for possible trade secret theft. An economic espionage conviction could carry up to 15 years in prison and a $5 million fine per count.
His lawyer, William Pernik, said he had received no information about a possible espionage case, telling the WSJ that his client “will fight these charges and allegations in court, not in the press.”
Pernik has stressed that Alfozan was charged with violating a federal recording statute, “not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent.”
OpenAI and the Saudi Embassy declined to comment when approached by the newspaper.
According to court documents, prosecutors claim that Alfozan, who joined OpenAI in July 2025, had intended to capture sensitive discussions about its AI technology. He allegedly maintained frequent contact with an unnamed member of the Saudi royal family throughout 2025 and 2026, with whom he discussed a potential job at an AI initiative in the kingdom.
His ties also included a role at Saudi investment firm Raed Ventures alongside Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, though the prince was not identified as the royal involved.
Prosecutors said that Alfozan had booked tickets to the kingdom for himself, his wife, and their infant son for October 12. After his arrest, a flight for his family was reportedly arranged by a member of the Saudi military, whom Alfozan’s lawyer identified as his wife’s brother-in-law acting in a personal capacity.
The Saudi consulate has offered to cover his full bail, arrange supervision, and withhold travel documents, while the defense offered an additional $1 million in his assets.
On Monday, Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse nevertheless denied release over flight concerns, describing the offer as “problematic.”
“It seems like a blank check: ‘We’re gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out,’” the judge said, noting that Saudi Arabia has no extradition treaty with the US.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, whom US President Donald Trump appointed earlier this month to lead a federal AI task force, said the case underscored why winning the AI race was “a national security prerogative” and pledged to safeguard “America’s cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats.”
The incident comes amid intensifying global technological competition, with Trump insisting that America must prevail in the AI race at any cost.
The US president has repeatedly rejected calls by industry leaders to slow the development of increasingly powerful models, stressing that “Whoever wins AI, wins.”

Russia’s once-feared Lancet kamikaze drone is losing its edge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
08:48:42 UTC
17:48:42 KST

- A Russian unit launched about 100 Lancet drones over three months and hit only three targets, pro-Russian militant Pavel Gubarev said.
- He put the cost at about $3.7 million to $6.1 million, saying Ukrainian air defenses stopped most drones.
A Russian drone unit fired about 100 Lancet loitering munitions over three months and hit only three targets, according to pro-Russian militant Pavel Gubarev, who said Ukrainian air defenses brought down most of the rest. The account points to a sharp drop in the effectiveness of one of Russia’s most widely used strike drones, Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi reported.
Gubarev said the drones were launched by a team from the Russian “Sparta” unit commanded by Senior Lt. Kirill Ozerov, call sign “Nevsky,” over a three-month period that began in mid-June. He did not name the section of the front where the unit operates.
The three targets hit were a self-propelled artillery gun, an infantry dugout and a roadside shop, Gubarev said. Ukrainian air defenses neutralized most of the remaining drones, and Russian forces destroyed some of them themselves because of poor coordination between units.
Gubarev put the price of a single Lancet at 3 million to 5.5 million rubles ($37,000 to $67,000), meaning the unit spent roughly 300 million to 500 million rubles (about $3.7 million to $6.1 million) on the three hits. The Oryx open-source project has estimated the cost of a Lancet at about $35,000, in line with his figures.
He blamed the unit’s leadership rather than its operators, saying commanders used the expensive drones without proper preparation while sending reports of supposedly successful results up the chain of command.
“There are no questions about the technical side of the UAV launches: the fighters did their job conscientiously and properly. The questions are for the commanders,” said Pavel Gubarev.
Gubarev, who declared himself “people’s governor” of Donetsk during Russia’s 2014 seizure of parts of eastern Ukraine, regularly comments on the Russian war effort on social media.
The Lancet is a family of loitering munitions built by ZALA Aero, part of Russia’s Kalashnikov Group. The drone has two sets of X-shaped wings mounted along a composite fuselage, with an optical seeker in the nose, the warhead, battery and electric motor in the middle, and a pusher propeller at the tail. Crews launch it from a catapult and fly it from a briefcase-style control station.
The stated range is more than 40 km (25 miles), and estimates based on the distances to targets it has struck suggest a maximum range of about 50 km (31 miles). Some versions carry a KZ-6 shaped-charge warhead weighing about 3 kg (6.6 pounds), which, according to available descriptions, is fixed inside the fuselage with mounting foam even though the charge was not designed to be used that way.
For much of the war, the Lancet was among Russia’s most effective weapons against Ukrainian artillery and armored vehicles. Ukrainian forces have since shot down growing numbers of the drones, including with interceptor drones that hunt them in the air.

Obama’s Ohio, Michigan speeches: Key takeaways on Trump, Iran war, midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
08:44:17 UTC
17:44:17 KST

Obama’s Ohio, Michigan speeches: Key takeaways on Trump, Iran war, midterms
The former US president warns of rising costs, corruption and threats to democratic values ahead of the November 3 vote.
Former President Barack Obama has railed against the Trump administration on a range of issues, including dragging the United States into “an unnecessary war” against Iran, as he campaigned for Democrats in Ohio and Michigan ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Speaking at rallies on Saturday, Obama accused President Donald Trump of “chaos and corruption”, as he urged voters to reject Republicans.
The speeches came just 10 days before the elections, with Senate and gubernatorial races taking place in both states.
Here are the key takeaways:
Obama blames Trump’s Iran war for rising fuel prices
“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said in Cleveland, Ohio, where he rallied in support of former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.
“Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for,” Obama said.
The former president defended the 2015 nuclear agreement reached under his administration, which restricted Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief.
“Iran didn’t have nuclear weapons because I had put a deal in place that everybody acknowledged kept them from getting nukes, and I didn’t have to fire a missile to do it. I just had to engage in diplomacy,” Obama said.
“He pulled out of it, starts this war.”
Obama blamed the conflict for rising oil and diesel prices, citing attacks on US military bases, American casualties and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
“Our allies and our bases have been attacked. Americans have been killed, hundreds of Americans have been wounded. We have run down our stock of missiles, and Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz where oil goes through to the world market,” he said.
The disruptions in oil flow through the strait, located between Iran and Oman, have pushed up energy prices worldwide. Before the war, a fifth of global oil and gas passed through the strait, which Iran has used as leverage in the war.
“This is the reason why the price of oil is up … This is the reason the price of diesel is up.”
The spike in diesel and petrol prices will likely cost the Republican Party, as the majority of Americans hold Trump responsible for starting the war and the subsequent increase in prices.
Obama also mocked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his focus on military culture and the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.
“These are not serious people,” Obama said.
Tariffs are making life more expensive for Americans
Obama criticised Trump’s tariffs, saying Americans were paying more for goods, including products made in the US using imported parts.
“When you impose tariffs, consumers pay the tab,” he said.
“It’s not just the goods that you use directly that have been imported … It’s also the car you build here in America. They might need a part from somewhere else, and now suddenly there’s a tariff on it.”
He questioned Trump’s trade dispute with Canada, a major US trading partner.
The two countries have been locked in a trade dispute, with Trump threatening 50 percent tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts from January 2027.
“And the big trade war he’s starting now is with that well-known evil empire Canada,” Obama said sarcastically.
“Canadians are the nicest people … they’re like our friendly neighbours to the north, and he’s like picking a fight with them.”
Obama also pointed to the growing US national debt, which has reached $40 trillion.
“Instead of bringing down deficits like he said with these tariffs, we’re now running a debt to the tune of $40 trillion.”
The figure refers to the total federal debt, which has accumulated over successive administrations, rather than the annual budget deficit.
Charges of corruption and enriching the wealthy
Obama accused the Trump administration of favouring wealthy Americans while common households struggled with rising costs.
“After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,'” Obama declared. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.”
He pointed to Trump’s 2025 tax and spending legislation, which extended tax cuts while reducing federal spending on programmes including Medicaid and food assistance.
“The only bill they passed of any significance in the last two years was a trillion-dollar tax break that mostly benefitted the richest Americans,” he said.
Obama also took aim at Trump’s White House renovations, including plans for a ballroom, changes to the Rose Garden and the addition of gold decorations.
“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama joked.
“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, just gold everywhere.”
Obama condemns Trump’s immigration crackdown
The former president said the US needed secure borders but criticised the methods used by immigration agents under the Trump administration.
“I believe that we do need to make sure that our border is orderly and secure and that people who want to come here do so lawfully,” he said.
“But I don’t recall anybody campaigning on sending masked agents running through our streets. I don’t recall anybody talking about law-abiding citizens being arrested, detained, or shot.”
“That’s not what we have to do to get our borders under control,” he added.
Obama attacks Ramaswamy over controversial Amy Acton advertisement
In Ohio, Obama criticised Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy over a campaign advertisement featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.
The advertisement features Acton’s mother questioning her honesty and her account of her childhood, without mentioning the allegations of sexual abuse that led to their separation decades ago.
It has drawn criticism from Republicans, including Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, although Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended it.
Obama condemned Ramaswamy’s decision to use Acton’s family history in the campaign.
“There’s got to be something inside you where you just say, you know, no office is worth stooping that low,” he said.
He also praised Acton’s career in public service and urged Ohio voters to support her on November 3.
Obama urges Michigan voters to back El-Sayed and Benson
In Detroit, Obama campaigned for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and gubernatorial contender Jocelyn Benson.
He praised El-Sayed’s Michigan roots and criticised his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, over his support for the US-Israel war on Iran and Trump’s trade policies.
“Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” Obama said, referring to his upbringing in the state, his family’s ties to the auto industry and his involvement in school sports.
Obama also spoke about attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim identity, comparing them with false claims about his own religion and birthplace during his presidential campaigns.
“Unlike Mike Rogers, Abdul hasn’t spent months cheerleading the Iran war … or called these tariffs ‘masterful’.”
The former president pushed back against those who call El-Sayed a “radical”, declaring that “Abdul shares my values”.
Obama also praised Benson for standing by Michigan’s 2020 election results despite threats and protests outside her home.
“When armed protesters showed up outside her home in 2020, demanded she overturn Michigan’s fair and free election results, Jocelyn stood her ground, stood up for you and your rights,” he said.
Obama calls midterms a ‘circuit breaker’ against Trump
Obama said the midterm elections offered voters a chance to limit Trump’s power during the remaining two years of his presidency.
“This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration,” he said. “It’s the circuit breaker in the system. We need to flip that circuit breaker.”
He also warned that dishonesty, intimidation and bullying were becoming accepted in US politics.
“We are not going to fix the economic system or the political system … so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes and where people in the highest offices in the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully,” he said.
“What we are missing in our public discourse is just basic decency.”

The attacks sparked fires, and emergency crews came under repeated strikes while responding to the incidents, the service said.

Van Gogh’s ‘Starry Night’ linked to July 1889 sky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
08:37:35 UTC
17:37:35 KST

AP Photo
A new study by South Korean researchers suggests Vincent van Gogh’s famous painting “The Starry Night” may have been inspired by an actual sky he observed in France around July 22, 1889, a month later than the date traditionally assigned to the masterpiece.
The findings, published last week in the journal Scientific Reports, are based on astronomical calculations, weather analyses and letters written by the Dutch postimpressionist painter to his brother.
Researchers led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, a telescope company executive and doctoral candidate at Kyung Hee University in Seoul, identified a predawn sky over Saint-Rémy-de-Provence that closely matches the celestial details depicted in the painting.
The moon’s crescent shape, Venus and the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus appeared in positions consistent with the scene around July 22, 1889, the team said. Their weather analysis also suggested that conditions would have allowed van Gogh to observe the sky.
Art historians have traditionally dated “The Starry Night” to June 1889, shortly after van Gogh entered an asylum in Saint-Rémy. The artist had cut off his left ear several months earlier following an argument with fellow painter Paul Gauguin.
Kim said the new findings challenge the established chronology. He and his team also examined van Gogh’s correspondence with his brother, including references to cicadas that they believe support a July date. Their analysis suggests a seizure commonly associated with that period may have occurred later in the month than previously thought.
Kim first traveled to France in 2019 to investigate the view, visiting in mid-June and again around July 22. He said the brilliant stars visible in the predawn July sky differed from those he observed in June.
However, the proposed date remains a hypothesis rather than a definitive conclusion. José Luis Aragón, a physicist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico who has studied the painting but was not involved in the research, said the study offered a careful, interdisciplinary approach. He noted that the moon’s appearance in mid-June did not match the thin crescent depicted by van Gogh.
Aragón also cautioned that the artist worked in a studio at the asylum, drawing on sketches and memory. The painting’s sky may therefore combine observations from several nights.
Still, he said, the research reinforces the idea that the painting was not pure fantasy and that van Gogh closely observed the real sky.

Royal Navy moves to buy U.S.-made Skydio X10D drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
08:36:54 UTC
17:36:54 KST

- Britain’s Ministry of Defence opened a tender for Skydio X10D reconnaissance drones with an estimated value of about $160,700 excluding VAT.
- Bids are due Nov. 19, and the contract is set to run until March 31, 2027.
Britain’s Ministry of Defence has opened a tender to buy Skydio X10D small drones, the American-made reconnaissance quadcopter already ordered by the thousands by the U.S. Army, with an estimated budget of £120,000 (about $160,700) excluding VAT, according to a notice on the Defence Sourcing Portal.
The tender was issued by Navy Commercial, the Royal Navy’s procurement office at Whale Island in Portsmouth, and published on Oct. 20 under the Procurement Act 2023. It does not say how many drones the ministry plans to buy or which unit will operate them. Delivery is listed for the South-East of England.
The contract is short. Bids are due by Nov. 19, the ministry expects to pick a supplier around Nov. 26, and the formal notice lists the contract as running from Nov. 30, 2026, to March 31, 2027, the end of the British government’s financial year. The listing on the Defence Sourcing Portal gives a slightly later start date of Dec. 10. The tender is open to any qualifying supplier, is marked as suitable for small and medium-sized businesses, and will be decided on price.
The X10D is a compact, rucksack-portable quadcopter built by Skydio in Hayward, California, for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. It carries day and thermal cameras, uses onboard artificial intelligence to fly itself around obstacles, including in complete darkness, and can track a subject day or night. The drone can switch radio channels automatically to keep its link under jamming and is designed to hold its position without relying on GPS.
The X10D has been on the U.S. Department of War’s Blue UAS list of drones cleared for military use since May 2024. In March, the U.S. Army ordered more than 2,500 X10Ds for over $52 million, the largest single-vendor small drone order in Army history. Spain awarded a contract worth up to €18 million (about $18.7 million) for the drone in February 2025, and Norway followed with an initial tender worth 101 million Norwegian kroner (about $9.4 million) in July 2025.
The UK Ministry of Defence already has experience with Skydio. In May 2022, Defence Equipment and Support’s Future Capabilities Group awarded a contract worth about £3 million (about $3.8 million) for the company’s earlier X2D drone, delivered with British partner Marlborough Communications, after buying and testing 90 Skydio drones in 2020.

2026-10-25

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.
The remarks come amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on February 28.
"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past."
An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
These military flare-ups have lulled in recent weeks.
Naval counter-blockade
Tehran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorisation -- moves strongly opposed by Washington and countries in the region.
In response, the US has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
In June, Iran agreed with the United States to a memorandum of understanding laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it.
Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.
"The current war has changed everything. We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same," said Araghchi.
"To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces."

WENCHANG, Hainan, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- China launched a Long March-8A carrier rocket from the southern island province of Hainan on Sunday, sending a batch of internet satellites into space.

He noted that financial difficulties and family circumstances can limit some young people's access to education, highlighting the importance of providing learning opportunities.

U Han Sein, vice chairman of the ELBC, said Chinese-language skills were becoming increasingly valuable as economic, trade and cultural exchanges between China and Myanmar deepened.
Ei Swe Zin, a Chinese-language teacher involved in the project, said cultural activities helped make lessons more engaging and encouraged students to develop an interest in the language.
"When we include cultural activities, students do not get bored while learning. They become more interested and enthusiastic about the language," she said, adding that language learning also helps students understand cultural nuances, including respectful forms of address and expressions used in different social situations. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- The Pentagon's latest move to label Confucius Institutes at U.S. universities as national security threats is an absurd overreach, exposing some U.S. politicians' warped threat perceptions and their dangerous political calculus of stoking anti-China sentiment ahead of the midterm elections.
By treating cultural and educational institutions as security risks, the Pentagon is stretching the concept of national security to the point of ridicule. In Washington's increasingly distorted security calculus, even teaching a language, introducing a civilization and promoting cultural exchange can be cast as threats.
More troubling still, this move appears to replace evidence-based assessments with political suspicion. Rather than demonstrating specific security risks posed by these institutes, Washington has once again resorted to insinuation and guilt by association.
The logic is both sweeping and dangerous: anything connected with China is treated as suspect, and even the peaceful sharing of language and culture must be viewed through the lens of geopolitical confrontation. This is not a serious approach to national security. It is an exercise in conjuring up threats.
The irony is hard to miss. During his visit to China in May, U.S. President Donald Trump praised the sculpture of Confucius on the facade of the U.S. Supreme Court. Yet institutions that introduce Chinese language and culture to American students are now portrayed as security threats.
Confucius may be welcome as a sculpture on an American landmark, but the living exchange of ideas rooted in his civilization is treated as a cause for alarm. This contradiction exposes the double standards shaping some U.S. politicians' approach to China.
In fact, the United States operates initiatives such as "American Spaces Programs" overseas to promote American culture. Hollywood blockbusters and brands like Coca-Cola have also carried American culture to the world for decades. By the Pentagon's logic, are all these also threats that should be banned?
Washington would also do well to reflect on its own record. For decades, the United States has waged wars abroad, carried out covert operations and intervened in other countries' domestic affairs, often with devastating consequences for peace and stability. Yet some American politicians seem more alarmed by cultural institutions than by the fallout from their own country's actions overseas.
National security should be based on credible evidence, not political prejudice. A country confident in its own institutions and values should have little to fear from people learning about another civilization. Turning cultural exchange into a security scare will not make the United States safer. It will only deepen mistrust, undermine mutual understanding and reinforce the divisions that threaten international peace. ■

BELGRADE, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Polling stations opened across Serbia at 7 a.m. local time (0600 GMT) on Sunday in snap parliamentary elections to elect the country's 250-seat National Assembly.
About 6.45 million registered voters are eligible to cast ballots at nearly 8,400 polling stations, including over 90 abroad, according to the country's electoral commission. Polls in Serbia are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. local time (1900 GMT).
Eighteen electoral lists comprising 2,418 candidates are competing for parliamentary seats.
The competing lists include "Aleksandar Vucic - United Serbia" led by the Serbian Progressive Party, "Student List - Students Win" backed by student groups, and "Ivica Dacic - Stability Factor!" formed by the Socialist Party of Serbia and its allies.
According to the electoral commission, more than 16,000 domestic and foreign observers are monitoring the vote.
Serbia elects its parliament through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency, with voters choosing electoral lists rather than individual candidates.
Electoral lists generally need votes equivalent to at least 3 percent of the number of voters who cast ballots to qualify for seat allocation. At least 126 seats are needed for a parliamentary majority.
Under Serbia's election law, election results must be published within 96 hours.
The newly elected National Assembly must hold its first sitting within 30 days. If it fails to elect a government within 90 days, the assembly must be dissolved and new parliamentary elections called. ■

U.S. Navy begins upgrading 22-year-old destroyer with new radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
08:11:17 UTC
17:11:17 KST

- USS Pinckney (DDG 91) began a depot modernization period at General Dynamics NASSCO to become the first U.S. Navy ship with the SPY-6(V)4 radar.
- The $149.6 million availability, part of DDG MOD 2.0, also adds new high-capacity air conditioning plants and runs through September 2028.
The U.S. Navy destroyer USS Pinckney (DDG 91) has entered General Dynamics NASSCO’s shipyard in San Diego for a second depot modernization period that will make it the first warship to receive the Raytheon AN/SPY-6(V)4 radar, the Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Maritime said.
The availability will also make Pinckney the first ship fitted with the Navy’s new High Efficiency Super-Capacity air conditioning plants, which are needed to handle the heavier electrical and cooling demands of the upgraded combat systems. The work is part of Destroyer Modernization 2.0, or DDG MOD 2.0, the Navy’s program to upgrade its older Flight IIA Arleigh Burke-class destroyers with a new radar, electronic warfare suite and combat system software.
“The collective effort by all stakeholders has finally brought us to the point of execution. Upon Depot Modernization Period completion, USS Pinckney will rejoin the Fleet equipped with the most comprehensive multi-spectral integrated sensor suite designed to maintain maritime superiority for decades to come,” said Capt. Tim Moore, program manager for DDG MOD 2.0.
The SPY-6(V)4 replaces the ship’s legacy AN/SPY-1D(V) radar. It uses four fixed array faces, each with 24 radar modular assemblies, for 360-degree coverage, and is a scaled-down version of the SPY-6(V)1 radar built into the Navy’s new Flight III destroyers, which use 37 assemblies per face. The radar will be fully integrated with Aegis Combat System Baseline 10 and is designed to detect and track ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, aircraft and surface threats at longer ranges than the older system.
The Navy is splitting the upgrade into two phases so that shipyards and contractors can learn from each installation. Pinckney completed the first phase in 2024, becoming the first warship to receive the AN/SLQ-32(V)7 Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program Block 3 suite, along with structural sponson modifications to carry the new equipment. It then deployed to the Pacific and Middle East, returning to San Diego in August after nine months at sea. Janes has reported that Pinckney became the first DDG MOD 2.0 ship to see combat, during operations against Iran in March.
The Navy awarded NASSCO $149.6 million on Sept. 5 for the current depot period, which is scheduled to run through September 2028. Raytheon installed the first SPY-6(V)4 array at the Navy’s land-based test site at Wallops Island, Virginia, in August, so engineers can integrate the radar with its power system before it goes aboard the ship and reduce testing time in the shipyard.
Pinckney leads a four-ship group of Flight IIA destroyers chosen to pioneer the DDG MOD 2.0 upgrades, along with USS Chung-Hoon (DDG 93), USS James E. Williams (DDG 95) and USS Halsey (DDG 97). Commissioned in 2004 and built by Ingalls Shipbuilding, the San Diego-based destroyer is named for William Pinckney, a Navy Cross recipient who rescued a fellow sailor aboard the aircraft carrier USS Enterprise during the Battle of Santa Cruz in World War II.

2026-10-25
