American are done paying for Trump’s family business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:03:17 UTC
02:03:17 KST

American are done paying for Trump’s family business
TEHRAN — Donald Trump won the White House promising to “Make America Great Again,” then promised Americans a short, cheap war on Iran. They got a closed Strait of Hormuz, Brent crude above $116 a barrel, and gasoline past $5 a gallon in several states. He and his family got a windfall.
Nine days before the November 3 midterms, the distance between those two experiences has become the central fact of American politics.
In CNBC’s final pre-election survey, 36 percent of registered voters named government corruption among their top issues, ahead of food prices at 34 percent and gasoline at 23 percent.
Fox News found 60 percent of voters extremely concerned. People are reading their grocery receipts and the headlines as one story.
A war with a customer list
The campaign of aggression against Iran has already cost tens of billions of dollars, paid from the public purse. Some of it is landing with companies the president’s sons own or advise.
Powerus, which Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are backing toward a stock listing, holds an Air Force contract worth up to $90 million for interceptors meant to counter Iranian drones.
Skeptics doubt the systems can stop Iran’s one-way attack drones, which have proved themselves in large numbers. Powerus is pitching them to Arab governments in the Persian Gulf anyway, the same clients Washington claims to be defending.
Trump Jr. also holds roughly $4 million in Unusual Machines, where he serves as an adviser. The “War” Department bought 3,500 drone motors and related parts from the company, and the Army has floated a follow-on order of 20,000.
Its shares jumped when his link became public. Rep. Jason Crow says firms tied to the sons have drawn about $3.7 billion in federal money this term.
The youngest Trump son, Barron, joined 1789 Capital days after the 2024 election. Among its holdings is Anduril, approved for a possible $2 billion interceptor sale to Kuwait.
Trump’s own portfolio includes Palantir, Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics and Northrop Grumman, whose revenues have swelled with U.S. military warmongering.
Richard Painter, who served as ethics lawyer in George W. Bush’s White House, told the Wall Street Journal that he sees no modern precedent. That is a notable benchmark, given the Bush administration’s own notorious record of foreign aggression and corporate enrichment.
Persian Gulf states, he says, are “under immense pressure to buy from Trump’s sons,” so the president will deliver what they want. It may be the first time, he adds, that a president’s family has made vast sums from a war launched without congressional authorization.
Arab monarchy money and a crypto pipeline
The Persian Gulf runs through the family’s earlier business too. In his upcoming book Princes and Thieves, Matthew Cole reports that Jared Kushner had access to at least two accounts tied to the UAE and Israel, together receiving about $2 billion, part of it Saudi-backed and moved through banks in Baku.
Dutch intelligence, which had penetrated his phone, helped trace the transfers. A third account, the report says, paid for an Israeli pledge to defend the Emirates against Iranian strikes.
Then came crypto. Days before the 2025 inauguration, an entity backed by Tahnoon bin Zayed, the UAE’s national security adviser, agreed to buy 49 percent of World Liberty Financial for $500 million.
An Abu Dhabi fund he chairs later bought $2 billion of the firm’s USD1 stablecoin. Months on, the administration eased AI chip exports to Emirati firms, including G42, which Tahnoon controls.
Trump also pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, whose company had paid $4.3 billion in fines, and accepted a $400 million jet from Qatar.
On October 22, a Circle shareholder sued in federal court, alleging violations of the Foreign Emoluments Clause.
Trump’s disclosures show $2.2 billion in earnings for his first year back, $1.4 billion of it from crypto, including about $636 million from a memecoin whose promoters advertised a dinner with him for its 185 biggest holders.
‘Slime, not crime’
Smaller scandals keep piling up. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned after the Wall Street Journal reported she asked a donor to cover a $100,000 credit card bill.
Adviser Corey Lewandowski faces a Justice Department inquiry. The New York Times says Alina Habba, Trump’s former lawyer, agreed to a $50 million deal with the family of a Venezuelan billionaire who later received a pardon.
Trump’s answer was to warn that dishonest allies “have to be prosecuted,” while his Justice Department charged a Virginia Democrat, state Sen. L. Louise Lucas.
Expect few convictions. Experts point to the Supreme Court: McDonnell in 2016 narrowed “official acts,” Snyder in 2024 excused gratuities paid after the fact, and Trump v. United States granted presidents sweeping immunity.
The Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section was effectively shut down in February 2025. What remains, some prosecutors say, is “slime, not crime,” despite overwhelming evidence of corruption that Americans across party lines can no longer ignore.
Nine days to judgment
Voters have noticed anyway. A Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll found nearly two in three Americans think Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, with most of the rise coming from Republicans and their leaners.
His approval sits at a record low of 33 percent, and Democrats have spent $182 million on corruption ads, more than the last four cycles combined, according to data from the firm AdImpact.
Vice President JD Vance calls the charge “laughable.” Trump’s pollster argues undecided voters will still choose on pocketbook issues. Perhaps. But $5 gasoline and a president’s sons selling drones are hard to pull apart.
The deeper question is what the money buys. In Matthew Cole’s account, Kushner held signing rights on an Emirati account while Abu Dhabi wanted the 2015 Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) dead.
Trump quit the agreement in May 2018. Months after he left office, Saudi Arabia’s sovereign fund gave his firm $2 billion, despite a screening panel finding its due diligence “unsatisfactory in all aspects.”
Today, at least some of the transactions happen in plain sight: Emirati stablecoin purchases, chip exports, drone contracts, and more.

Ste Marie imbues Monos Vancouver office with "residential quality"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ste Marie imbues Monos Vancouver office with “residential quality”
Canadian interiors studio Ste Marie has designed the Vancouver headquarters of luggage brand Monos to emphasise simplicity and shift mood throughout the day.
Located in the city’s Mount Pleasant neighbourhood, the Monos office was created to reflect the brand’s development to date and provide space for continued growth.
Ste Marie was presented with an open-ended brief, allowing the studio to develop a “flexible framework” for a company that is “still exploring what it could become” and would allow its team to collaborate, experiment and host.
“Monos is a brand grounded in design, mindfulness, human connection, and we understood this as an opportunity to create a place where those values could be put into practice,” said Ste Marie.
“A place where their people could come together to work, create, exchange ideas, test new things, host events and gather as an extended community.”
The studio, which previously designed the interiors for a Monos store in Toronto, approached the workplace like a residential project and organised the spaces into three overlapping areas.
“Like an apartment, it accommodates everyday activity as naturally as moments of hosting,” said the studio. “The residential quality also supports Monos’ culture of openness.”
The first area features low, soft modular sofas for lounging and conversation, and enclosed banquettes below conical pendant lights that facilitate personal exchanges, small meetings or shared meals.
An elongated communal table at the centre of the open plan provides a flexible surface for meetings, product development, testing, dining and gathering.
Here, the custom millwork is arranged in perpendicular planes that form vertical supports and horizontal overhead light boxes.
At the back is a kitchen and tea room with solid-surface counters and handleless cabinets, continuing the minimalist schema that runs throughout.
“These areas can expand and contract as needed: a meeting can become a meal, a work surface can become a display, and a lounge can transform into an event space,” Ste Marie said.
The hardness of the polished concrete flooring and rift-cut timber millwork is offset by soft furnishings, natural-fibre rugs and sheer curtains.
Dimmable lighting enables the mood to shift from early morning focused work to more casual afternoon meetings and then evening events.
“The result is a workplace that feels considered but not overly designed, with the warmth and informality of a personal space and the flexibility of a creative studio,” said Ste Marie.
Ste Marie was founded by Craig Stanghetta and has developed a reputation for its cinematic hospitality spaces across North America.
Other recent projects by the studio include a trio of venues in Edmonton, a series of amenity spaces within a renovated 1960s tower in Chicago and a Vancouver restaurant influenced by Hong Kong’s “love motels”.

Operation al-Khalil exposes limits of Israeli aggression
TEHRAN – The resistance operation in al-Khalil (Hebron), which took place just days before the Israeli elections, was far more than an isolated security incident.
It raises fundamental questions about the limits of power within the Israeli regime’s security establishment and its ability to prevent armed resistance operations in the occupied West Bank.
Despite continued raids, tighter military restrictions, an expanding campaign of searches, arrests, detentions, and home demolitions, armed resistance remains ongoing. This exposes the gap between the ability to establish control on the ground and the ability to achieve lasting security.
The operation is significant because of its timing and the context in which it occurred. Raids by Israeli Occupation Forces (IOF) alongside settler terrorism on Palestinians, their land, and their property in the West Bank have been escalating, alongside threats to expand the aggression.
The question is not only what security consequences the resistance operation has produced, but what it reveals about the shortcomings of the regime’s approach in the West Bank. The IOF continues to pursue policies aimed at imposing new realities through aggression and the complete control daily life in the occupied territories.
The armed resistance operation in al-Khalil that killed and injured IOF troops cannot be understood separately from the conditions in the city and its surrounding areas, where IOF attacks on Palestinians continue and overlap with settler terrorism.
On September 24, homes and other structures were demolished in the area of Jinba near al-Khalil, displacing eight families comprising 55 Palestinians, including 32 children. Some were forced to seek shelter in caves.
On October 12 and 13, children and their vehicles were attacked with rocks and sticks as they made their way to school. On October 17, settlers attacked the village of Ma’in near al-Khalil, injuring three Palestinians, one of whom was shot with live ammunition. They also stole 380 sheep. On October 19, farmers were attacked while harvesting olives.
These incidents are also inseparable from the IOF restrictions imposed on Palestinians at the Ibrahimi Mosque in al-Khalil and the continued measures enforcing its division by time and space.
Palestinians face conditions in which Israel’s pressure extends beyond military operations into the details of everyday life and their ability to remain on their land, amid the ongoing threat of ethnic cleansing.
The al-Khalil operation raises questions about the occupation regime’s ability to prevent armed resistance, even under heightened alert and strict security measures. Military superiority, a heavy military occupation, and the capacity to carry out raids and arrests do not necessarily mean an ability to anticipate every operation or prevent it from taking place.
This is where the central contradiction emerges. The IOF can expand its raids and impose sweeping restrictions on Palestinians in the West Bank, but it cannot automatically turn this into lasting, guaranteed security. Controlling territory is not the same as being able to control every security or political development that occurs within it.
The fact that an armed resistance operation took place in al-Khalil at this particular moment exposes the IOF’s security failure to anticipate the operation, issue an early warning, and prevent it from happening. It also puts claims of comprehensive security control to a serious test and serves as a reminder that the regime’s security policy in the West Bank, however extensive, prolonged, or intensified, cannot eliminate the underlying factors sustaining the aggression against Palestinians.
This becomes even more significant given the Netanyahu government’s reliance on military force as its primary tool for establishing deterrence and reshaping the situation in the West Bank. As arrests and terror expand, the possibility of renewed confrontation remains strong. This is a natural consequence of any occupation.
The al-Khalil operation comes at a sensitive electoral moment for the Netanyahu coalition, which seeks to present its strategy of maintaining security control over the West Bank as proof of the success of its policies. An armed resistance operation occurring amid this rhetoric and strategy raises questions within the regime itself about the effectiveness of the approach and the Netanyahu government’s ability to deliver on its security promises.
Remarks by Netanyahu and Katz, about a large-scale offensive in the West Bank have been translated into expanded raids, sieges, mass arrests, demolition of homes and infrastructure, similar to the patterns seen in refugee camps across the northern West Bank. The rhetoric is reminiscent of similar aggression used during the Second Intifada in 2002 under Ariel Sharon.
The regime’s continued reliance on military force raises a fundamental question about the limits of this approach, which has failed to deliver security. Establishing security control does not guarantee safety or eliminate the causes of the conflict with the Palestinian people.
Nor can expanding the aggression guarantee complete security as long as the occupation, its policies, and its violations of Palestinian rights remain. The regime refuses to acknowledge these underlying factors and openly declares its intention to settle the conflict by force, presenting this outcome as inevitable.
Looking back, the occupation regime’s past experiences with the use of excessive force have failed to deliver the strategic outcomes.
In other words, force cannot settle a struggle over land. The strategic significance of the al-Khalil operation lies not simply in its immediate security impact, but also in what it reveals about the difficulty of turning IOF superiority into a definitive resolution amid the West Bank aggression.
The regime possesses overwhelming military power and an extensive, integrated security and military apparatus. It can impose realities on the ground and carry out its plans against Palestinians, but it cannot guarantee lasting security and stability.
From this perspective, many believe that the return of armed resistance operations amid the choices of occupation, settlement expansion, and ongoing aggression against Palestinians reinforces a crucial point: the issue goes beyond an isolated intelligence failure. The more pressure Palestinians face, the more likely such operations are to recur as a consequence of IOF policies and settler terrorism.
Armed resistance operations do not emerge in a vacuum. They arise in response to the occupation regime’s policies imposed on a people whose entire existence is under threat, even on their own land. Palestinian land is being seized and subjected to Judaization, while Palestinians face growing threats to their rights, presence, future, land, and holy sites.
With a large-scale IOF assault and forced displacement underway in al-Khalil, the West Bank faces the possibility of an escalation that could spiral out of control.
The regime’s real dilemma is not simply how to tighten its control over the West Bank, but its belief that control through force can bring the resistance to an end. Every military operation carried out by the IOF may alter certain realities on the ground, but it cannot erase Palestinians’ rights to their land or their other rights, nor can it extinguish their aspirations for freedom.
The regime’s military superiority does not, by any means, guarantee that the armed struggle can be brought to a definitive end as long as its political roots remain unresolved and resistance can rise again from the ashes.

‘PMLA case not examined’: ED moves Supreme Court against HC order quashing proceedings against NewsClick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:49:01 UTC
01:49:01 KST

NEW DELHI: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has moved the Supreme Court challenging the Delhi high court’s order quashing a money laundering case against news portal NewsClick and its editor-in-chief, Prabir Purkayastha, over alleged violations of foreign direct investment (FDI) rules.The ED argued that the high court quashed its Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR) without examining the merits of the case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). It also flagged a five-month delay in the pronouncement of the judgment.The matter is yet to be listed for hearing.
Why Delhi HC quashed ED's case against NewsClick
In a judgment dated May 29, Justice Neena Bansal Krishna of the Delhi high court described the continuation of an FIR registered by the Delhi Police’s Economic Offences Wing (EOW) as “nothing but a gross abuse of the process of law”. The judge held that quashing the FIR for the predicate offence also warranted the closure of the ED’s ECIR.Also Read | ‘Gross abuse of law’: Delhi HC quashes FIR, ED case against Newsclick, founderThe court ruled that the investment was an "economic decision that did not spell out any criminal offence”. Citing the Union ministry of information and broadcasting’s reply to NewsClick, Justice Krishna noted there was no cap or restriction on FDI in digital media at the time.The single-judge bench ruled that the investment followed acceptable practices and that the allegations, even if accepted, did not establish cheating or criminal breach of trust.
The alleged victim in the cheating case should have been M/s Worldwide Media Holdings LLC, but the company had filed no complaint. Instead, the complaint came from “merely an informant”.Justice Krishna also rejected the fund-siphoning allegation, noting that a digital media company would naturally incur expenses on salaries, consultation fees and rent.The high court further dismissed the ED’s attempt to sustain the money laundering case on the basis of criminal conspiracy under the IPC, holding that the agency must establish the “illegal objective” or “means” allegedly adopted by NewsClick and others.“Pertinently, extensive investigations were carried out by the ED for about a year and a half, and the petitioners as well as their employees have been summoned and examined many a times, but nothing incriminating till date has been found or placed on record," the order said.
“Aside from bald assertions of a criminal conspiracy, there is not a whisper of any incriminating allegation, which would even remotely suggest the commission of the offence punishable under Section 4 of the PMLA,” it added.The bench further stated that the request for a copy of the ECIR had become "infructuous" after the report was quashed.
The case
The EOW’s 2020 FIR alleged that PPK Newsclick Studio Pvt Ltd, NewsClick’s parent company, received Rs 9.59 crore in FDI from US-based Worldwide Media Holdings LLC in 2018-19 in violation of foreign investment rules, causing a loss to the government exchequer.It alleged that the company’s shares were grossly overvalued to circumvent the 26% FDI cap for digital news websites, and that over 45% of the investment was siphoned off through salaries, consultation fees and rent for ulterior motives.The ED subsequently registered a money laundering case against NewsClick, Purkayastha and others.PPK Newsclick Studio sought quashing of the FIR, arguing that it contained "vague" allegations.(With PTI inputs)

Silence about attacks on nuclear facilities is unforgivable
Jam-e-Jam criticized the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for its response to attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities. The article argued that military strikes carried out by the United States and Israel against Iran’s nuclear sites in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious violations of international law and the prohibition on aggression.
According to the paper, both the governing bodies and the Secretariat of the IAEA failed to issue even a statement condemning these actions, a situation unprecedented in the agency’s history. The newspaper claimed this failure exposed a major institutional weakness and raised concerns about the consistent application of principles that the agency is supposed to uphold. It argued that the IAEA cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks on safeguarded facilities as a secondary concern. Therefore, the agency should clearly reaffirm that attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities are unlawful, unacceptable, and should never be tolerated under any circumstances.
Donya-e-Eqtesad: Decoding an Emirati flight to Tehran
Donya-e-Eqtesad examined the repeated landing of an Emirati aircraft in Tehran. These flights sparked speculation about possible contacts between the UAE and Iran ahead of a potential new phase of regional tensions. The visits occurred at a time of intensified diplomatic activity across the region. The newspaper also noted that Trump’s support for Netanyahu before Israel’s national elections increased concerns about possible new attacks against Iran. Since the UAE aligned itself with the United States and Israel after the outbreak of conflict and was reportedly targeted by Iranian retaliatory actions, the return of a government-linked Emirati aircraft to Tehran attracted attention. Combined with earlier reports regarding possible arrangements related to frozen Iranian assets, the flights fueled speculation about behind-the-scenes communication between the two countries. Nevertheless, the true purpose of the flights remains unclear, leaving open the question of whether they were intended to ease tensions or serve another mission.
Ettelaat: E3’s proposal for mediation amid tensions
Ettelaat discussed the announcement by Germany, France, and the United Kingdom (known as European trio) that they are prepared to act as mediators between Tehran and Washington over the Iran nuclear issue. According to the newspaper, these three countries possess extensive experience in talks concerning Iran’s nuclear program and have long participated in diplomatic efforts aimed at ensuring its peaceful nature. The European initiative remains focused on preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, a goal that Berlin, Paris, and London continue to regard as essential for reducing regional tensions. European governments are therefore seeking to keep the door open for negotiations while responding to the rapidly evolving security situation in the Middle East. At the same time, Iran’s response to the proposal remains uncertain. Since the European troika has largely been sidelined in recent phases of the nuclear dispute, it remains to be seen whether Iran and the United States will once again bring these countries back into the negotiating process.
Etemad: Washington’s messages not genuine diplomatic initiatives
Etemad interviewed former Iranian parliamentarian Heshmatollah 
 
Falahatpisheh about the likelihood of war versus successful negotiations. While diplomatic efforts to reduce regional tensions continue, assessments of potential Iran-US talks remain cautious. Falahatpisheh argued that Washington’s recent messages are not genuine diplomatic initiatives but rather ultimatums containing strict demands. He believes the United States seeks to restrict significant parts of Iran’s nuclear and military capabilities, and that its proposals appear closer to demands for surrender than a basis for agreement. At the same time, he noted that Iran is trying to highlight the costs and vulnerabilities of any military confrontation, taking into account both US electoral considerations and Iran’s military posture. In his view, this strategy can strengthen deterrence while keeping diplomatic channels open.
Javan: No violations in the Strait of Hormuz
In an article, Javan addressed developments in the Strait of Hormuz. Contrary to misleading narratives from Trump and CENTCOM, field reports indicate that vessels involved in oil smuggling or other violations have reduced or halted their activities. The newspaper suggested that military measures and restrictions may be influencing maritime calculations in this strategic waterway. Meanwhile, rising oil prices, with crude exceeding $117 per barrel, demonstrated that developments in the Strait of Hormuz are not merely military issues but also have immediate consequences for global energy markets and the international economy. In this context, warnings from the IRGC Navy about expanding responses to US actions, alongside statements from the speaker of Parliament regarding the costs of conflict with Iran, reflected two complementary messages: Iran’s ability to affect one of the world’s most important energy corridors and a warning about the broader economic and strategic consequences of escalating tensions.

Photo: AP

“Unfortunately the speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there,” Zelensky told the Hudson Institute think tank.
He said Kyiv was also waiting for US interceptor missiles to protect it from Russian strikes.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham separately “underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access to Starlink” in a call with Donald Trump on Friday, Downing Street said.
However, Donald Trump told reporters he would speak to Musk if there was still an issue.
“If there is a problem, I will get it straightened out,” he said.
The US leader has pivoted back toward Moscow over the past two weeks, announcing a diesel deal that he hopes would bring down oil prices sent soaring by the Iran war and postponing sanctions on Russia.
Moscow has in exchange freed a US detainee — and apparently given Donald Trump’s wife a gift.
Melania Trump said she had worked with the Russian and Ukrainian leaderships on the Oleshky plan.
Civilian leaders from both countries would visit the devastated city to assess aid needs, she said.

Richard Metson (麥人杰) was among the artists honored at the 17th Golden Comic Awards ceremony on Thursday, with awards presented in seven categories and prizes totaling NT$2.75 million (US$84,595).
Metson was presented with the Special Contribution Award, while five artists were honored in the Comic of the Year category.
The other awards were for Best Cross-media Application, Best Editor, Best New Talent and Online Popularity, as well as the Golden Comic Grand Prize.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Culture
Twenty-four works from 185 submissions were shortlisted for this year’s awards.
Minister of Culture Li Yuan (李遠) presented the Special Contribution Award to Metson, recognizing his more than 40 years of “dedication to comic creation.”
It was Metson’s second award following his first win in the China Times National Comics Contest in 1984 with Heavenly Questions (天問).
He is a pioneering Taiwanese comic artist whose work spans comics, animation, film, video games and illustration, the organizers said.
Metson has created a wide range of works, from sci-fi classics Birdman (鳥人) and Zero Legend (零代傳說), and comedy series Brain Twisters (腦筋急轉彎) to alternative graphic novels Deadline (期限) and Black Book (黑色大書).
He collaborated on the graphic novel anthology Sept Reves du Louvre (Seven Dreams of the Louvre), directed animation for the landmark Taiwanese film Grandma and Her Ghosts (魔法阿媽) and developed major animation series, including Happy Star Cat (快樂星貓).
Metson said he had initially thought the phone call informing him of the award was a scam because he had not submitted an application.
He wondered why a scam ring would target a comic artist, he said.
When he won his first award in 1984 with Heavenly Questions, people had disliked him because he did not treat them to a meal to celebrate, he said.
“This time, I will buy dinner,” he said.
Metson’s Twin Crowns: Little Prince and Princess Saga (雙寶記:星星穿越宇宙而來) won the Golden Comic Grand Prize.
Five works received Comic of the Year awards: Plant Collectors’ Notebooks Vol. 5 (採集人的野帳5), The Banana Sprout Vol. 3 (芭蕉的芽Vol.3), Wonder Land (良田:柚子異色精選集), To Be the One You Love (喜歡你喜歡的樣子) and Adeus Adeus (再見了再見).
Three Unmarried Women Musical (三個不結婚的女人) claimed the Best Cross-media Application Award.
Lai Hsuan-pei (賴萱珮) won the Best Editor Award with Our Messy Love (難搞的戀愛體質).
Wu Kuan-xiong (吳冠熊) won the Best New Talent Award with Blue Whale, Wandering Boy (藍鯨與龍少年).
The Online Popularity Award was won by Yuzu (柚子) for Wonder Land.

Storm leaves after killing one and injuring 616
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:44:02 UTC
01:44:02 KST

Tropical Storm Champi left one person dead, injured 616 and caused some damage to infrastructure before moving away from Taiwan yesterday afternoon, the Central Emergency Operations Center said.
With the storm on a course toward southern Japan, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) lifted its sea warning last night at 8:30pm. It lifted its land warning at 2:30pm.
As of 5pm yesterday, Champi had led to the death of one person and injured 616 since beginning to affect Taiwan on Thursday as a typhoon, the center said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
The death was reported in Pingtung County’s Liouciou Township (琉球), where a man was on Thursday swept away by storm-driven waves on a beach, the center said.
Most injuries were minor scrapes and bruises, with no one reported missing, it said.
Of the 9,027 reports of damage received, 3,287 involved fallen trees, including 1,282 in Taipei, the most of any administrative region, followed by 646 in Taichung. Another 3,033 involved essential infrastructure, while 1,014 involved billboards and signs, the center said.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Power Co
It said more than 340,000 households lost power during the storm, and about 22,000 were still without electricity as of yesterday evening, but were expected to have service restored by 11pm.
Yilan County recorded 650mm of accumulated rainfall from Thursday through 4pm yesterday, the highest in the nation, while Taoyuan and Hsinchu County each received more than 500mm. Taipei recorded 469.5mm, the center said.
Yesterday alone through 4pm, Miaoli County had recorded 302mm of rainfall, Hsinchu County and Taipei had recorded about 250mm, Chiayi and Nantou counties had recorded 170mm, and Yunlin County had recorded 150mm.
Photo: I-hwa Cheng, AFP
A total of 4,960 people had been evacuated by 4pm yesterday as a precaution against landslides, including residents in New Taipei City, Taoyuan, Keelung and Tainan, and Yilan, Hualien, Nantou, Yunlin, Pingtung, Hsinchu, Chiayi and Taitung counties, the center said.
As of 5pm yesterday, Champi was centered about 320km northeast of Taipei, moving north-northeast to northeast at 14kph to 21kph. It had maximum sustained winds of 101kph, with gusts of up to 126kph, the CWA said.
CWA forecaster Lin Ping-yu (林秉煜) said Champi’s outer circulation would bring intermittent rain north of Miaoli County last night and early today.
Showers would gradually ease and become limited to areas north of Taoyuan and the mountainous areas of Taipei and New Taipei City before tapering off early today, Lin said.
Most areas in Taiwan would be partly cloudy to sunny today and tomorrow, with some rain in the east, Lin said, adding that Hualien and Taitung could see heavier rain, while mountainous areas of central and southern Taiwan could get scattered afternoon showers.
Champi also disrupted air and sea transport to Taiwan’s outlying islands, as well as international flights.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
At Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, 563 flights were canceled on Friday, while another 261 had been canceled as of 10:15am yesterday, the airport operator said.
Flights to and from Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) were also disrupted yesterday, with several flights canceled and others diverted.
The airports expected flight operations to gradually recover while urging travelers to check their flight’s status with their airlines before heading to the airport, as schedules remained subject to change.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Agriculture yesterday said Champi had caused an estimated NT$133.36 million (US$4.1 million) in agricultural losses across Taiwan as of yesterday afternoon.
The brunt of the losses reported to date have occurred in Yunlin County, accounting for more than 80 percent of the total, with garlic crops sustaining the heaviest losses, it said.

Life expectancy in Taiwan increases to 81.27 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:58 UTC
01:43:58 KST

Taiwan’s life expectancy reached 81.27 years, up from 80.77 years a year earlier, with cancer remaining the leading cause of death for the 44th consecutive year, the Ministry of the Interior said yesterday.
Various types of cancer accounted for 54,838 deaths last year, or 27.48 percent of all deaths, the ministry said in a statement.
Life expectancy would have been 3.7 years more, or 84.97 years, if cancer deaths were excluded, it said.
Source: Ministry of the Interior
Life expectancy was calculated after excluding deaths from each of the 10 leading causes of death and compared with the overall average, it said, adding that the greater the difference, the greater the effect of the cause of death on life expectancy.
The 10 leading causes of death in Taiwan last year were cancers, heart disease, pneumonia, cerebrovascular disease, diabetes, hypertensive diseases, accidents, nephritis, nephrotic syndrome and nephrosis, chronic lower respiratory diseases and suicide, Ministry of Health and Welfare data showed.
Excluding deaths from heart disease and pneumonia raised life expectancy by 1.54 years and 1.13 years respectively, the interior ministry said.
The gap between life expectancy and the figure calculated excluding cancer deaths narrowed from 4.1 years in 2015 to 3.7 last year, suggesting that cancer’s impact on life expectancy had eased slightly, it said.
Men lost more years of life than women to most of the 10 leading causes of death last year, except for diabetes, hypertensive diseases and kidney diseases, it said.
Men lost 0.75 years of life expectancy to accidents, compared with 0.36 years for women, the statement said.
The differences might be related to occupation, physiological factors, diet and healthcare, or lifestyle, it said.
The data help show how different causes of death affect life expectancy, it said.
More information is available on the interior ministry’s Web site in the “Statistics” section.

Institute touts milk test to monitor health of cows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:57 UTC
01:43:57 KST

The Taiwan Livestock Research Institute has developed a technique for dairy farm management evaluation that can help stabilize milk production by identifying nutritional problems up to two weeks earlier than conventional indicators.
Total milk fat percentage and milk yield used to be key indicators for monitoring the health of dairy cattle, but those indicators can lag ill health by days, the institute said on Tuesday.
Wang Ssu-han (王思涵), an associate researcher at the institute, said that it analyzed 2,073 bulk tank milk samples and found that milk fat composition is highly subject to summer heat, which can cause heat stress in cows, reducing feed intake and changing the composition of their milk.
Photo: CNA
The institute used the analysis to develop an evaluation technique that dairy farmers use to detect health issues in cattle a week or two weeks earlier than before, Wang said.
The technique can categorize milk fatty acids into two types: “newly synthesized” and “preformed,” she said.
Newly synthesized fatty acids are derived from the process of dairy cows digesting feed and their mammary glands synthesizing fatty acids, while preformed fatty acids come directly from diet or body fat, she said.
Analyzing the fatty acid profiles reveals health issues earlier, she said.
For example, levels of newly synthesized fatty acids in milk can indicate how well cows’ rumens are functioning and the quality of their feed, she said.
Preformed fatty acids help detect issues such as insufficient food intake, she added.
With health issues spotted earlier, farmers can more promptly adjust starch, fiber and concentrate in feed and increase the milk fat percentage, Wang said, citing one farm application in which adjusting the feed helped restore milk fat content to 3.75 percent from 3.5 percent.
With that percentage gain, revenue loss of about NT$0.92 per kilogram of raw milk would be prevented, she said.
For a mid-sized dairy farm with daily milk production of 2,000kg, that would avoid monthly revenue loss of up to NT$55,000, she added.
Dairy farmers are advised to monitor long-term data trends instead of using a single figure for decisionmaking when they apply the technique, the institute said.
Milk fatty acids data are warning signals for dairy farm management, it said.
Farmers who observe a sustained negative trend in the milk fatty acid composition of their cows should check the physical condition of their animals, as well as improve potential issues such as moldy feed or poor cowshed ventilation, it said.

As Israeli election nears, campaign turns ugly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:57 UTC
01:43:57 KST

Days ahead of close-fought Israeli elections, campaigns have gone into overdrive with poor-taste jibes and inflammatory attacks against candidates, sometimes crossing red lines.
Fueled in part by a boom in artificial intelligence (AI)-generated images flooding social media, candidates and activists are seeking to portray their opponents as weak, untrustworthy or damaging for the country as they play on stereotypes and fears to sway public opinion.
The electioneering has at times turned personal, with some candidates who lost loved ones in the wars following Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack even having their bereavement dragged into the campaign.
Photo: AFP
Ahead of Tuesday’s vote, polls show Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc neck-and-neck with that of his main centre-right rival Gadi Eisenkot.
On Wednesday, Eisenkot posted a video on social media wishing Netanyahu a happy 77th birthday that featured a slate of AI-generated characters including a Hamas member speaking from a tunnel.
“What can we wish for the person who has been protecting us for 20 years?” the militant says, evoking theories that the prime minister has deliberately helped Muslim militants to stay in power in Gaza, charges vehemently denied by Netanyahu.
Soon after, an AI depiction of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei pops up, telling Netanyahu: “One more round without victory, and I’ll make you a bomb as a present.”
Netanyahu has also liberally weaponized AI-generated content against his rival. In July, he posted a video depicting Eisenkot rejecting a hug from a young man wearing a T-shirt with the slogan “Israel unity” and instead embracing Arab-Israeli candidate Mansour Abbas.
The clip sparked widespread outrage over claims the young man had been made to resemble Eisenkot’s son who was killed fighting in Gaza in 2023, something Netanyahu’s party denied.
In an interview broadcast by Channel 13, Eisenkot said he had felt “deep contempt for Netanyahu and his entourage” after watching the video.
Netanyahu’s camp has used AI throughout the campaign to stoke fears over a possible opposition coalition including Arab-Israeli parties.
Clips have ranged from Jewish opposition politicians taking off masks to reveal Arab-Israeli candidates underneath, to Arabs looming over what appears to be a crumbling parliament building.
Billboards for Netanyahu’s Likud party with the phrase “The Right or Palestine” alongside the faces of Arab-Israeli politicians have also sprung up across the country.
“It’s incitement, especially from Prime Minister Netanyahu’s camp,” said Thair Abu Ras, head of the Forum for Regional Thinking at the Van Leer Jerusalem Institute.
“This whole notion of having an Arab party in the coalition is illegitimate in the eyes of the right wing, and they’re trying to enforce that kind of way of thinking on the Eisenkot coalition as well,” he said.
Apparently racialized comments have been leveled at Eisenkot, the son of Moroccan Jews.
This month, a senior commentator on the pro-Netanyahu Channel 14 television station described him as “a monkey.”
While the term is not necessarily a racial slur in Hebrew, the remark drew widespread condemnation from opposition politicians and from Netanyahu himself.
The election is the first since Hamas’ October 2023 attack. A number of candidates are people whose lives were transformed that day or in the wars that followed, but trauma or bereavement have not spared them from personal attacks.
Laly Derai, whose son was killed fighting in Gaza in 2024, is running for the new far-right Amcha Israel party, which advocates universal conscription into the Israeli military — an increasingly contentious issue due to exemptions for religious students.
She said she has faced a coordinated smear campaign against her, which has at times invoked her son’s death and accusations that she is betraying his memory. Posters calling for her to withdraw her candidacy so as not to “put the country in danger” have sprung up in the area around the settlement where she lives in the occupied West Bank.
“They’re trying to break me but, paradoxically or not, this campaign has reinforced my decision to enter politics precisely to put an end to this hate-filled rhetoric,” she said.
Speaking to public broadcaster KAN, she said she had received “phone calls at all hours of the day and night, disgusting comments on social media, signs posted in our towns, including near our children’s school buses — all of this just because we dared to propose something new.”
Relatives of hostages formerly held by Hamas have also been caught in the crosshairs.
On an unofficial Facebook page for supporters of Netanyahu’s Likud party, an image was posted on Tuesday pitting one mother of a former hostage against another.
One mother, Likud candidate Talik Gvili, looks calm against the backdrop of an Israeli flag, while Einav Zangauker — a vocal critic of Netanyahu — looks frenzied around protesters tinted in red.
“It is us or them,” the caption reads.

Expert discusses deterring  transnational repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:51 UTC
01:43:51 KST

Harsher penalties without early threat detection and efforts to identify those behind the action would not deter transnational repression, Taipei District Court national security judge and Institute for National Defense and Security Research adjunct fellow Hsu Kai-chieh (許凱傑) said on Friday.
Taiwan should draw on the experiences of Canada and Australia, which have measures to share threat information and penalize preparatory acts involving foreign interference before attacks occur, he said.
Amendments must clearly define what constitutes a legal violation and how “foreign forces” are identified, ensuring that people are not accused of breaking the law simply because of their political views or correspondence with people in China, he added.
Photo: Huang Yun-hsuan, Taipei Times
“Defensive democracy does not lower the standards of the rule of law. Rather, it means ensuring that democracies have the means, through rigorous legal procedures, to prevent authoritarian states from exploiting the openness of democratic societies to oppress their people,” he said.
The prevention of transnational repression requires early warnings, investigations to identify those behind the acts and protection for victims, he said.
The government should ensure that people who might be targeted receive timely information about threats, Hsu said.
For example, Canada allows intelligence agencies to share threat information with people and organizations outside the government, he said, adding that it helps potential targets take precautions.
Meanwhile, Australia criminalizes preparatory acts involving foreign interference, as well as providing funding or substantial support to foreign intelligence services, Hsu said.
Such provisions give law enforcement agencies opportunities to disrupt operations before targets are attacked, he added.
The Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法) covers some forms of such conduct, but there is room for improvement in provisions addressing threats, coercion, unlawful detention and the illegal collection or use of personal data when such acts involve foreign infiltration, he said.
He also called for greater interagency cooperation, saying that an operation could involve surveillance, cyberattacks and direction from overseas, but as some information is held separately by the police, cybersecurity agencies and intelligence services, investigators could struggle to link seemingly unrelated incidents.
US legislative proposals and Germany’s experience could provide useful references for Taiwan as it develops coordination channels and reporting mechanisms, Hsu said.
Information sharing must comply with evidence-gathering rules and protect intelligence sources, ensuring that investigative leads can be turned into evidence that stand up in court, he added.
Hsu also warned that the public might hesitate to report threats, because they fear retaliation.
The government should provide reliable channels for seeking help, security advice and legal assistance, as well as clear procedures for receiving reports, assessing risks and providing protection, he said.
Making victims feel safe enough to seek help would also allow authorities to preserve evidence earlier and prevent further harm, he added.

For months, US President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have openly hinted at a military intervention or takeover of Cuba, ramping up economic, political and legal pressure on the country.
“To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba — now is the time,” Rubio said on social media.
Photo: Reuters
“The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA,” he said.
The unusual post appeared to confirm that the CIA is active in Cuba after a long history of covert operations including backing the disastrous Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961.
The call was mocked by Cuban officials.
“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on social media. “There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”
The CIA later uploaded a video to social media offering instructions in Spanish for those who believe they have information of interest to the intelligence agency, encouraging them to first and foremost visit an official US installation in person if they can safely travel to one.
For those hoping to contact the CIA online via the cia.gov Web site, the agency instructed users to access the Internet on a secure network such as a VPN using a private browser and a burner e-mail account unassociated with any personal details. Those sharing information should be prepared to include their city, job, level of access and contact information with their message.
Trump, speaking at a rally in Florida earlier on Friday, underlined his ambitions to impose regime change in Cuba.
“Those beautiful [US military] ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards [46m] off the coast,” he said. “They’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”
Cuban Minister of Foreign Affairs Bruno Rodriguez quickly dismissed Trump’s threats.
“Our coastline is full of beautiful beaches, but there are also razor-sharp limestone spikes, an inhospitable environment for those who make it to our shores with hostile purposes and lust for domination,” he posted.

Tien Kung III, PAC-3 to anchor defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:49 UTC
01:43:49 KST

Taiwan’s Tien Kung III (天弓三型, “Sky Bow III”) and US-made Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) missiles would remain the backbone of the nation’s air defense in the next three to five years, a defense official said on condition of anonymity.
They made the remarks as they pointed to delayed US arms sales and production constraints affecting the domestically-developed Tien Kung IV (天弓四型, “Sky Bow IV”) missile, which means that the Chiang Kung (強弓, “Strong Bow”) program would not enter service until 2028.
A planned US arms sale to Taiwan worth NT$420 billion (US$12.92 billion) has yet to be announced, delaying key equipment deliveries, including extended-range Patriot PAC-3 missiles and the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System, they said.
Photo: Screen grab from the Defense Visual Information Distribution System’s Web site
Meanwhile, following a year-long budget fight with the legislature, the Ministry of National Defense has opted to fund the Tien Kung IV missile procurement through the government’s annual budget instead of special budgets, the source said.
The ministry has indicated that the missile would provide the key high-altitude interceptor capability for the “T-Dome,” the military’s planned networked air defense matrix for Taiwan proper.
The Tien Kung IV’s vector-thrust maneuverability and high maximum altitude are deemed essential capabilities for Taiwan to counter the advanced ballistic missiles of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army, sources said.
At the current funding levels, the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) can begin delivering Tien Kung IV missiles no earlier than 2028, the official said.
The government plans to bridge the capability gap with a proposed NT$13 billion supplementary budget for materials and assembly lines for the missiles, they said.
Meanwhile, NCSIST has transferred the technology used in more than 50 percent of the missile’s components to the private sector, including parts for active seekers and active electronically scanned arrays, the official said.
Until these efforts bear fruit, the Tien Kung III and PAC-3 missiles must bear the brunt of defending Taiwan’s airspace, the official said.
NCSIST has successfully conducted stress tests on its sprint production capacity for the Tien Kung III missile, they said, adding that Taiwan can produce 96 Tien Kung missiles a year.
The system would be the armed forces’ mainstay interceptor for at least three years, the official said.
Taiwan’s 13 Tien Kung III air defense missile positions, including planned and completed ones, can readily accommodate the Tien Kung IV thanks to commonalities between the two systems’ radar and launch vehicles, they said.
The NCSIST-developed air defense battalion battle management system is capable of integrating Tien Kung III, Tien Kung IV and PAC-3 missiles, which must suffice until the US approves and delivers the anticipated arms package, they added.

Bayern Munich expect coach Vincent Kompany to miss an extended period as he continues his hospital treatment for a virus after collapsing on the training pitch on Friday. “Vinnie will be given all the time he needs. We’re not starting to put together any timeframes. We need to firstly figure out what it is and then we’ll discuss calmly what recovery time is to be. We won’t be talking about days, but weeks. We need to all be clear on that,” he said.
Photo: NTB Scanpix via AP

“All the football operations are in our hands and we’ll work together as a team to keep the club moving forward,” he added.
Bayern’s second team’s game was postponed after Kompany’s collapse, but Eberl said the club did not consider trying to postpone today’s Bundesliga game. “I think the greatest joy for Vinnie would be for us to play well tomorrow and, ideally, get a positive result,” Eberl said. “That would probably be one of the best things we could do to help him recover.”

“I caught a pretty nasty virus last week, and of course I didn’t listen to my body — and then at some point my body just said, ‘enough is enough!’”
The defending champions sit on top of the Bundesliga table ahead of today’s game, one point above Freiburg. Their next Champions League match is on Nov. 3 in Madrid against Atletico.

Messi receives top Spanish award from heir to throne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:48 UTC
01:43:48 KST

AFP, OVIEDO, Spain
Lionel Messi received Spain’s most prestigious sports award on Friday in recognition of his glittering career and his work for disadvantaged children’s access to health and education.
The Argentine forward, 39, was named winner of the Princess of Asturias Award for Sports in June, with the jury hailing “the most successful footballer of all time” and his social work.
Photo: EPA
Dozens of fans wearing Argentina soccer shirts cheered and chanted Messi’s name as he arrived to the sound of bagpipes and drums at the ceremony in Oviedo, capital of the northern Spanish region of Asturias.
Messi collected a formal roll of parchment from Princess Leonor, the heir to the Spanish throne after whom the awards are named, who lauded his “unique career.”
“He turned the extraordinary into routine by reading the game and deciding on the most effective option in fractions of a second, while respecting the collective essence above ego,” Leonor said.
One of the greatest soccer players of all time, Messi has won eight Ballon d’Or titles, a World Cup and dozens of trophies at club level.
He spent 21 years at Barcelona where he played in a side that dominated Spain and Europe under Pep Guardiola and Luis Enrique.
After leaving the Catalan club in 2021, Messi spent two years at French giants Paris Saint-Germain and plays for Inter Miami in MLS.
Argentina’s all-time top goal scorer, assist provider and caps holder called time on his international career earlier this year after losing the World Cup final to Spain in New Jersey.
“The most important thing is to know how to lose and how to win,” Messi told an event with children in Oviedo on Thursday, saying that attitude was “fundamental” in soccer.
Founded in 1981, the Princess of Asturias Awards are the most prestigious in the Spanish-speaking world and come with prize money of 50,000 euros (US$56,000).
They encompass the arts, sciences and sports and are handed out annually in honor of efforts to improve human coexistence, solidarity and global cooperation.
British author Julian Barnes, trailblazing US astronaut Christina Koch and punk star Patti Smith were among the other winners who received their prize on Friday.
Previous winners of the sports award include tennis greats Serena Williams and Rafael Nadal, marathon record-breaker Eliud Kipchoge and US skier Lindsey Vonn.

Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung urges AI, drone ties with Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:48 UTC
01:43:48 KST

Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) yesterday called for Taiwan and Europe to build trusted supply chains in artificial intelligence (AI) and drones, saying closer cooperation could strengthen economic and national security.
Speaking at the opening of the annual conference of the Formosa Club, which connects pro-Taiwan parliamentarians across Europe, Lin said Taiwan’s semiconductor, AI server and emerging drone industries complemented Europe’s expertise in precision manufacturing and industrial technology.
“These require trusted partners because they directly involve national security and critical infrastructure,” he said.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
Russia’s war against Ukraine had demonstrated how excessive economic dependence could become an instrument of coercion, Lin said, adding that Taiwan offered a partnership grounded in trust and shared values.
Taiwan was developing a complete drone supply chain encompassing hardware, critical components and cybersecurity standards, he said.
As an example of industrial cooperation, Lin cited a proposed technology park in Poland planned by the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association.
The project would focus on AI data centers, smart cities and electric vehicles, he said.
Lin described economic cooperation as one pillar of Taiwan’s “integrated diplomacy,” alongside partnerships with fellow democracies.
He urged like-minded countries to jointly resist transnational repression, accusing China of using domestic legislation to extend its jurisdiction overseas and threaten freedom of expression.
“No country should be allowed to use domestic law as an instrument for exporting a chilling effect beyond its own borders,” he said.
Member of the European Parliament Michael Gahler, who chaired the conference, called for parliamentary support for Taiwan to translate into broader, institutionalized cooperation at the government level.
He advocated arrangements facilitating investment in both directions, saying their substance mattered more than whether they were called bilateral investment agreements.
Europe could deepen practical engagement with Taiwan while maintaining its “one China” policies, Gahler said, distinguishing those policies from Beijing’s “one China” principle.
Democracies needed to coordinate their responses to the long-term threats of war, hybrid warfare and economic coercion from Russia and China, he said.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the club, which was founded in 2019, are scheduled to cohost a forum on Tuesday focusing on cooperation between Taiwan and Europe in AI and drone technology.

EDITORIAL: Militarism, messaging, partnerships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:43 UTC
01:43:43 KST

Two strands of a concerted misinformation campaign affecting Taiwan need to be resisted. The first is “US skepticism,” the idea that in the event of aggression against Taiwan by the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA), Washington would be unlikely to intervene militarily. The second is “Japanese neo-militarism.”
Both originate from and serve the purposes of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). The first is designed to shake the resolve of Taiwanese and the second to reduce obstacles to PLA aggression in the Taiwan Strait.
A US operational warfare guidance report released on Oct. 7 titled How the Army Fights describes how the US military intends to counterbalance its “pacing threat” — the PLA — by improving its warfighting infrastructure across the region. That is to be achieved by ensuring that forward deployments of weapons, equipment and supplies are present along the First Island Chain, enabling a rapid response to PLA actions.
This year’s Keen Sword military exercises, which started on Monday and run through Thursday, are operational practice runs by Japan and the US to protect Japan, including its Ryukyu Islands, with deployments on Okinawa, Miyako, Ishigaki and Yonaguni — only 110km from Taiwan — as well as on the main islands of Shikoku and Kyushu.
The addition of Indo-Pacific, Pacific and European nations — including France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the Philippines, Australia and Canada — shows that other nations also see the benefit of the exercises.
The larger scale and wider participation at this year’s Keen Sword exercises demonstrate the evolving structure of the regional deterrence. They are the physical manifestation of the concepts laid out in the US’ operational warfare guidance report, just as they are the first trial run of Japan’s new Joint Operations Command, launched on March 24 last year to unify operational command of Japan’s ground, maritime and air self-defense forces.
The participation of the Philippines extends the scope of the exercises south along the First Island Chain, while the implications of the US report stretch north to South Korea, too, as the Chosun Daily reported in an article titled “US Army’s new guidance calls for full force against China in First Island Chain: New guidelines emphasize immediate action, impacting South Korea’s defense strategies.”
The article said that the new stance “necessitates changes to military assets on the Korean Peninsula, which hosts the second-largest US troop presence after Japan,” and quotes US Forces Korea Commander General Xavier Brunson as describing South Korea as a “fixed aircraft carrier between China and Japan.”
With these preparations in place, it is difficult to entertain any idea of “US skepticism.” The wide regional participation surely also quashes any suspicion of “Japanese neo-militarism,” yet the CCP continues to peddle this unfounded narrative to divert from its own blatant militaristic drive.
An article published in the English-language Chinese state media publication Global Times titled “Japan-US ‘Keen Sword’ pierces the ‘facade of peace,’” accuses Japan of “attempting to advance its maritime expansionist claims through military deployments and to exert pressure through force to secure control over the seas.”
The article said that “will send the wrong signal, exacerbate tensions in the Taiwan Straits [sic] and the East China Sea, and undermine regional peace and stability.”
The psychological projection of the CCP’s own intent is astonishing.
The article also contends that, during World War II, Japan “forged the Axis bloc with Germany and Italy; today, it leans on the Japan-US alliance alongside participating NATO nations,” attempting to tie Japan’s strategy with fascists, and to drive a wedge between the US and Japan.
For Taiwanese not to fall for this disinformation, they must first understand it for what it is. Then it is possible to discount it or push back against it.
However, more can be done.
Deterrence messaging is not just for Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and the PLA’s military planners, it is for the Chinese public, too. Chinese must be made to understand the cost of aggression in the Taiwan Strait and that it can be avoided if their government draws back from its destabilizing militarism and agrees to come to the table with the elected representatives of Taiwan’s government, without preconditions, and with the understanding that it would need to compromise on its red lines.
The most troubling message coming out of Washington for Taipei is not any single statement but the cumulative effect of a series of signals suggesting that US President Donald Trump is rethinking Taiwan’s strategic value while viewing the US-China relationship through the lens of a transactional great-power bargain. The danger behind Trump’s new softness toward Beijing is a potential US-China bargain that undermines Taiwan’s core interests. During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) recent state visit to Washington, Trump and Xi appeared to rewrite the history of World War II. In a Sept. 25 fact sheet on Xi’s visit, the White House said,

CDC warns storm raises the risk of some diseases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:42 UTC
01:43:42 KST

Strong wind and heavy rain brought by Typhoon Champi increases the risk of some diseases, so people should take protective actions during cleanup activities, CDC Deputy Director-General and spokesman Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said yesterday.
Wind and heavy rain can disrupt soil and sediment, stirring up pathogens and causing them to spread into the environment, increasing the risk of contracting diseases such as melioidosis, leptospirosis and tetanus, Lin said.
Melioidosis is an infectious disease caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, bacteria found in tropical and subtropical soil and surface water, he said.
Photo: CNA
The bacteria can be transmitted through cuts or abrasions exposed to contaminated soil or water, breathing in dust or water droplets, or consuming contaminated water or food, especially during typhoons or flooding after typhoons, he said.
Leptospirosis is a bacterial infection caused by Leptospira bacteria, which spreads from infected animals to humans through wounds or mucous membranes coming into direct contact with contaminated water, soil or animal urine, as well as consuming contaminated water or food, he said.
Elderly people and people with chronic medical conditions, including diabetes and liver disease, have increased risk of severe melioidosis infection, which can cause pneumonia, sepsis or septic shock, Lin said.
People who frequently come into contact with wastewater, wildlife, aquaculture or livestock, as well as veterinarians and others who work with animals, and people who live or work in areas with severe rodent infestations are the main groups susceptible to leptospirosis, he said.
However, following a typhoon, torrential rain and flooding, the pathogens are easily flushed in large quantities onto the ground and into standing water, so people with open skin wounds who walk through water without proper protection are susceptible to the two diseases, he added.
Standing water after heavy rain is an ideal breeding ground for mosquitoes, increasing the risk of vector-borne infectious diseases such as dengue fever, Lin said, adding that people should also pay close attention to food hygiene after a typhoon to prevent gastrointestinal infections.
The CDC urges people to wear appropriate protective gear when cleaning and restoring their living environment after a typhoon or flooding, thoroughly clean and tidy the surroundings before and after a storm to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, do not consume water or food that has spoiled or been contaminated, and thoroughly clean and disinfect the home environment, he said.
Protective gear includes long waterproof boots, thick waterproof rubber gloves, medical masks, and protective eyewear or face shields, he said, adding that before cleaning up, people who have open wounds should dress and bandage them, and strictly avoid direct contact with contaminated water or mud.
The CDC recommends using bleach for environmental cleaning and disinfection, he said.
Wipe flood-affected surfaces with bleach diluted 1:100 with water, disinfect kitchenware and tableware with boiling water, or a solution of 40ml of bleach and 10 liters of water, then thoroughly rinse them with clean water before use, Lin said.
People should also wash their hands thoroughly with soap to eliminate pathogens, he said, adding that if they experience fever, headache, muscle soreness, diarrhea or jaundice after contact with floodwater, they should see a doctor immediately and inform the doctor about their exposure to floodwater.

Brewers’ Misiorowski sets pitch record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:41 UTC
01:43:41 KST

Jacob Misiorowski stepped on the mound for a World Series debut like no other.
“I had so much adrenaline built up,” he said.
He threw a pitch the likes of which had never been seen in the Fall Classic.
Photo: AP
The Miz broke the World Series velocity record with his very first delivery, a 103.5mph (166.6kph) fastball to the Tampa Bay Rays’ Yandy Diaz that was taken high out of the strike zone for a ball. He allowed one run over five innings to get his first postseason win as a starter, helping the Milwaukee Brewers to a 3-2 victory in Friday night’s opener.
“I don’t even know how to tell you how I felt,” the 24-year-old right-hander said a half-hour after the end of a crazy ninth inning, prolonged by a game-extending video review. “I still don’t know how I felt. I feel like I’m still trying to take everything in and understand what happened.”
Misiorowski gave up four hits and one walk, striking out a season-low three.
Aroldis Chapman of the Chicago Cubs had the previous mark for fastest Series pitch at 103.2mph in the ninth inning of Game 2 in 2016, an offering that resulted in a groundout to second by Cleveland’s Coco Crisp. The previous high by a Series starting pitcher since tracking began in 2008 was 101.1mph by the New York Mets’ Noah Syndergaard to Kansas City’s Ben Zobrist that was taken for a ball in the first inning of Game 3 in 2015.
Miz reached 100mph with 38 pitches, topping the previous Series high of 24 by Chapman in Game 5 of 2016. The most by a starting pitcher in the Series had been six by Tampa Bay’s Tyler Glasnow in the 2020 opener against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Tampa Bay scored in the fourth when Jonathan Aranda walked, took third on Junior Caminero’s double over center fielder Garrett Mitchell and came around on Liam Hicks’ grounder to first baseman Jake Bauers.
Nearing the end of his first full major league season, Misiorowski has reached 100mph with 134 of 260 postseason pitches. However, his spin rate was down, a sign of a season in which he has pitched 188 innings — up from 141 1/3 innings last year. And he got just seven swings and misses, five on his fastball.
Tampa Bay batters fouled off 20 of his 78 pitches and tipped another.
During the regular season, Misiorowski reached 100mph with 1,115 pitches, including a high of 105.5mph to the Chicago Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27.
“What we’re used to seeing in the regular season was Miz just mow through people and have two strikeouts an inning. That’s unrealistic,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. “This is the best team in the American League.”
Miz’s first pitch was so fast the scoreboard at American Family Field could not keep up, flashing 103.4mph— one-tenth of a mile less than it registered on MLB’s Statcast system.
“He’s such a special pitcher,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I felt like for him to be out of the game at five innings, there’s a small win in that.”
Misiorowski threw fastballs on 10 of his first 12 pitches, then mixed in more offspeed stuff. In all he tossed 48 fastballs, 17 cutters, seven sliders and six curveballs.
Miz finished with 30 pitches at 101mph or higher, 11 of 102mph or more and three at over 103mph.
Warming up in the bullpen, he could not take in the introductions before Milwaukee’s first World Series game in 44 years. He thought about how far he had come, how he was at Double-A Biloxi two years ago.
“It was crazy,” he said. “It’s everything I dreamed of.”

Three arms programs facing delays: MND
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:37 UTC
01:43:37 KST

Three of Taiwan’s 24 US arms procurement programs are facing delays: the purchase of MK-48 heavyweight torpedoes, AGM-154C Joint Standoff Weapons and F-16V Block 70 jets, the Ministry of National Defense (MND) said in a report submitted to the Legislative Yuan.
Of the 24 ongoing procurement programs, 21 were progressing as scheduled, the report said.
The military planned to procure 24 MK-48 heavyweight submarine-launched torpedoes for combat use and four for training, at a total cost of NT$5.46 billion (US$167.96 million).
Photo: Hotli Simanjuntak, EPA
All the torpedoes were scheduled to be delivered by this year, but supply chain disruptions and the need to restart production lines had led to repeated delays.
The latest schedule calls for all the torpedoes to be delivered by 2028, the ministry said.
Taiwan also procured AGM-154C missiles under the F-16A/B performance upgrade program, known as the Feng Chan project, but the US had to restart production lines, source materials and resolve system integration issues as Taiwan had opted for the latest version of the missiles, it said.
The delays have pushed the completion of missile deliveries to 2028, it added.
The upgrades to Taiwan’s F-16A/B jets were completed in 2023, the ministry said.
Lastly, the procurement 66 F-16V Block 70 jets, for which NT$247.23 billion was allocated between 2020 and this year, is also delayed.
All 66 aircraft were scheduled to be delivered this year, but the relocation and restart of the production line, along with supply chain disruptions, have put the deliveries at risk, the ministry said.
The first two aircraft arrived at the air force’s Chihhang Base in Taitung on Oct. 2, and the remaining jets are to be flown to Taiwan in batches after preparations are completed, it said.
Other procurement programs have made progress, with all M1A2T tanks, Switchblade 300 drones and airborne operations parachute equipment scheduled under to be delivered this year, the ministry said
Deliveries of third-generation land-based communications systems, Stinger man-portable air defense systems, Harpoon coastal defense systems, MS-110 reconnaissance pods and MQ-9B drones are also expected to continue this year, the ministry added.
The third-generation land-based communications system program runs from 2020 to 2029, with more than NT$8.7 billion allocated. The procurement covers 154 communications nodes, 24 relay systems and eight network management centers.
Equipment is being delivered in batches, and the program is expected to be completed in 2029, it said.
The Patriot II system upgrade and Patriot III procurement program runs from 2007 to next year, with more than NT$179.1 billion allocated, the ministry said.
The procurement includes upgrades to three Patriot II missile system units, six Patriot III missile system units and 102 extended-range Patriot III missiles, it said.

Taiwan plans to build rare earths plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:37 UTC
01:43:37 KST

The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) plans to build a rare-earth demonstration plant that could meet half the nation’s needs by the end of 2030, as Chinese export controls heighten concerns over industrial supply chains, the institute president said.
In the planning stage, the facility aims to produce 500 tonnes of rare earths annually, ITRI president Chang Pei-zen (張培仁) said in a recent interview.
Construction is targeted for completion by the end of 2028, followed by work to refine production processes and reach the planned output.
Photo: Reuters
The ITRI intends to build the plant in an industrial park to facilitate its eventual transfer to a private company. Funding would need to be budgeted by the National Science and Technology Council, while commercial arrangements, including possible government price guarantees for investors, remain under discussion, Chang said.
Taiwan’s demand for rare earths is relatively small, but the materials are indispensable, he said, adding that the Ministry of Economic Affairs hopes to develop a domestic supply chain and expand production capacity to address concerns about export restrictions.
China’s controls have highlighted risks extending beyond the supply of raw materials to components used in industrial equipment.
Reuters on Thursday reported that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) was exploring alternatives to rare earth components in factory equipment to reduce the risk of disruptions at its advanced chip plants.
TSMC did not comment.
Rare earth magnets are used in motors that move parts in industrial machinery, including equipment in highly automated semiconductor factories, Reuters said.
Supply restrictions could affect manufacturers even when rare earths are not incorporated directly into their finished products.
The ITRI already operates an experimental rare earth production line, but its annual output is only about 5 tonnes, Chang said.
The proposed plant’s target would represent a 100-fold increase.
Equipment at ITRI’s headquarters in Hsinchu County handles rare earth separation and conversion into metals, while some equipment for making high-end magnets is at its Southern Region Campus in Tainan, Chang said.
Rare earth processing is technically challenging, as different elements have very similar properties, making them difficult to separate, he said.
Developing and fine-tuning the separation process can involve hundreds or even thousands of stages and requires substantial experience, Chang said.
The institute aims to refine its production processes by the end of 2030 as it works toward the annual output target. Alongside the technical work, further discussions will be needed on how to provide prospective private investors with sufficient assurances to participate, he said.
