====================================================================================================

Ancient wheat, modern revival: Türkiye reclaims agricultural heritage through heirloom seeds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
23:16:24 CST
00:16:24 KST

ANKARA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- A hundred years ago, Hatice Alkan kept a sack of wheat seeds in her dowry chest, a traditional blessing of abundance and prosperity.
Alkan raised children, grew old, but forgot the seeds. She would never have imagined that her great-grandson would plant them and help revive a traditional wheat variety known as "red wheat" a century later, and that this would also spur a wider effort to recover and cultivate Türkiye's ancestral seeds that have fallen out of use in modern agriculture.
Across the Anatolia peninsula, farmers, researchers and local institutions have worked to recover crop varieties that may have been displaced by alternatives offering higher yields, more uniform growth and easier harvesting.
Beyond their agricultural value, these heirloom varieties can preserve genetic diversity and traits shaped by generations of cultivation under specific environmental conditions.
In northeastern Türkiye, one such crop is Kavilca, an ancient wheat variety traditionally grown in the provinces of Kars and Ardahan. The region's harsh continental climate, marked by some of the coldest winter temperatures in Türkiye, has helped shape local agricultural practices.
Kavilca is valued for its adaptation to these conditions, making its continued cultivation significant for both regional farming heritage and the conservation of traditional crop varieties.
In 2017, Mirasimiz Yerel Tohum Project, or "Our Heritage, Local Seeds," was launched as a national initiative under the auspices of Emine Erdogan, wife of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry.
Its collection efforts seek out seeds kept in household chests and wrapped in cloth, echoing traditional practices in Turkish brides' dowry chests.
Once collected, seeds can be identified, conserved in seed banks, multiplied, and studied for potential use in agricultural research and breeding. Some varieties may subsequently be registered or made available for wider cultivation, linking household preservation practices with more systematic efforts to protect Türkiye's agricultural genetic resources.
Meanwhile, the Turkish government also helps farmers to reduce the financial burden of adopting traditional varieties.
In 2021, 56 tonnes of kavilca seeds were distributed to 160 producers in Kars and Ardahan to expand cultivation. The farmers received a grant subsidy to cover 75 percent of eligible costs, as an incentive to cultivate a crop that might otherwise remain marginal.
At the Ataturk Agricultural Research Farm, operated by the Ankara Metropolitan Municipality, 45 local seed varieties and cultivars have achieved genetic and developmental stability after three years of selection and cultivation.
Products grown from heirloom seeds, including the traditional Ayas tomato and Ankara melon, have reached modern supermarket shelves, offering a potential route from conservation to commercial production.
Agricultural engineer Fatma Zehra Mutlu told reporters that the seeds would be distributed free of charge to local farmers, where they could complete their growing cycles under natural conditions.
Meanwhile, more than 1,500 indigenous seed samples were collected nationwide between 2020 and 2022 and stored in the national seed gene bank, according to reported figures. The government has also pursued the certification and registration of native varieties to support their formal market circulation.
Türkiye was updating its National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan to align with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the international roadmap adopted in 2022 to halt and reverse biodiversity loss, said Ibrahim Yumakli, Türkiye's minister of agriculture and forestry, last Friday at the Leaders' Summit of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia.
Describing the protection of biodiversity as a responsibility to future generations, the minister said Türkiye hopes to use the upcoming COP31 climate conference in Antalya to help translate climate commitments into concrete action and strengthen connections among climate policy, biodiversity conservation, land, and food security. Across China: Climbing Hainan gibbon population demonstrates China's environmental protection efforts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
23:16:10 CST
00:16:10 KST

Hainan gibbons are seen in Bawangling, part of the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park, in south China's Hainan Province, May 28, 2026. (Photo by Li Wenyong/Xinhua)
HAIKOU, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Before the morning mist fully lifts, the clear calls of Hainan gibbons already echo through the valleys of Bawangling, part of the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park in south China's Hainan Province.
The tropical rainforest in central Hainan is China's most concentrated, best-preserved, and largest contiguous continental-island-type tropical rainforest, and it forms an important part of the world's tropical rainforest system. Established in 2021, the national park covers about 4,269 square kilometers.
According to the park administration, 91 new wildlife and plant species have been discovered in the past five years, and more than 95 percent of Hainan's primary forest and over 55 percent of its natural forest have been effectively protected.
As the world's most endangered gibbon, the Hainan gibbons have long been the rainforest's "top star," with their swinging figures through the canopy the most direct proof of improving ecology in Hainan and also China at large.
Listed as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the Hainan gibbon once teetered on the brink of extinction, with fewer than 10 individuals remaining in just two groups. The Bawangling area is the species' only known habitat.
The gibbons are back in the spotlight as Saturday marks International Gibbon Day.
Data from the National Forestry and Grassland Administration showed that the population of Hainan's resident gibbons has increased to 44 in seven groups, making it the only gibbon species in the world with a continuously growing population.
Hainan gibbons have long arms and oval faces. The apes are gentle by nature and have unique calls. They feed mainly on ripe berries, tender leaves and twigs, and flower buds, and sometimes also eat honey, insects and bird eggs. Adult males have black fur, while females have golden fur. Females give birth to only one baby gibbon every two to three years.
In recent years, Hainan has stepped up efforts to improve and expand the gibbons' habitat. Measures include relocating residents from core protected areas, restoring degraded ecosystems and building ecological corridors.
Local authorities have also set up professional monitoring teams to conduct on-site monitoring and track the population through surveys. In addition, Hainan's forestry authorities have also established a global think tank for the national park, forming a joint global research mechanism.
Chen Qing, a forest worker involved in gibbon monitoring, has spent years observing the primates through binoculars, photographing them and recording their movements and behavior in a notebook.
Chen has also joined forest protection efforts organized by the Hainan forestry authorities and civil society organizations, planting fruit trees and building rope bridges for the gibbons.
"When we were short-handed, I brought my family members to the front line," Chen said. "We have restored and improved a large area of their habitat."
The gibbons' growing population reflects China's broader efforts to protect its natural environment, authorities said.
Fu Mingkai, a local guide, said the rainforest is a globally important gene pool of germplasm resources and home to many plants and animals unique to Hainan.
"For example, the Hainan gibbon and the Hainan peacock pheasant, both of which have very high requirements for their habitat, have been found here," he said.
Their presence and population recovery show that the rainforest is healthy and full of vitality, he added.
"Thanks to strict protection in recent years, the vegetation has recovered and biodiversity in the rainforest is improving," Fu said.
"The rainforest is the Hainan gibbon's home, and it is my home too," Chen said. "I am sure that one day there will be more gibbons singing songs in the morning to awaken the primeval tropical rainforest." ■
A Hainan gibbon is seen in Bawangling, part of the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park, in south China's Hainan Province, May 28, 2026. (Photo by Li Wenyong/Xinhua)

Democrats want to kill Trump’s diesel deal. Working Americans will pay the price

For a party that claims to champion working Americans, this is a peculiar way of demonstrating its concern.
Diesel is the lifeblood of the American economy. It powers the trucks that carry food to supermarkets, the tractors that harvest crops, the machinery that builds homes and roads, and the locomotives that move freight across the vast country.
Yet the people who depend on it have too often been treated as an afterthought by the Washington establishment. They live and work in the industrial towns, farming communities and sprawling rural counties that coastal political elites dismiss as flyover country.
Just recall Hillary Clinton’s infamous 2016 description of millions of Trump supporters as a “basket of deplorables” – a perfect crystallization of the contempt that many ordinary Americans felt was directed at them by the Democrats.
A decade later, that perception is unlikely to be helped by the Democratic lawmakers’ threats to investigate businesses for participating in an arrangement intended to bring additional fuel to the market.
The timing makes those threats extra galling. America is facing an energy crunch aggravated by the Trump administration’s own military campaign against Iran. There is no reason to pretend otherwise. Yes, the president’s decisions helped disrupt global energy markets, and Americans are entitled to demand answers about their consequences.
But recognizing that responsibility does not mean opposing every subsequent attempt to alleviate the damage.
Trump’s decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel represents an effort to increase available supplies at a time when the market desperately needs relief. It is a pragmatic response to an immediate economic problem, whatever one thinks of the circumstances that created it.
And now Democrats are determined to make that response costly for the companies willing to participate.
Congress has every right to examine whether the administration acted within its legal authority. But threatening private businesses with investigations for engaging in transactions authorized by the federal government is another matter entirely. If those companies comply with the law, why should they have to fear becoming targets of a future congressional majority?
The actual volume of Russian diesel involved is almost beside the point. Moscow initially pledged to release some 300,000 metric tons of diesel, with further shipments promised in the following months – a modest quantity compared to America’s enormous fuel consumption.
But that’s not what the markets will be reacting to. They react to expectations, regulatory certainty and the willingness of businesses to undertake transactions without fearing political retaliation. And now, even a lawful, government-authorized energy deal could expose companies to years of investigations simply because a different party took power.
Just imagine the chilling effect.
Today, the dispute concerns a relatively small quantity of fuel from one supplier. Tomorrow, the same approach could be applied to other commodities, trading partners or commercial arrangements that fall afoul of Washington’s shifting ideological priorities.
In effect, the Democrats want to hold American energy security hostage to domestic political warfare.
And for what? The ostensible objective is to keep pressuring Russia.
For years, Moscow has faced sweeping Western sanctions, restrictions on financial transactions and efforts to shut its energy exports out of international markets. None of this has forced Russia to accept any of the West’s demands.
Russia has shown it can adapt and endure economic pressure. While not entirely painless, sanctions have consistently failed to produce the political outcome their advocates have called and hoped for.
Meanwhile, Moscow has repeatedly signaled that it remains prepared to negotiate to reasonable counterparts that would take Russia’s own security concerns and national interests into account. Whether those positions are acceptable to Washington is a matter for diplomacy – and refusing to talk altogether is not diplomacy.
Trump is willing to acknowledge that Russia remains a major power with which the US must eventually find a workable relationship. It’s the baseline level of recognition of political reality one expects from the leader of a major world power.
What the Democrats are doing is the international-politics equivalent of pressing their hands to their ears and shouting ‘La La La’ at the top of their lungs.
The truck driver paying more at the pump, the farmer counting operating costs for the next season and the small-business owner watching expenses climb have little interest in Washington’s political theater. They want affordable fuel, predictable costs and a government that remembers whom it is supposed to serve.
Threatening investigations to discourage companies from helping supply the American market is not sending the message the Democrats seem to think it’s sending. It suggests that, to them, political obedience matters more than keeping the country running.
And ordinary Americans could once again be left paying the bill.

Report: Netanyahu told diplomats to back Argentina's call for Falklands talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:08:39 UTC
00:08:39 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructed Israeli diplomats to support Argentina's call for negotiations over the future of the Falkland Islands and acknowledge Argentina's historical connection to the territory, The Telegraph reported Saturday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The reported shift in Israel's position follows Britain's decision last month to impose sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. According to The Telegraph, the move reflects growing tensions between Jerusalem and London over Britain's policies toward Israel and the Palestinians.
The Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas, are a British territory in the South Atlantic, roughly 480 kilometers (about 300 miles) east of Argentina's coast. The dispute dates back centuries and culminated in 1982 when the two nations fought a war over the islands. Although Britain won, the Argentinians still claim the islands.
The diplomatic push comes as Israel seeks closer ties with right-leaning governments in South and Central America, while facing growing criticism from traditional European allies over the Gaza war and settler violence in the West Bank.
The change would not amount to formal Israeli recognition of Argentina's sovereignty claim over the islands, but has raised concerns in Britain that Israel could go further if London imposes additional sanctions on settlements, the newspaper reported.
However, an Israeli Embassy spokesman in London, Alex Gandler, denied that Netanyahu had issued such an instruction. Israel's Foreign Ministry also denied the report, saying: "The report is incorrect. There is no change in our position on the issue."
I categorically deny this allegation. No such directive exists.
Israel's Ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, addressed the dispute at a UN session last week, calling for direct negotiations between Britain and Argentina. Sources cited by The Telegraph described his remarks as a significant departure from Israel's previous position, particularly because they acknowledged Argentina's historical connection to the islands.
Danon said Israel recognized the importance Argentina attached to the issue and its efforts to resolve it through diplomatic channels and in accordance with international law. He also called for direct, constructive and practical dialogue and said any progress should take into account relevant historical, legal and human considerations.
One source told The Telegraph that the wording of Danon's statement had been approved at the highest levels of the Israeli government. The source described the intervention as the first time Israel had become involved in the dispute.
The report linked the shift to Israel's close relationship with Argentine President Javier Milei, who has strongly supported Israel throughout the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack. Milei attended Israel's Independence Day celebrations this year, where he lit a ceremonial torch.
Israeli officials cited by The Telegraph also pointed to deteriorating relations with Britain, particularly over the sanctions and critical statements by British leaders. The newspaper reported that the Israeli position could further strain ties amid the dispute over Israel's West Bank policies.
Britain's decision to sanction settlements has brought bilateral relations to their lowest point in decades, following London's recognition of Palestinian statehood last year and its criticism of Israel's conduct in the war in Gaza.
The sanctions announced last month by British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband expanded Britain's human rights sanctions framework to cover violations of international humanitarian law. The measures allow restrictions on individuals and entities involved in settlement construction, expansion and financing.
The new regulations took effect days before the October 19 deadline for bids on a construction tender in the E1 area of the West Bank, east of Jerusalem. Britain and other countries had warned contractors that participating in the tender could expose them to legal and reputational consequences. The planned construction between Jerusalem and the Ma'aleh Adumim settlement is opposed by Western governments because it could sever the territorial contiguity needed for a future Palestinian state.
Britain has also announced plans for a trade ban on settlements, joined by Canada and France. The British government has said the measure could take six to nine months to enter into force because of the legislative process required.
The measures followed Britain's adoption of the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion, which found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful. Separately, the Fourth Geneva Convention prohibits an occupying power from transferring parts of its civilian population into occupied territory.
In response to Britain's moves, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced the closure of the British Consulate in Jerusalem. Seven British diplomats will continue to operate in the city under a reduced diplomatic presence.
At a UN Security Council meeting in February, Sa'ar had invoked the Falklands dispute while accusing Britain of hypocrisy over its opposition to Israeli settlements. Addressing then-British Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper, he argued that Britain's position on Israeli residence in the West Bank contradicted international law and the Balfour Declaration.
"It is our country; it's not 13,000 kilometers from our country, like the Falkland Islands. The Argentinians call it the Malvinas Islands – a dispute you haven't solved with Argentina until today," Sa'ar said.
Despite the political tensions, Israeli government sources told The Telegraph that the two countries continued to cooperate closely on security and hoped to maintain the relationship.
Israel also has practical reasons to stop short of formally endorsing Argentina's claim. Intelligence cooperation with Britain gives Israel an additional channel into the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, while Israeli companies have commercial ties with British firms involved in the Sea Lion oilfield project near the Falklands.
Britain's Foreign Office has not commented on The Telegraph's report.

Beyond Iran’s famous cities: villages that deserve a place on every traveler’s itinerary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:08:09 UTC
00:08:09 KST

Beyond Iran’s famous cities: villages that deserve a place on every traveler’s itinerary
TEHRAN - Iran’s historical cities are renowned for their grand mosques, Persian gardens, traditional bazaars and Silk Road heritage. Yet beyond the familiar destinations of Isfahan, Shiraz and Yazd, to name a few, lies another side of the country: a landscape of mountain villages, ancient mud-brick settlements and rural communities whose traditions offer a different perspective on Iranian life.
Scattered across the country’s mountains, valleys and desert margins, these places reveal the diversity of Iran’s geography, architecture and cultural heritage. Some are easily reached on a day trip from a nearby city, while others require more time and effort to explore. Together, they offer travelers an opportunity to look beyond the country’s best-known attractions and discover the character of its rural regions.
Kandovan, life inside volcanic rock
In northwestern Iran, Kandovan stands out for its unusual architecture. Located near Tabriz, the village is known for its cone-shaped rock formations, in which generations of residents have carved homes and other living spaces.
Often compared with Cappadocia in central Turkey, Kandovan belongs to a small group of settlements where people have continued to inhabit rock-cut dwellings into modern times. Its distinctive landscape, shaped by volcanic activity and centuries of human adaptation, gives the village an appearance unlike that of most Iranian settlements.
Unlike archaeological cave sites preserved primarily as historical attractions, Kandovan remains a living community. Its homes illustrate how residents have adapted traditional building practices to the surrounding geology and climate.
The village is also one of the more accessible rural destinations for travelers visiting Tabriz, making it a convenient introduction to Iran’s countryside.
Palangan, a village climbing the Kordestan’s mountains
In Kordestan province, western Iran, Palangan is celebrated for its stepped architecture and dramatic mountain setting. Traditional houses rise above one another along the slopes, creating a compact settlement that appears to grow out of the surrounding terrain.
The village offers a glimpse into rural Kurdish life, including local food traditions and the close relationship between communities and their natural environment. Its river, mountain scenery and stone-built houses make it a popular destination for visitors from nearby areas.
Local restaurants serving river fish provide an opportunity to sample regional cuisine, while the surrounding hills offer a setting for walking and exploring.
Palangan is among several stepped villages found across the Kurdish mountain regions of western Iran. Although some rural settlements in the area remain relatively difficult to reach, Palangan can be visited from nearby urban centers, including Sanandaj, with onward travel arrangements.
Masuleh, where rooftops become streets
Further north, in Gilan province, Masuleh offers another striking example of architecture adapted to mountainous terrain. Its traditional houses are built along a steep slope, with the roof of one building often serving as a walkway or courtyard for the house above it.
The arrangement gives the village its distinctive stepped appearance and makes pedestrian movement an integral part of its architectural character.
Set amid the mist-covered mountains of northern Iran, Masuleh is known for its humid climate, lush surroundings and frequent clouds that drift through the settlement. Its popularity among domestic travelers means that its streets can become crowded, particularly during busy travel periods.
Nevertheless, walking trails leading into the surrounding mountains offer opportunities to escape the busiest areas and appreciate the landscape. Within the village, rooftops and narrow paths remain important spaces for everyday encounters, reflecting a strong sense of community.
Masuleh is therefore both a scenic destination and an example of how traditional settlements developed in response to steep terrain and local living conditions.
Gazor-Khan, gateway to the Alamut Valley
For travelers interested in history and mountain landscapes, Gazor-Khan in Qazvin province offers a combination of both. The village is best known as the gateway to the ruins of the UNESCO-listed Alamut Castle, a fortress associated with the Nizari Ismaili community, whose members became known in medieval sources as the Assassins.
Perched high above the Alamut Valley, the fortress occupied a strategic position and became an important center of the Nizari Ismaili state. Its history is closely associated with Hassan-i Sabbah, who established his base there in the late 11th century.
The Mongol campaign led by Hulagu Khan resulted in the fortress's capture and destruction in the 13th century. Although much of the original structure has disappeared, the remaining ruins and surrounding mountain scenery continue to attract visitors.
Beyond the historic site, Gazor-Khan is a quiet mountain village surrounded by orchards, including apple, apricot and cherry trees. In spring, flowering trees add color to the landscape, while hiking routes provide opportunities to explore the valley.
The journey requires more planning than a visit to villages close to major cities, but the combination of history, scenery and rural life makes it a rewarding destination.
Abyaneh, a living link to Iran’s past
Located near Kashan, at the foot of Mount Karkas, Abyaneh is among Iran’s best-known historic villages. Its red earthen buildings, wooden balconies, narrow lanes and traditional dress give it a distinctive appearance.
The settlement is often associated with Iran’s pre-Islamic past, although its long history spans multiple periods. Its architecture reflects the use of locally available materials, particularly the red soil that gives the buildings their characteristic color.
Abyaneh is also notable for the preservation of elements of local language and cultural traditions. Some older residents speak a distinctive local dialect, while traditional clothing remains an important part of the village’s cultural identity.
Men have traditionally worn dark coats and loose trousers, while women’s clothing is known for its colorful patterns and white headscarves. These customs provide a visible connection to regional traditions that have endured alongside broader changes in Iranian society.
Abyaneh’s popularity, however, has brought challenges. Visitors can fill its narrow streets, particularly during peak travel periods, and the village can sometimes feel more like an open-air heritage site than an ordinary rural community.
Nain, desert heritage beyond the main tourist routes
Between Yazd and Tehran, Nain offers a quieter encounter with Iran’s desert heritage. Although technically a small town rather than a village, it deserves attention for its historic architecture and relatively understated place on many travel itineraries.
The town is known for its historical Jameh Mosque, an old bazaar, traditional water reservoirs and the remains of Narenj Castle. Together, these structures reflect the architectural and engineering traditions that helped communities survive in Iran’s arid central regions.
Traditional water reservoirs, known as ab-anbars, were designed to store water for use during dry periods. Along with other water-management structures, they demonstrate the importance of adapting settlement patterns and architecture to scarce water resources.
Parts of Nain’s historic fabric have deteriorated, and some old buildings remain in poor condition. Yet the town’s less commercialized atmosphere can offer a different experience from more heavily visited heritage destinations.
Its contrast between historic quarters and newer neighborhoods also reveals how traditional settlements have evolved as residents adapt to contemporary life.
Kharanaq, traces of an ancient Silk Road settlement
Northeast of Yazd, Kharanaq is known for its abandoned mud-brick settlement and atmospheric ruins. The village developed along historic travel routes and is associated with the network of settlements that supported movement across central Iran.
Its old buildings, narrow alleys and earthen walls form a dense architectural landscape. Some structures are believed to date back many centuries, although the history of individual buildings varies.
Walking through the abandoned quarter offers a sense of how communities once organized their homes and passageways in a desert environment. From elevated points, visitors can see the settlement against a backdrop of surrounding mountains and open terrain.
The ruins are also vulnerable. Weathering, erosion and uncontrolled visitor access can accelerate the deterioration of fragile earthen structures. Exploring the area responsibly means avoiding unstable buildings, staying on established paths where possible and respecting any restricted areas.
Kharanaq can be combined with visits to Meybod and the Zoroastrian pilgrimage site of Chak Chak, making it a possible addition to a wider itinerary from Yazd.
Meybod, desert architecture and ingenious design
Meybod, another historical settlement near Yazd, offers a broader view of the architectural traditions of Iran’s central desert. Although it is a town rather than a village, its historic structures make it a worthwhile stop for travelers interested in the region’s cultural heritage.
One of its principal attractions is Narin Castle, a large earthen fortress whose origins extend back into antiquity. The town also preserves traditional water reservoirs and a historic pigeon house.
Pigeon houses were constructed to shelter birds and collect their droppings, which were used as agricultural fertilizer. Their design reflects the resourcefulness of communities that relied on locally available materials and developed practical solutions to meet everyday needs.
The pigeon house in Meybod is among the notable surviving examples of this building tradition in Iran.
Together, the castle, water-storage structures and pigeon house illustrate how architecture in the desert served practical purposes while also becoming part of the region’s distinctive cultural landscape.
Why Iran’s rural destinations matter
Exploring Iran’s villages and smaller historic settlements offers more than a change of scenery. These places reveal how people have adapted to different environments, from the volcanic formations of the northwest to the steep mountains of Kordestan and the water-scarce landscapes of the central plateau.
Their architecture reflects local responses to climate, geology and available resources. Their languages, clothing, food and customs also demonstrate the country’s regional and ethnic diversity.
For travelers whose itineraries focus on Iran’s famous cities, adding even one or two rural destinations can broaden their understanding of the country.

Netanyahu says Israel mulling over crypto ahead of possible sanctions
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he is exploring the use of cryptocurrency to circumvent potential financial sanctions on Israel, drawing criticism from opposition figures who said it would turn the Jewish state into an economic pariah like Iran.
“We need to prepare ways to evade banking sanctions through an alternative economic system,” Netanyahu said in an interview with Israel’s Channel 10. “You know what that means – the currencies that can bypass them. I’m working on that too.” Asked whether he meant crypto, the Prime Minister said: “Very correct.”
Netanyahu was speaking ahead of the Oct 27 election, where he faces a strong challenge from former general Gadi Eisenkot.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said the Prime Minister’s proposal for evading potential sanctions “belongs to countries like Iran, Russia, and Venezuela – nations whose banks are cut off from the world, whose companies cannot accept payments, and whose young people are fleeing”.
“That’s his vision,” Lapid added in a post on social media platform X.
In September, 12 major countries, led by Britain, pledged coordinated measures against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the moves would also cover individuals and companies providing financing, construction and other services to the settlements.
That raised fears of sanctions on Israeli banks that could rattle the tech-export-driven economy.
“The concern is that foreign banks will cease providing correspondent services to their Israeli counterparts, effectively severing Israel’s ability to conduct international economic activity,” said Yair Avidan, a former banking supervisor at the Bank of Israel.
Netanyahu “is finally admitting that Israel faces a real danger of diplomatic isolation and economic sanctions, yet instead of explaining how he intends to prevent them, he is already talking about preparing a ‘sanctions-bypassing economy’”, said former finance minister Avigdor Liberman, leader of Israel Beytenu, an opposition party. He vowed to “break Israel out of diplomatic isolation and eliminate the threat of sanctions” if the opposition takes power.
In the interview, Netanyahu also warned that decades of US military aid would end, forcing Israel to finance its defence on its own.
“If you think we will continue receiving what I secured twice – tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defence budget – you’d better prepare yourselves and get used to the idea that this will not continue,” he said. “That is because America has changed, not because Israel has changed. It will end. It is only a matter of time.”
Netanyahu said Israel has two more years with US President Donald Trump, but must prepare for a less favourable Washington after he leaves power.
The US and Israel have agreed a memorandum of understanding which runs through 2028 and provides US$3.8 billion (S$4.9 billion) annually, largely for military procurement from the US.
Washington extended a supplement of at least US$15 billion during three years of war triggered by Hamas’ October 2023 attack on Israel, which claimed the lives of 1,200 Israelis.
Netanyahu said Israel could afford higher defence spending after robust growth, despite three years of war. “For years, we kept defence spending under control to encourage economic growth,” he said. “Now the economy must support defence, because without security, there will be no economy.” BLOOMBERG

Review under way on array that detects nuclear tests
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:00:02 BST
00:00:02 KST

An independent review has been commissioned into ways of reducing the ground vibration reaching the Eskdalemuir seismic array, the installation that gives Britain its contribution to global nuclear test detection, and it covers putting sensors down boreholes and processing the signal differently, according to answers given in Parliament.
Luke Akehurst, the Labour member for North Durham, put four questions to the Ministry of Defence on the array, its monitoring equipment and the restrictions it places on wind farm development nearby.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Monitoring equipment at the Eskdalemuir Seismometer Array is continually reviewed to ensure it meets national requirements and the requirements of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test-Ban Treaty Organisation International Monitoring System.
“There is currently an ongoing independent review of mitigation proposals for reduction of seismic ground vibration received at the Eskdalemuir seismic array and the effect on the detection capability of the array, commissioned by the Ministry of Defence and Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. This includes a review of borehole emplacement and digital signal processing approaches.”
Asked when the science behind the restrictions on wind energy development around the array was last independently reviewed, Pollard said: “The current methodology used to assess the impact of wind turbines on the Array’s ability to detect underground seismic events has been developed using specialist scientific advice and remains the basis for safeguarding decisions. The methodology itself was retained as part of the revised safeguarding approach published in March 2026 following public consultation.”
On whether upgrading the array could allow more onshore wind to be built, Pollard said: “The Ministry of Defence (MOD) has worked closely with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNEZ) over onshore wind deployment in the vicinity of the Eskdalemuir Seismic Array, which supports the United Kingdom’s obligations under the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. As part of this work, the MOD supported experimental testing of alternative technologies and has considered assessments undertaken by specialist technical advisers and independent seismology experts.
“DESNZ has recently consulted on a revised approach to managing onshore wind turbine interference in the vicinity of the Array. The MOD and DESNZ have also commissioned an independent scientific review of alternative technological solutions.
“Previously, evidence made available to the Department has not demonstrated that proposed alternative technological solutions provide viable mitigation for operational use. The consultation responses and independent scientific review are currently being considered and DESNZ will publish a government response reflecting the outcome of both processes soon.”
Eskdalemuir sits in Dumfriesshire and feeds the International Monitoring System run by the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organisation in Vienna, which watches for the seismic signature of an underground nuclear explosion anywhere in the world. Turbine blades and towers transmit vibration into the ground, and that noise competes with the signals the array is there to hear. A safeguarding zone restricts development around the site, and that zone has become contested as onshore wind expands across southern Scotland.

Congress alleged that crores of voters across the country had been unfairly deprived of their voting rights due to large-scale deletions and discrepancies in electoral rolls.
NEW DELHI: The Congress will hold marches, conduct door-to-door visits and organise awareness meetings to address alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. The party will also ensure all eligible citizens are registered by the end of December, senior party leader and former Union minister Bharatsinh Solanki said on Saturday.Congress plans to appoint booth-level agents to verify voter lists and flag discrepancies to election authorities.Addressing a press conference, Solanki, an All India Congress Committee (AICC) observer, said the campaign would cover rural and remote areas as well as urban centres. It aims to put a special focus on disadvantaged communities and young voters. The party will distribute pamphlets and hold meetings to raise awareness about the issue, he added.Solanki alleged that crores of voters across the country had been unfairly deprived of their voting rights due to large-scale deletions and discrepancies in electoral rolls. He accused the Centre and the Election Commission of allowing electoral procedures to be misused."The country's democracy and Constitution are under threat amid rising inflation, unemployment and corruption. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi have launched a nationwide campaign to raise awareness about electoral malpractices," he said.
Congress to appoint booth-level agents
As part of the campaign, the Congress will appoint a booth level agent-2 (BLA-2) at every polling booth to work alongside booth level officers (BLOs) and verify electoral rolls through door-to-door visits, Solanki said.
The party will submit complaints to the relevant authorities over discrepancies and, if necessary, approach district election officials, the state election machinery and the Supreme Court, he added.
Solanki flags discrepancies in Latur

How French presidential hopefuls turn unrest into campaign ammo – RT reports

The unrest came ahead of the French presidential election scheduled for the spring of 2027, in which Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term. His potential successors, however, have scrambled to use the protests to score votes.
Le Pen has urged a tougher crackdown on rioters to restore order. “Our country is caught in a vice, if not held hostage, between violence and powerlessness,” Le Pen said, pledging support for police and demanding tougher penalties for rioters. National Rally president Jordan Bardella blamed far-left militants and criminals from the suburbs for the unrest, proposing to suspend family benefits for repeat offenders and make vandals pay for damage.

While Attal insisted that the priority should be the defense of people and property, Philippe called for the “reestablishment of the authority of the state, the punishment of looters and vandals, as well as a detailed method for restoring discussion with high school students and trade union organizations.”
Recent polls show Le Pen – who has long ridden a wave of public discontent over immigration, crime, and the rising cost of living – holding a commanding lead over her rivals ahead of the 2027 election. An OpinionWay survey published on Thursday put her at 36% in the first round, compared to 16% for Melenchon, and 12% for Philippe. A separate Ifop-Fiducial poll conducted after the October 17 unrest also placed Le Pen ahead in every hypothetical second-round matchup, including 56% against Philippe and 68% against Melenchon.

Fire destroys Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain retreat
The Eagle’s Nest mountainous retreat built for Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler in the Bavarian Alps has been devastated by a blaze, the German police have said.
The former tea house for the leader of the Third Reich, which was constructed on the peak of the Obersalzberg in southern Germany in 1938, sits at an altitude of 1,834 meters (6,000 feet).
A fire alarm at the Eagle’s Nest went off on Friday evening, and it was completely engulfed in flames by the time emergency services arrived, the police said.
The high elevation complicated the work of some 200 fire fighters, who were only able to extinguish the blaze on Saturday morning, they added.
“It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved,” a police spokesperson told Bild tabloid.
The police said that a suspect had been arrested in connection with the fire, but revealed no further details.
According to Bild, the detained person was a motorcyclist whom the officers encountered on their way to the burning retreat, but his involvement in the case currently remains unclear. Investigators believe arson caused the fire, the paper’s sources claimed.
Following reports of the blaze, the Bavarian authorities announced plans to rebuild the structure, Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said.
“We will not allow ruins to remain there,” DPA quoted him as saying.
The Eagle’s Nest was one of the few historic building from Hitler’s era to avoid damage by bombing during the World War II. The retreat hosted a museum and a restaurant since the 1950s, becoming a popular tourist destination. It was preserved as “a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship,” according to its website.

Thousands protest in Turkey over journalists’ arrests, media shutdowns
ISTANBUL – Thousands rallied in Istanbul and Ankara on Oct 24 against what they described as growing pressure on journalists in Turkey, including arrests, media shutdowns and the appointment of state administrators.
“Enough. We can no longer breathe,” shouted marchers in the crowds, which were composed mainly of journalists, rights groups and opposition party representatives.
Press freedom has been increasingly constrained in Turkey since a failed coup attempt in 2016, with sweeping prosecutions and digital censorship.
But recent weeks have seen what rights advocates say is mounting pressure on independent journalism.
Eleven journalists have been jailed in the past two months and several media outlets shut down, according to the Turkish Journalists’ Union.
At least 3,000 people gathered on the Asian side of Istanbul, according to police.
They held up photos of jailed journalists, chanting: “We will not be silenced. Enough is enough!” and “We will not bow to pressure”.
Earlier in October, police raided Turkey’s most-watched news channel, Halk TV, halting broadcasts and installing a government-appointed administrator.
The move was the latest against media outlets seen as critical of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his government.
It followed the closure of the website and social media accounts belonging to leading digital news outlet T24 over what authorities described as “LGBT propaganda”.
“This gathering is not simply about standing up for journalists,” veteran journalist Zafer Arapkirli told AFP after the Istanbul protest.
“It is also about defending respect for society’s right to access information and news through journalists and independent media,” said the columnist for the BirGun daily.
Intimidation
For Arapkirli – who himself faces lawsuits – the more intense the pressure becomes, the stronger the response and the determination to stand against it must be.
“What the regime wants is to intimidate, silence and frighten society through such pressure – by arresting individual journalists, seizing media outlets, banning news coverage and blocking access to social media,” he said.
“We must show that we will not allow this to happen.
“We have done so up to now. I believe we are now moving towards demonstrating this determination on a much larger scale.”
In Ankara, at least 3,000 protesters gathered, according to a police count.
They shouted: “No to censorship” and “Freedom for jailed journalists”.
“Today’s protest was important both because it brought journalists together to make their voices heard and because it defended citizens’ right to access information,” Gokcer Tahincioglu, coordinator for the shutdown T24, told AFP in Ankara.
“Journalists are determined to get one message across: we want to practise journalism, and we want to be able to do so freely,” he said.
Praising the solidarity after the now shut T24, Tahincioglu said: “We want to regain the conditions necessary to report freely as soon as possible.” AFP

====================================================================================================

Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:30:01 UTC
23:30:01 KST

A drug from Amgen could give patients with a notoriously aggressive form of lung cancer significantly more time to live when added to an immunotherapy from AstraZeneca, a study found.
Full results from a late-stage trial released Saturday show that adding Amgen's immunotherapy Imdelltra to AstraZeneca's Imfinzi drug slashed the risk of death by 58% in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, a fast-growing disease that has spread beyond the lung where it began.
The drug combination extended their median overall survival to 21.1 months compared with 12.7 months with AstraZeneca's drug alone, the trial found.
That means half of patients in the group that took the combination regimen were alive for at least roughly 21 months. The trial tested the combo as a maintenance therapy in patients who received initial treatment with Imfinzi and chemotherapy, and whose cancer had not progressed.
"I think there are moments in medicine when you see a piece of data that is so profound that it's going to transform the standard of care for patients, and I think, honestly, we're at that moment," said Dr. Paul Burton, Amgen's chief medical officer, in an interview.
The combination "has the potential to take on one of the most aggressive cancers that we deal with today, and almost convert it into a chronic disease," he said, adding that "these data say that's a possibility."
The results also suggest a greater commercial opportunity for Imdelltra, which posted $288 million in sales during the second quarter, up 115% year over year. The drug already generated $627 million in global sales in 2025 and appears to be on its way to becoming a blockbuster medicine, or hitting the $1 billion sales threshold.
Small cell lung cancer remains difficult to treat because, even if chemotherapy initially works well for most patients, the disease often returns or progresses within months, said lead trial investigator Dr. Jacob Sands, who is the associate chief of the Lowe Center for Thoracic Oncology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.
He said immunotherapy has helped a small subset of patients achieve years of disease control, but most have not experienced similarly durable benefits, highlighting the need for better treatments. There are roughly 31,000 new small cell lung cancer cases in the U.S. each year, and an estimated 60% to 70% of those people are diagnosed with extensive-stage disease.
Sands said the benefits in the trial were seen across subgroups of patients, including those whose cancer spread to the brain or liver. Disease that has spread to those organs is associated with poorer treatment outcomes.
He added that with longer-term follow-up data on the patients, the 21-month figure "may evolve further and hopefully will substantially improve," similar to what Amgen saw in a Phase 1 trial on the immunotherapy combination. In that early-stage trial on a smaller number of patients, a long-term follow-up showed the benefit was sustained for years.
Using Imdelltra earlier
Amgen said the findings also suggest that using Imdelltra earlier in a patient's treatment could meaningfully alter the trajectory of the disease. Imdelltra is currently approved for patients whose small cell lung cancer has progressed while they are on, or after, platinum-based chemotherapy.
Researchers specifically tested whether adding Imdelltra could help patients live longer than continuing Imfinzi alone, which is already approved as a first treatment for this type of lung cancer. Amgen said nearly 80% of patients who started taking both drugs were alive at one year compared with 53% receiving Imfinzi alone.
Imdelltra's "big impact" on controlling the disease and ultimately how long people live highlights the importance of including it in first-line maintenance treatment, Sands said. That refers to ongoing therapy given after an initial heavy treatment, such as chemotherapy or surgery.
Burton added that it positions Amgen's drug to be an "indispensable backbone therapy" for small cell lung cancer, regardless of the other immunotherapy that can be paired with it.
Imdelltra binds to DLL3, a protein on cancer cells, and CD3, a protein on T cells, which are a type of immune cell that can kill cancer. By binding to both, Imdelltra brings T cells into close contact with tumor cells, helping the immune system destroy the cancer.
Imfinzi, made by AstraZeneca, is an immunotherapy that blocks a protein called PD-L1, which cancer cells use to evade the immune system. The drugs work together in complementary ways: Imfinzi helps remove the brakes on the immune response, while Imdelltra brings T cells directly to cancer cells and helps activate them to attack the tumor.
The study, which was presented at a major cancer meeting called the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress, did not test whether the combination was better than other first-line treatment approaches.
Still, the findings suggest Amgen's drug could be another option offered to small cell lung cancer patients earlier in their treatment. Kate Brenan, a 44-year-old mother of two from Denver, sees that as a win on its own.
She was diagnosed with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer in early January 2024. Brenan underwent six rounds of a common combination chemotherapy, followed by chest radiation and later whole-brain radiation after the cancer spread.
In September 2024, she started Imdelltra and has had no evidence of disease ever since.
"I think that it's remarkable how quickly things are changing in the world of small cancer treatment options," Brenan told CNBC, adding that Imdelltra potentially becoming an earlier treatment option "can only be a good thing for the patients moving forward, and I'm really excited about that."

Xinhua Commentary: Marking Taiwan Recovery Day with shared resolve to advance China's reunification
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
22:25:02 CST
23:25:02 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- As China prepares to mark the 81st anniversary of its recovery of Taiwan and observe the Taiwan Recovery Day on Oct. 25, the occasion offers an opportunity to revisit a glorious chapter of history, in which people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait jointly resisted foreign aggression, and to draw strength from the past to advance reunification.
China's recovery of Taiwan in 1945 was a hard-won victory in the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression during World War II, and a defining moment in the nation's struggle to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Starting in 1840, China endured a period of immense suffering amid foreign aggression and the decay of feudal rule. Japan's aggression marked some of the darkest chapters in modern Chinese history. Following its war against China in 1894, Japan seized Taiwan and the Penghu Islands in 1895, subjecting Taiwan to five decades of colonial rule.
Faced with both internal turmoil and foreign invasion, the Chinese people valiantly fought against the invaders, ultimately defeating Japanese aggression to safeguard the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
On Oct. 25, 1945, after China's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the broader World Anti-Fascist War, Taiwan was recovered. This historic day, forever etched in the history of the Chinese nation, deserves to be remembered by people on both sides of the Strait.
Throughout the struggles against foreign aggression and for national liberation, Taiwan shared the fate of its motherland China. Patriots in Taiwan resisted Japanese colonial rule through political, military and cultural struggles, with more than 650,000 giving their lives during the five decades of Japanese occupation.
Driven by the conviction that "to save Taiwan, one must first save the motherland," over 50,000 people in Taiwan went across the Strait to join the fight against Japanese aggression, risking their lives to defend the dignity and honor of the Chinese nation.
Historical archives and photographs capture the island's jubilant celebrations when China recovered Taiwan in 1945. Families decorated their homes with lanterns, brought out ancestral tablets, and burned incense to share the good news with their forebears. Residents poured spontaneously into streets to cheer, while the sound of firecrackers rang out into the night.
These memories, forged through bloodshed and sacrifice, testify to the deep-rooted bonds between people in Taiwan and their fellow Chinese on the mainland, as well as the shared destiny of people on both sides of the Strait.
China's recovery of Taiwan was an important outcome of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, and provides compelling evidence that the Chinese government resumed the exercise of sovereignty over Taiwan.
The Cairo Declaration, issued in 1943, stipulates that all territories Japan had stolen from China, including Taiwan and the Penghu Islands, shall be restored to China. The Potsdam Proclamation of 1945 reiterates that "the terms of the Cairo Declaration shall be carried out."
In September 1945, Japan signed the instrument of surrender, pledging to fulfill the obligations set out in the Potsdam Proclamation. On Oct. 25 that year, the Chinese government announced that it was resuming its exercise of sovereignty over Taiwan. A ceremony to accept Japan's surrender in Taiwan Province of the China war theater of the Allied powers was held in Taipei.
From that point forward, China had recovered Taiwan de jure and de facto through a host of documents with international legal effect. Taiwan's status as an inalienable part of the Chinese territory was thereby reaffirmed, and the question of Taiwan's status was resolved.
However, an unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation.
The fact that the two sides of the Taiwan Strait have yet to be fully reunified is a scar left by history on the Chinese nation, but the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed.
Driven by their political interests and secessionist agenda, Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and other secessionist forces have repeatedly claimed that Taiwan's status remains undetermined, distorted historical accounts in textbooks, pursued educational policies that remove Chinese cultural elements, and propagated a separatist narrative in an attempt to sever historical ties across the Strait and mislead younger generations in Taiwan.
Since Lai Ching-te took office in 2024, the DPP authorities have conspicuously avoided mentioning China's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and China's recovery of Taiwan. The DPP authorities have also repeatedly downplayed or whitewashed Japan's colonial rule over Taiwan. Such actions betray the fundamental interests of the Chinese nation.
Achieving national reunification is a responsibility shared by all Chinese people, including people in Taiwan. The establishment of the Taiwan Recovery Day enables people on both sides of the Strait to commemorate this historic moment together.
The Taiwan question originated in a weak and ravaged China, and will be resolved as China achieves national rejuvenation. Commemorating Taiwan's recovery today is an opportunity to draw strength and resolve from the sacrifices of the war and the recovery of lost territory, while reaffirming the determination and confidence to advance national reunification. ■

Moreover, the CEO said the initiative would firm up efforts to build export capacity and complement Ghana's trade fairs by connecting Ghanaian producers with international buyers and improving the visibility of high-quality made-in-Ghana products.
"The Accra Trade House provides a permanent marketplace that complements our trade fairs, buyer-seller engagements, and international market entry programs," he said.
According to him, the trade house would be expanded to some Ghanaian missions abroad to broaden the reach of Made-in-Ghana products.
The maiden Friday Market brought together producers of Ghanaian fabrics, local beverages, leather and wood products, cocoa, shea and coffee derivatives, and fashion products, among others.
Meanwhile, officials familiar with Ghana's foreign trade promotion schedules have told Xinhua that the country is actively preparing to participate in the 2026 China International Import Expo scheduled for November in Shanghai. ■

Protecting minorities: A test for Syria's new political order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:22:24 UTC
23:22:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Protecting minorities: A test for Syria's new political order
Damascus - Almost two years on from the fall of Assad’s regime in 2024, continued violence targeting Syria’s ethnic minorities is placing the country’s post-war recovery under strain as the government struggles to manage persistent sectarian tensions.
Earlier this month, pro-government demonstrators gathered in Kurdish areas of Hasakeh and Raqqa, vandalising Kurdish symbols and calling for the government to take full control of the region.
This comes amid the ongoing integration of the Kurdish-led SDF into the Syrian state.
The unrest followed a series of mob attacks and acts of vandalism targeting Christian homes, vehicles and shops in Al-Suqaylabiyah, a predominantly Greek Orthodox town in Hama province.
These are not isolated incidents. Post-Assad Syria has seen “several minority communities that have feared systemic discrimination and unfair treatment - particularly the Kurdish, Druze and Alawite communities,” Caroline Rose, a senior director at the Soufan Center, tells The New Arab.
Al-Suqaylabiyah has already experienced a previous spate of mob violence over the past year, while Syria continues to witness sectarian killings on an almost daily basis.
The country’s post-war recovery was also blighted by a series of massacres targeting Syria’s Alawite and Druze minorities in 2025.
Syria’s decade-long civil war deepened sectarian hostility. Assad sought to frame the conflict as a sectarian war between Syria’s minority communities and Sunni “Islamists” and “terrorists”.
As the revolution progressed, opposition to Assad became increasingly Islamist and sectarian in nature. During the conflict, communities on all sides were targeted, with many villages and neighbourhoods suffering killings and displacement.
The collapse of the regime saw many displaced communities return to their destroyed homes, in many cases living alongside those they believed had destroyed them in the first place.
While the government has repeatedly moved to clamp down on outbreaks of violence, two years into Syria’s “transitional period”, it has struggled to address many of the underlying grievances that allow disputes to escalate into communal violence.
Rebuilding trust in the security services
It is this legacy of civil war grievances that allows disputes, often rooted in personal conflicts or criminal activity, to escalate into communal violence. The recent violence in Al-Suqaylabiyah began with a fight between two men, one of whom returned to his village to rally a mob.
Although Damascus has made efforts to deploy its security services to quell unrest, in many parts of Syria this does not necessarily create a greater sense of security among local communities.
“Local officials and security chiefs come mainly from the networks that toppled Assad, often recruited for their loyalty. Minority recruitment into the security forces remains limited,” explains Dr Nanar Hawach, an independent expert specialising in Syria, to The New Arab.
“The already few minority recruits mostly hold desk or traffic jobs, and the armed patrols in their areas are often drawn from elsewhere,” he adds.
“As a result, many ethnic minority residents hesitate to report threats to the officers who patrol their streets, who they may not trust.”
Over the past two years, although the government has made significant strides in filling the security vacuum that emerged after the collapse of the regime, the Interior Ministry remains understaffed according to analysts.
One way to address this, alongside the communal sense of distrust, would be to encourage the recruitment and active deployment of security personnel from minority backgrounds, particularly in areas where minorities make up a substantial proportion of the local population.
However, Gregory Waters, an independent researcher and senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, cautions against establishing a system of local communal policing on ethnic or religious lines which he believes in the long run may serve to “solidify sectarian divisions” by clearly demarcating that “this is a Christian town with Christian police, and that is a Sunni town with Sunni police”.
He argues that alongside more personnel, the local security services need to improve their coordination with local communities, in order to be quickly made aware of and pre-emptively halt sectarian mobilisations before they become violent.
However, analysts agree that establishing civil peace requires more than simply securitising the issue.
Achieving a sense of justice
Local disputes have long been common in many of these communities, although they have taken on a more sectarian character in post-Assad Syria because of grievances that emerged during the civil war.
“For many of those people returning home, seeing their hometowns destroyed has a very visceral impact,” says Waters.
He suggests that this sense of grievance manifests as anger stemming from the perception that “the people responsible were let off the hook”. Those affected perceive a lack of genuine transitional justice.
The Syrian government has begun the long and complicated process of trying those responsible for crimes committed during the civil war. In August, Bashar Al-Assad and several senior regime figures were sentenced to death in absentia.
Despite this, many lower-level figures have not yet been arrested. According to Waters, this gives aggrieved communities “an excuse to cause problems”, even when those targeted by retaliatory violence were not actually responsible for the original crimes.
However, many within minority communities are sensitive to perceived state overreach. Genuine arrests linked to transitional justice can also be misrepresented, with such actions “often get[ting] blown up and distorted through misinformation and fake news”, explains Waters.
The arrests “become construed as the government targeting ethnic minorities – which can aggravate these communities further”.
Waters suggests that building genuine civil peace requires more than simply imposing justice. Instead, he argues, there needs to be “a systemic whole-of-sector approach, that brings together local leadership, revolutionary figures, security chiefs, and most importantly, those who are causing the civil disturbances”.
Local governance and the economy
Governance disputes appear to be a driving force behind much of the recent violence in northeast Syria.
The integration of the SDF into the government is “sparking fears amongst Kurdish communities about the loss of Kurdish political autonomy, Kurdish language rights and security control in the region,” says Rose.
“These fears have been exacerbated by increasing fuel prices and the general cost of living, which have also contributed to public demonstrations.”
Meanwhile, Arab communities in the northeast are frustrated by the slow pace of integration. Reflecting long-standing grievances over what they perceive as corruption and discrimination under SDF rule, some want Damascus to take a more direct role in governing the region.
There is an economic dimension to this issue. The risk of violence erupting is heightened by the lack of real livelihoods for young men, and the sense that material support remains scant.
“You have unemployed young men, angry that their homes and workplaces are destroyed with nowhere else to channel their frustration,” says Waters. “These are the types that are sparking incidents.”
Alongside economics, part of the frustration is rooted in the sense that “communities have limited influence over how their areas are governed,” Hawach explains to The New Arab.
“Alongside security officials, local civilian leaders are often recruited from opposition networks. Minority candidates may be viewed with a degree of distrust, particularly Alawites, given their association with the former regime.”
Hawach suggests that the authorities could address these concerns by giving local communities more meaningful decision-making powers. He points to the Ismaili Council in the town of Salamiyah as a key example.
The Ismaili Council, which represents Syria’s Ismaili community, established contact with HTS before the fall of the regime and helped facilitate the city’s handover to advancing opposition forces.
Since then, the council has worked closely with local security chiefs and community leaders to ensure that occasional incidents of violence do not spiral into broader communal conflict.
“Syria could develop these local bodies with genuine authority over local services, public employment and disputes,” suggests Hawach.
Ultimately, ensuring civil peace in Syria will require the Syrian government to not only develop its security architecture but also address the grievances that cause local disputes to escalate.
Without meaningful accountability, economic development and greater local representation, efforts to restore stability risk leaving the underlying causes of communal tension unresolved.
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues

flash forest scatters millions of seeds across canada’s wildfire-damaged landscapes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:15:07 UTC
23:15:07 KST

flash forest scatters millions of seeds across canada’s wildfire-damaged landscapes
biodegradable capsules packed with native seeds and beneficial fungi help restore wildfire-damaged landscapes across northern quebec.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
flash forest plants for life after wildfires
Across the blackened forests of northern Quebec, drones fly above the remains of burned trees, launching small, seed-filled capsules into the earth. Each carries the beginnings of a new tree, packed with ingredients intended to help it grow in damaged soil. The system is developed by Canadian company Flash Forest, which is using aerial technology to replant landscapes devastated by wildfire, including remote areas that are difficult to reach on foot.
The work follows Quebec’s devastating 2023 wildfire season, when around 4.5 million hectares of forest burned across the province. Flash Forest has since expanded its planting operations across Canada. According to its latest impact report, the company planted 686,147 trees across five sites in 2025, covering 429 hectares of burned forest. The technology allows large areas to be seeded quickly while keeping heavy planting equipment off the forest floor.
tiny engineered pods give seeds a place to grow
At the center of Flash Forest’s operation is a biodegradable seed pod designed to support a young tree through its earliest stages of growth. Each capsule contains nutrients, moisture-retaining additives and mycorrhizal fungi, which can help developing roots absorb nutrients from the soil. Customized drones propel the pods directly into the ground, where the seeds can germinate without first spending years growing in a nursery.
The capsules are manufactured to consistent dimensions so they can pass through the drones’ automated feeding mechanisms. Their composition is developed around the needs of the seeds, with materials intended to retain moisture and support early growth. By sowing seeds directly into the landscape, the company also avoids the transplant shock that can affect nursery-grown saplings. Yet even with this engineered starting point, germination remains dependent on the conditions of each planting site.
collecting millions of seeds in northern quebec
Behind the automated planting process is a remarkable effort to gather seeds from the forests themselves. Flash Forest has been working with the Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation to restore areas damaged by the 2023 wildfires, which destroyed wildlife habitats and affected traditional hunting grounds. When northern Quebec faced a shortage of native seeds, the team worked with local partners to collect jack pine cones directly from trees, traveling by snowmobile and climbing through forests in temperatures as low as -30°C.
The winter operation yielded approximately 8.5 million jack pine seeds, which were incorporated into planting pods within five months of collection. For Benny Blacksmith of the Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation, the aerial process offers a way to restore habitats while avoiding further disturbance to the land. He describes the impact of the fires on wildlife, recalling how even small animals disappeared from affected areas, disrupting the food sources of larger species. The community hopes to see native trees such as white birch and black spruce return to the damaged landscape.
the longer process of rebuilding a forest
Flash Forest’s work continues after the drones have finished planting. The company surveys each site to assess existing vegetation before returning to monitor seedling growth. Experimental plots compare the performance of its engineered pods against untreated seeds and areas left to regenerate naturally. Some sites in Quebec have already experienced delayed germination following warmer temperatures and reduced rainfall, with further monitoring planned for fall 2026.
Wildfire is itself part of the natural cycle of boreal forests. Jack pine cones can open in response to heat, releasing seeds onto the exposed ground, although increasingly severe fires and changing climate conditions can interrupt this process. Flash Forest’s technology offers a way to introduce new seeds where that recovery is struggling. The drones can put them into the ground in a matter of seconds. Whether they establish themselves, and what kind of forest eventually grows around them, will become apparent over the years ahead.
project info:
project: Flash Forest automated reforestation
company: Flash Forest | @flashforest.ca
founders: Bryce Jones, Cameron Jones, Angelique Ahlstrom
location: Canada
founded: 2019
project partners: Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation

NEW DELHI: The National Medical Commission (NMC) is considering a revised proposal to rotate heads of departments (HoDs) in medical colleges every five years, instead of the three-year tenure proposed earlier, following feedback from stakeholders.Under the revised proposal, rotation would be restricted to professors, rather than including both professors and eligible associate professors as envisaged in the draft amendment published in May 2025, M K Ramesh, president of the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB), told TOI.Ramesh said the commission had received substantial feedback on the earlier proposal and that valid points raised by stakeholders would be considered. Suggestions included rotation periods of five or 10 years, as well as doing away with mandatory rotation altogether.The original draft amendment to the Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations, 2023, proposed rotating the HoD post every three years among eligible professors and associate professors, based on seniority. Nearly a year and a half after the draft was published, the proposal remains unresolved.
Ramesh said the proposal would need to be taken up afresh and that the revised draft would be moved shortly. Once initiated, the process would be completed within six weeks, he said.He did not confirm whether the NMC would invite stakeholders to comment again on the revised proposal or take a decision based on the feedback already received.The delay had also prompted an RTI application by Dr A N Dattatri, professor and head of the department of pharmacology at Karnataka Medical College and Research Institute, Hubballi, seeking the PGMEB’s detailed note on stakeholder feedback and its views on the proposal. In a reply dated September 16, 2026, the board said the matter was under consideration and declined to disclose the information, citing Section 8(1)(i) of the RTI Act.The proposed change could affect how leadership positions are assigned in medical college departments. The five-year rotation plan remains a proposal and has not yet been formally notified.

US lawmakers plot to derail Trump’s Russian diesel deal
A number of American lawmakers intend to block the Trump administration’s deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel through April and are threatening action against US companies involved in the trade. The bipartisan group is also planning to block the US Treasury from issuing such a waiver in the future.
US President Donald Trump announced the deal earlier this month, as US diesel prices hit a record $6.50+ per gallon in September and prices in parts of California topped $8. Under the waiver, struck just weeks ahead of the impending November midterm elections, Moscow agreed to immediately put 300,000 tons of diesel into the market, and commit to further releases.
The disruption of global energy markets, caused by the Iran war and the Ukraine conflict, has resulted in rising gas prices in the US, further denting the positions of Republicans ahead of the vote. Diesel is the key fuel type extensively used in agriculture and freight; its price affects the cost of virtually all goods, resulting in further cost-of-living issues. Rural communities, smalltime farmers, and truckers are particularly vulnerable to diesel prices spikes.
Senate Democrats are now seeking to investigate the diesel deal, the Washington Post reported on Thursday, citing an unnamed Senate Democratic aide. According to the aide, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee has requested companies involved in the scheme to preserve documents ahead of a possible probe by the panel.
“[The companies] should have liability concerns as well as investigative concerns,” the aide told WaPo.
Further action against the diesel deal has been taken by Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-1), an outspoken hawk, Ukraine backer, and proponent of sanctions against Russia. The proposed legislation, titled the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act of 2026, would effectively block Russian oil imports for good.
The bill would nullify the standing Russian oil waiver, “immediately rendering General License 135 ineffective and prohibiting future waivers or general licenses authorizing the importation of Russian energy products,” as well as strip the Treasury from the ability to expend funds “on agreements that violate the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022,” the legislation that sanctioned Russian energy products, including diesel, in the first place.
Apart from the energy part, the bill also would “reinforce critical intelligence support for Ukraine,” obliging spy agencies to cooperate with Kiev and to “notify congressional intelligence committees within 24 hours of any interruption.”

Dawn of a new era in naval battle: What does the Iranian style bring?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:05:37 UTC
23:05:37 KST

Dawn of a new era in naval battle: What does the Iranian style bring?
October 24, 2026 - 17:35
For decades, American aircraft carriers symbolized Washington’s military might and served as instruments for imposing its will on other nations. However, the 2026 aggression against the Islamic Republic of Iran marked a turning point. Iranian anti-ship missiles targeted the American fleet, forcing it to retreat — a development that brings the end of the U.S. military presence in the region’s waters closer. As the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Sayyid Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, wrote on September 28, 2026: “It will not be long before the Arabian Sea rids itself of them [the aggressor enemy] too.”
