Zelenskyy imposes sanctions on suppliers to Russia’s defense industry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:02:32 EEST
23:02:32 KST

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has signed decrees enacting decisions by the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC) to impose sanctions on Russian entities and individuals. These parties are involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles or supply equipment and components to Russian defense industry enterprises for use in military aircraft, armored vehicles, missile systems, and drones.
Relevant decrees, Nos. 1058/2024 and 1059/2024, are dated October 24 and have been published on the head of state’s official website.
The first sanction list includes 51 individuals and 44 legal entities involved in the manufacture of ballistic missiles—weapons that the Russian Federation uses to attack critical and civilian infrastructure, as well as to shell Ukrainian cities and communities. These entities produce and supply raw materials, equipment, and tools used to create long-range strike systems, including the Iskander, Kalibr, Kh-101, and Kinzhal.
The sanction package specifically targets Russian enterprises that manufacture weaponry, components, and related software, as well as the executives of these companies.
All individuals subject to these sanctions are citizens of the Russian Federation. Of the 44 entities on the first list, 42 are registered in the Russian Federation, while two are registered in the People's Republic of China.
Additionally, sanctions have been imposed on 32 Russian citizens and 35 Russian companies that are part of the production and supply chains for high-precision industrial equipment, tools, components, electronics, and raw materials intended for entities that serve Russia’s defense-industrial complex.
Sanctions have also been imposed on enterprises belonging to the Russian industrial group Rusal—entities that are significant to the aggressor state and involved in the production of military aircraft, armored vehicles, missile systems, drones, and other military hardware.
"We are systematically identifying enterprises involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles and other weaponry, and applying sanctions against them. We are also working to extend these sanctions to other jurisdictions. Taken together, these measures should significantly weaken the capacity of the Russian military-industrial complex to manufacture weapons," noted Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Advisor and Presidential Commissioner for Sanction Policy.

The psychology behind Taylor Swift’s billion-dollar media empire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:00:46 UTC
23:00:46 KST

The intense, one-sided connections fans feel toward pop star Taylor Swift and their fear of missing out on shared cultural moments strongly predict whether they will attend her concerts and watch her films. These predictive links highlight how the psychological need for social belonging drives large-scale consumer behavior, according to a recent study published in Psychology of Popular Media.
A parasocial relationship occurs when an audience member develops a one-sided bond with a media figure, such as a musician, actor, or internet personality. While the celebrity is unaware of the individual fan, the fan experiences genuine emotions and reactions that mimic real-life friendships.
Taylor Swift has cultivated an exceptionally robust parasocial dynamic with her audience over her career. By interacting with followers online and weaving personal details into her music, she has built an environment where fans feel they truly know her. When her Eras Tour launched, it shattered records, selling over two million tickets in a single day. The researchers noted that Swift used the resulting ticketing challenges to align herself with her fans, strengthening their perceived bond.
Such pervasive cultural conversation often triggers a phenomenon known as the fear of missing out, commonly referred to as FoMO. Researchers divide this concept into two distinct categories. Trait fear of missing out is a long-standing personality characteristic where a person generally worries that others are having rewarding experiences without them. State fear of missing out is a temporary, situation-specific anxiety in response to a particular event.
The researchers anchored their investigation in Self-Determination Theory. This psychological framework suggests that human beings are motivated by a fundamental need for relatedness, or the desire to feel connected to others. In the context of entertainment, people might consume specific media to satisfy this need, either by bonding with a celebrity or by joining a community of fellow fans.
Lindsey Conlin Maxwell and Caroline Neese of the University of Southern Mississippi, along with Alec C. Tefertiller of Baylor University, designed the study to see how these psychological elements influenced audience behavior. They used Swift and her wildly popular Eras Tour as an ideal testing ground. The team aimed to determine if long-term personality traits could predict parasocial bonds and if those bonds predicted purchasing tickets for concerts and movies.
To capture these emotions at their peak, the researchers conducted a national survey during the opening weekend of the concert film, “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour,” in October 2023. They recruited 303 adults in the United States using an online task platform. The respondents answered questions designed to measure their baseline personality traits, their current feelings about the movie release, and their perceived relationship with the pop star.
The survey asked participants to rate their agreement with statements about missing out on rewarding experiences in general, capturing their trait-level anxieties. It also asked specific questions about whether they feared others would enjoy watching the concert film more than them, measuring their temporary state of anxiety. Additionally, the questionnaire evaluated the depth of their parasocial relationship with Swift and recorded their actual behaviors regarding concert and movie attendance.
The data revealed that an individual’s general fear of missing out was a strong predictor of their parasocial relationship with Swift. The researchers noted that this long-standing personality trait explained roughly one-third of the variations in how strongly people felt connected to the singer. People who routinely worry about being left out of social experiences appear highly motivated to build imaginary bonds with media figures to alleviate that apprehension.
Both the personality trait and the parasocial relationship predicted concert-related behaviors. As scores on the parasocial relationship scale increased, respondents were nearly twice as likely to have attempted to buy Eras Tour tickets. They were also substantially more likely to have actually attended one of the live stadium shows.
Similar patterns emerged for the concert film. High levels of baseline anxiety about missing out, as well as a strong perceived relationship with Swift, predicted whether someone had already seen the movie during its opening weekend. These factors also predicted whether a person intended to see the film in theaters later or watch it once it became available on streaming platforms.
One of the most notable results involved temporary, event-specific anxiety. The researchers tested whether attending the live concert satisfied fans to the point of reducing their anxiety about the movie release. The data showed the exact opposite pattern.
People who had already attended the live Eras Tour experienced higher levels of temporary anxiety about missing out on the movie than those who had not attended the concert. Attending the concert did not quench the desire to engage with the media event. Going to the live show actually increased the likelihood that someone wanted to see the theatrical release.
The researchers suggest that a parasocial relationship can become so potent that individuals seek repeated positive experiences with the celebrity to maintain the bond. Because fans experience a strong sense of relatedness when participating in these events, the desire to rejoin the community and relive the excitement remains high. The shared euphoria among thousands of fans, known as collective effervescence, likely fuels this ongoing demand.
The attempt to replicate the concert experience inside movie theaters capitalized on this collective effervescence. By trading friendship bracelets and singing together in theaters, fans who could not attend the live shows found a way to participate in the cultural phenomenon. This shared environment allowed audiences to maintain their parasocial relationship with the singer while simultaneously relieving their anxieties about missing out.
While the study provides a detailed look at consumer motivations, it carries a few limitations. The participants were drawn from a convenience sample, and they were allowed to self-select into a survey they knew was about Taylor Swift. As a result, roughly two-thirds of the respondents identified as fans, and the demographic makeup was predominantly female and white, which could affect how well the results apply to the broader population.
The research relied on self-reported survey data, which is useful for identifying predictive links but cannot definitively prove cause and effect. It remains possible that other unmeasured variables influence both the psychological traits and the purchasing habits of the respondents.
Future investigations could explore how fans develop interpersonal relationships with one another based on their mutual parasocial connections to a single celebrity. The researchers also recommend looking closer at how social media amplifies the fear of missing out during major entertainment events. Measuring the direct impact of shared euphoric experiences could further explain why people are so driven to participate in massive cultural moments.
The study, ““It’s You and Me, There’s Nothing Like This”: Parasocial Relationships, Fear of Missing Out, and How Fans Consume the Products in Taylor Swift’s Media Empire,” was authored by Lindsey Conlin Maxwell, Alec C. Tefertiller, and Caroline Neese.

All Boxers built to one standard, says minister
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:00:37 BST
23:00:37 KST

All six hundred and twenty three Mechanised Infantry Vehicle Boxers are being delivered to a common build standard, which has made variant and build configuration effectively the same thing.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for an updated breakdown of the 623 vehicles by variant, build configuration and role, referring back to an answer given in June 2021.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “I refer the hon. Member to the answer I gave on 18 December 2025 to Question 100025, which set out the number of Mechanised Infantry Vehicle (MIV) Boxers contracted for by variant. This information remains extant. As the Boxer programme has developed, build configuration and variant have become effectively interchangeable, with all 623 MIV Boxer vehicles being delivered to a common build standard. Consequently, a separate breakdown by build configuration is no longer relevant.
“The Department keeps under review its approach to the disclosure of information, taking account of a range of factors. An updated breakdown by role could pose a risk to operational security and, therefore, I am unable to provide this information.”
A common build standard means the hulls and drive modules come off the line identically whatever mission module they eventually carry, which is the design logic of the vehicle: the mission module can be lifted off and another fitted. Ministers confirmed earlier this month that Boxers will be able to recover one another in the field and that the vehicle has been built with the electrical and physical margin to take a remote weapon station later.
Boxer is being built in Britain by Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land at Telford and Stockton-on-Tees, with WFEL at Stockport, under contracts covering the 623 vehicles for the British Army.

Fighter jets typically house their main radars behind a radome in the nose, while conventional airborne early-warning aircraft often carry large radar arrays in prominent structures above the fuselage.
Although aircraft wings offer a large surface area, their relatively thin cross-sections leave limited internal space for radar equipment.
Top Chinese military aircraft designers have now proposed a revolutionary method to integrate large antenna arrays into aircraft wings, using flight manoeuvres and coordinated formations of unmanned aircraft to expand radar coverage.
The design was outlined in a study published online on October 10 in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Measurement & Control Technology, which presented wing-mounted radar as a new approach to building multifunctional, high-performance airborne early-warning systems.

NEW DELHI: The long-awaited 666-bed super speciality block at Dr Ram Manohar Lohia (RML) Hospital has secured fire safety clearance, bringing the Rs 482-crore facility a step closer to becoming operational and expanding access to specialised treatment at the Central government-run hospital.The 11-storey block will add 666 beds to the hospital’s existing capacity of 1,538, taking the total to 2,204. It will house 18 operation theatres, 99 intensive care unit (ICU) beds, 196 high dependency unit (HDU) beds and three catheterisation laboratories.
The facility will strengthen treatment in oncology, oncosurgery, hepatology, gastrointestinal surgery and liver transplantation. It will also have two linear accelerators for cancer treatment and a nuclear medicine department equipped with positron emission tomography (PET) scan facilities.The fire safety clearance removes a key hurdle to commissioning the facility, which is expected to expand the hospital’s capacity to handle complex cases and provide critical care. The timeline for making the block operational, however, has not been specified.The development comes as Union health minister JP Nadda reviewed healthcare services and infrastructure development at RML Hospital on Friday, emphasising patient-centric care and wider access to advanced medical facilities.Once operational, the new block is expected to significantly expand RML Hospital’s tertiary care capacity, catering to patients from Delhi and neighbouring states.

The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions.
Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE's northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have heightened concerns about maritime security and the conflict's environmental fallout.
Ras Al Khaimah, a northern UAE emirate known for its beaches and luxury resorts, is also home to Wynn Resorts' planned casino resort on Al Marjan Island.
The Las Vegas-based operator, which won the UAE's first commercial gaming licence in 2024, said in February it expected the resort to open in the first quarter of 2027.

Residents reported unusual odours in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE's environment ministry said they posed no health risks. The smell remained pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday.

How Operation Santa Claus grew from Christmas donations to ‘engine’ of change

Unknown Publisher

How Operation Santa Claus grew from Christmas donations to ‘engine’ of change
Fundraising drive has evolved over its nearly 40 years from simply disbursing funds to building sustained relationships with NGOs
Over nearly four decades, Operation Santa Claus (OSC) has grown from a quirky holiday fundraiser into an “engine” for community change in Hong Kong.
For some beneficiaries, the journey was a full circle. Rachel Chow Chiu-yan learned about the fundraising drive in Young Post when she was a student, later pitched for funds on behalf of a group helping teenage girls and later joined the charity.
“Ten to 20 years ago, Operation Santa Claus disbursed some funding to charities that saw it as seed money. Now, after successful pilot schemes, the initiatives have been replicated,” Chow, former senior manager of the programme, said.
The drive was established by the South China Morning Post and public broadcaster RTHK in 1988.

LUCKNOW: Indian Railways has decided to extend its Optional Travel Insurance Scheme (OTIS) to passengers booking reserved tickets through Passenger Reservation System (PRS) counters from October 27, in compliance with Supreme Court directions.In an order issued on Saturday, the Railway Board directed all zonal railways to make necessary arrangements for implementing the scheme at reservation counters.The decision follows the Supreme Court's October 6 order in the Union of India versus Radha Yadav case.Under the scheme, passengers can opt for insurance by paying a premium of 45 paise per passenger, offering coverage of up to Rs 10 lakh in case of death or permanent total disability arising from a railway accident or untoward incident.The policy also provides Rs 7.5 lakh for permanent partial disability, up to Rs 2 lakh towards hospitalisation expenses and Rs 10,000 for transportation of mortal remains.According to the Railway Board, insurance will remain optional, and reservation staff must inform passengers about its availability before booking.
Passengers opting for insurance must provide a mobile number and pay the premium through digital payment modes only.
The premium will be collected along with the ticket fare.Insurance policy details will be communicated to passengers through their registered mobile numbers.The Board clarified that the existing terms and conditions applicable to IRCTC e-ticket insurance will also apply to tickets purchased at reservation counters.Divisional railway managers and commercial officers have been directed to monitor implementation, while zonal railways must submit compliance reports confirming operational readiness.

Harmonized regulatory frameworks urged in Africa to advance pharmaceutical self-reliance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
21:32:57 CST
22:32:57 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Industry experts and stakeholders on Friday called for concerted action to establish a robust ecosystem for bioequivalence testing to ensure locally manufactured generic medicines across Eastern and Southern Africa are safe, accessible, and scientifically proven.
The call was made during a regional workshop focused on developing a White Paper on bioequivalence testing and regulatory harmonization in Eastern and Southern Africa, held in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia. The five-day event, which ran from Oct. 19 to 23, highlighted the critical need for harmonized regulatory frameworks and expanded domestic testing capacity to eliminate costly reliance on overseas facilities.
Jointly organized by the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the Ethiopian government and the World Bank, the workshop brought together national regulators, pharmaceutical manufacturers, experts and researchers, as well as development partners to establish a comprehensive regional framework for bioequivalence testing.
Experts and policymakers at the gathering emphasized that relying on external testing facilities imposes significant economic burdens and causes regulatory approval delays for locally manufactured generic drugs. They stressed the urgent need to expand domestic testing capacity to support sustainable pharmaceutical growth across the region.
Addressing the workshop, Girum Hailu, a senior policy and partnership specialist at IGAD, highlighted several critical gaps affecting the sector, including limited regional bioequivalence testing facilities, heavy dependence on overseas testing, high study costs, and inconsistent regulatory requirements across borders.
To overcome these challenges, experts advocated for advancing regulatory harmonization aligned with international standards, implementing phased, risk-based compliance pathways for legacy products, and establishing shared regional testing capacity backed by strong oversight mechanisms to support local manufacturers.
Stakeholders also underscored the vital importance of making bioequivalence services more affordable and accessible to local pharmaceutical manufacturers, outlining priority investments and capacity-building measures for accredited centers across the region. ■

Yang Jianxing, cultural counselor of the Chinese Embassy in Nigeria, said the restoration of Taiwan was an important outcome of the Chinese people's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and part of the collective memory of the Chinese nation.
"The exhibition features a series of precious historical photographs and detailed textual records, showcasing the firm resolve of the Chinese people as a whole to uphold the one-China principle and safeguard national sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity," Yang said.
Hu Jieguo, secretary-general of the China Council for the Promotion of Peaceful National Reunification in Western Africa, said Taiwan was liberated from Japanese colonial rule and returned to China 81 years ago.
"This victory was not a gift, but was paid for with the blood, sweat, and tears of millions of Chinese sons and daughters who stood united against foreign aggression," Hu said, noting that the commemoration in Nigeria carries special significance as China and Nigeria share historical experiences of resisting foreign invasion and colonialism.
Gui Tao, deputy editor-in-chief of Xinhua News Agency Africa Regional Bureau, said the exhibition, held in five African countries including Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa, Nigeria and Mozambique, looks back at an important chapter of history and affirms peace, justice and historical fact.
"The African people, including the people of Nigeria, endured the suffering brought by colonialism, just as China did, and went through the same historical process of striving for national independence, state sovereignty and national dignity," Gui said.
Three Taiwanese businesspeople from China's Guangdong Province shared their experiences of working and living on the Chinese mainland through video.
Chen Chi-An, executive vice president of the Guangzhou Taiwan-Funded Enterprises Association, said there are more than 2,900 Taiwan-funded companies in Guangzhou, with many Taiwanese students also studying and living in the city.
"Over the past several decades, I have been able to give back to and work together with young people from the mainland, which is what makes us Taiwan businessmen happiest," Chen said.
Wu Chun-Jui, president of the Taiwan Businessmen Association Dongguan, said Dongguan has a favorable business environment and that Taiwan businesspeople have established self-funded hospitals and schools there.
"We hope to take this opportunity to remember this period of history. The great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is unstoppable," Wu said.
Hsu Fu-hsien, president of the Taiwan Merchant Association Shenzhen, said he has worked in Shenzhen since 1990 and has built his family and career there.
"I have grown up here, got married here, and my children have also grown up here in Shenzhen," Hsu said, expressing hope that the exhibition would allow African people and overseas compatriots to see the reality of Taiwanese businesspeople living and working on the Chinese mainland.
Sheriff Ibrahim, head of the Centre for Contemporary China-Africa Research in Nigeria, said Nigeria recognizes the one-China principle and that the Nigerian government has continued to reaffirm this position.
"There is a certain similarity between China's efforts to maintain national unity and Nigeria's own experience in maintaining its territorial integrity," Ibrahim said, expressing confidence that China would eventually achieve peaceful reunification with Taiwan.
Charles Onunaiju, director of the Center for China Studies in Nigeria, said China's experience of foreign intervention and colonial aggression is closely connected with the issue of national reunification.
"African countries have their own historical experiences and are therefore able to understand China's position on safeguarding national unity and sovereignty," Onunaiju said.
A book edited by Xinhua News Agency was also presented at the exhibition. The Taiwan businessmen associations from Guangzhou and Shenzhen donated books to Nigerian officials and experts. ■

====================================================================================================

British jets escort French jets on ‘nuclear strike’
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:18:23 BST
22:18:23 KST

RAF Typhoons have escorted French Rafales simulating a nuclear strike mission over the Mediterranean, the first time British aircraft have taken part in a French nuclear exercise, according to the government.
Exercise Rummy ran on 20 and 21 October, with the Rafales launching from Saint-Dizier air base in eastern France, the home of the French air force’s airborne nuclear component. No nuclear weapons were involved, and the Ministry of Defence said the exercise was conducted under robust safety and security arrangements and focused on how the two air forces work together.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said: “This exercise marks a new chapter in the defence nuclear relationship between the United Kingdom and France.
“As Europe’s nuclear powers, we have a shared responsibility to contribute to the security and stability of the Euro-Atlantic region. This exercise demonstrates the depth of our partnership, the credibility of our deterrents and our determination to stand together in the face of emerging threats.
“In an increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt: the UK and France remain united in our commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations.”
Catherine Vautrin, the French Minister of the Armed Forces and Veterans, said: “Having independent nuclear forces does not exclude coordination. Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom keeps deepening: on Tuesday night, UK Typhoons participated for the very first time to a French nuclear exercise alongside Rafales.
“Through coordination, our nuclear forces demonstrate that they can contribute even more significantly to the overall security of the Alliance and to the peace and stability of the Euro Atlantic area.”
The exercise falls under the Northwood Declaration, the agreement signed last year under which the two countries said that no extreme threat to Europe could arise which would not prompt a response by both, while each retains sovereign and independent nuclear forces and national decision making. Britain and France are the only nuclear armed states in Europe, and the declaration established a joint nuclear steering group to coordinate their policy, capabilities and operations.
Saint-Dizier is the base of the 4th Fighter Wing, which operates Rafales carrying the ASMP-A supersonic stand-off missile that forms the airborne half of the French deterrent. The French maintain both an airborne component and ballistic missile submarines, while Britain has relied on submarines alone since the WE.177 bomb was withdrawn in 1998.
That changes with the purchase of twelve F-35A aircraft and British entry into NATO’s nuclear mission, which will return a nuclear role to the Royal Air Force after more than a quarter of a century. Air Marshal Johnny Beck told a committee this year that the aircraft were not bought for the nuclear role, while the government has presented the purchase as the means of joining the mission.
The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise, funding the Dreadnought ballistic missile submarines, SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, a new sovereign warhead and the supporting infrastructure. The refreshed Lancaster House agreement between Britain and France covers an expanded joint deployable force, deeper nuclear cooperation and work on the next generation of weapons.

In the capital’s luxury shopping districts along Avenue Louise, Boulevard de Waterloo, and in the Rue Neuve and Sablon areas, more than half of the storefronts have been covered with particleboard panels.
"Naturally, we hope that the police will be able to contain the unrest this time. But we have a grim history. Hopes aren't always realized," Antoine, the owner of a city center electronics store, told TASS.
According to him, the emergency installation of panels on a small shop featuring two glass display windows and a door costs owners between 1,500 and 2,000 euros. Although the panels are firmly screwed into the structural framework, such defensive measures "will only deter opportunistic rioters who aren't specifically targeting a particular store."
Last weekend, street unrest that began as student protests devolved into the looting of city center shops. This week, calls to "take to the streets for social justice on October 24" have once again circulated widely across Belgian social media. Shop owners are discussing online the possibility of legally using civilian or non-lethal weapons to defend against rioters. However, Belgian self-defense law justifies the use of force only to protect life and physical well-being, not property.
Brussels authorities have also undertaken extensive preparations. Reinforced police units are stationed at major intersections in the city center, and the number of patrols circulating throughout the city significantly exceeds that of an ordinary day.
By midday, the situation in the city remained calm. The areas around Brussels’ three main railway stations - North, South, and Central - where groups of protesters typically gather, are under heightened police surveillance, though the situation there remains peaceful for now.

Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:15:00 UTC
22:15:00 KST

Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- Queen Mary University of London
- Summary:
- A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.
- Share:
A small device that delivers gentle electrical pulses through the ear could offer a new approach to treating stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home.
Although the treatment did not significantly lower blood pressure compared with a placebo device across all participants, researchers observed encouraging results in patients with more severe hypertension. The findings suggest that stimulating nerves in the ear could eventually help certain people whose blood pressure remains elevated despite taking medication.
The results come from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension, a journal of the American Heart Association. Researchers emphasize that larger studies are needed to determine whether the approach can provide meaningful benefits and which patients might respond best.
How Ear Nerve Stimulation Could Lower Blood Pressure
The experimental treatment uses a technique called transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), which aims to influence the autonomic nervous system. This network of nerves automatically controls essential bodily functions, including heart rate, digestion, and blood pressure.
By delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear, researchers hope to influence the body's natural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure without requiring an invasive procedure.
The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, uses two small clips positioned on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage located just in front of the ear canal. These clips deliver gentle electrical stimulation, allowing patients to administer the treatment themselves without visiting a clinic.
Clinical Trial Tests the Device in 63 Patients
The clinical trial, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), enrolled 63 people with uncontrolled hypertension. All participants were already taking at least one medication to lower their blood pressure, but their readings remained above recommended levels.
Researchers randomly divided the participants into two groups. One received active nerve stimulation, while the other used a sham device designed to serve as a comparison. This approach helped investigators assess whether the electrical stimulation produced benefits beyond those associated with using the device itself.
Participants used their assigned devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks. For the following 10 weeks, they reduced their sessions to once per week.
The results showed that the treatment was safe and generally comfortable for participants. Most also followed the prescribed schedule, suggesting that the technology could be practical for regular use at home.
However, when researchers compared blood pressure changes across the entire study population, they found no statistically significant difference between patients receiving active stimulation and those using the sham device.
Promising Results in Patients With Severe Hypertension
Despite the lack of a significant overall benefit, the researchers identified a potentially important finding among participants who entered the trial with more severe hypertension.
A prespecified subgroup analysis, meaning the researchers had planned this comparison before examining the results, revealed a greater reduction in blood pressure among these patients when they received active nerve stimulation rather than the sham treatment.
This finding raises the possibility that the technique may work better for people with particularly difficult-to-control blood pressure. However, the trial was relatively small, and the subgroup results require confirmation in larger studies before any conclusions can be drawn about its effectiveness.
Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said:
"This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham.
"As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension."
A Potential New Option for Hard-to-Control Blood Pressure
High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular disease and increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. It places additional strain on blood vessels and the heart, potentially causing serious damage over time.
Although medications help many patients manage their condition, a substantial number continue to have blood pressure readings above recommended targets even while receiving treatment.
This ongoing challenge has encouraged scientists to explore additional approaches that could complement existing therapies.
Ear nerve stimulation is one such possibility. Because the device is small, does not require surgery, and can be used at home, it could offer a convenient option if future research establishes that it reliably lowers blood pressure in certain patients.
For now, the findings represent an early step rather than proof of an effective new treatment. The researchers say larger clinical trials will be essential to confirm the encouraging results in patients with severe hypertension and identify which groups, if any, could benefit most from this approach.

A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:01:22 UTC
22:01:22 KST

A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- University of Vermont
- Summary:
- A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts.
- Share:
Researchers at the University of Vermont have discovered a surprising pattern in human language that challenges a scientific theory widely accepted for more than 70 years. Their findings suggest that the meaning of words is shaped by something more fundamental than emotion: our understanding of power, danger, and order.
The study, published in Science Advances, introduces a new approach called "ousiometrics," which uses mathematical methods to measure the essential meaning of language. Its most striking finding is that the words people use show a consistent and widespread preference for safety over danger.
This hidden safety bias could transform how researchers study language, understand human behavior, and develop artificial intelligence systems that interpret what people say and write.
Scientists Discover a Hidden Safety Bias in Human Language
Since the 1950s, much of the scientific understanding of word meaning has relied on a framework developed through pioneering research by psychologist Charles Osgood and others. Known as the VAD model, it describes meaning through three emotional dimensions: valence (positive vs. negative), arousal (excited vs. calm), and dominance (controlling vs. submissive).
This approach became influential in psychology, linguistics, and artificial intelligence, particularly in systems designed to identify the emotional tone of written language.
However, the University of Vermont researchers found evidence that this long-established model overlooks important aspects of how meaning is organized.
Their analysis examined billions of individual uses of more than 20,000 words across a wide range of real-world texts. Using advanced computational techniques, the team identified a different underlying structure. They found that the three dimensions in the traditional VAD model are not independent of one another, as previously assumed.
Instead, their results indicate that word meaning can be more effectively described through three separate dimensions: power (weak vs. powerful), danger (safe vs. dangerous), and structure (ordered vs. chaotic).
The research, supported by the US National Science Foundation, Google, MassMutual, and other funders, found that this new framework accounted for more than 90% of the variation in measured word meaning. The traditional VAD approach explained approximately 72%.
That improvement could be especially important as large language models, automated content moderation, and other AI technologies increasingly depend on understanding human communication.
Why Human Language Favors Safety Over Danger
One of the study's most unexpected discoveries emerged when the researchers examined how words actually appear in everyday communication.
Across books, news reporting, social media, and spoken language, words associated with safety appeared much more frequently than those associated with danger.
This finding offers a new explanation for a familiar phenomenon called the Pollyanna principle, which describes the tendency for human language to lean toward positive rather than negative words.
For decades, researchers generally interpreted this pattern as evidence that people favor positive emotional expressions. The new analysis suggests that something more fundamental may be responsible.
According to the researchers, the apparent preference for positivity largely reflects an underlying preference for safety.
"The Pollyanna principle's positivity bias," the study concludes. "is, in fact, a one-dimensional projection of an underlying safety bias."
"This is a big observation that comes out of this work," said Peter Dodds, director of the UVM's Complex Systems Institute and senior author of the study. "Expressions of safety are crucial to all language."
Could Human Language Be Shaped by Survival?
The discovery raises an intriguing possibility: the structure of human language may reflect evolutionary pressures associated with staying alive.
From this perspective, words do more than communicate feelings. They also help people recognize threats, evaluate uncertainty, establish trust, and coordinate actions with others.
Being able to distinguish between safety and danger is essential to survival. The researchers suggest that this basic human priority may also influence how meaning is organized in language.
Throughout daily life, people constantly exchange information about whether individuals, places, situations, and behaviors are threatening or safe. The new findings suggest that these distinctions may be more central to communication than previously recognized.
They also offer a different interpretation of why positive language is so common. Rather than simply expressing happiness or approval, many positive words may convey a sense of security, stability, or predictability.
Julia Zimmerman, a postdoctoral researcher in UVM's Computational Story Lab and a co-author of the study, said the three newly identified dimensions reflect experiences that are fundamental to human life.
"Power, danger, and structure," she said, "are relevant to every person that's ever lived."
Researchers have also long recognized that people tend to favor language associated with goodness and low aggression. The team argues that these familiar tendencies may arise from the same deeper pattern.
"We now understand," the team writes, that these are "shadows of an underlying linguistic safety bias."
Although the results are consistent with a possible connection between language and survival, they do not establish that evolutionary pressures directly caused the safety bias.
A Discovery That Could Change How AI Understands Language
The findings have implications that extend well beyond linguistics.
Many artificial intelligence systems use sentiment analysis to determine whether language expresses positive, negative, or neutral feelings. Some approaches also draw on the traditional VAD framework to measure emotional meaning.
If that framework does not fully capture the underlying structure of language, systems built around it could overlook important distinctions in what people communicate.
The researchers suggest that incorporating power, danger, and structure could eventually help AI models interpret language more accurately and explain their assessments more clearly. This may be particularly useful when analyzing trust, risk, and decision-making.
In linguistics, the findings offer a different way to understand the foundations of meaning. Instead of treating emotional tone as the primary organizing principle, the new framework emphasizes distinctions related to strength, safety, and predictability.
Psychology could also be affected. Decades of studies have used the VAD model to investigate emotions, perception, and behavior. A different set of fundamental dimensions could encourage researchers to reconsider how some of those findings are interpreted.
The discovery may also interest neuroscientists. The human brain is highly sensitive to threats and signals of safety, and the newly identified linguistic bias suggests that these biological priorities may be reflected in language. This potential connection could help researchers explore relationships between brain activity and symbolic communication, although further research would be needed to establish them.
A New Tool Measures the Hidden Meaning of Words
To investigate these patterns, the researchers created analytical methods designed to measure meaning across enormous collections of written and spoken language.
One of their central innovations is the "ousiometer," a tool that rapidly evaluates the essential meaning of large bodies of text and produces an average meaning score.
(The word "ouisa" comes from Ancient Greek and is a root for the English word "essence.")
The ousiometer builds on an earlier tool developed by the research team called the "hedonometer" (a happiness meter). While that instrument measures the overall emotional tone of language, the new approach examines broader patterns of meaning.
The researchers demonstrated that the ousiometer can analyze material from remarkably different sources, including Jane Austen's novels, Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories, the New York Times, Wikipedia, Twitter, and transcripts of talk radio programs.
The tool can also track how meaning shifts as a story unfolds.
For example, the researchers analyzed an English translation of Victor Hugo's Les Misérables and mapped its changing meaning throughout the novel.
They called this changing pattern an "ousiometric trajectory." The visualization resembles the twisting shape of a multicolored protein, with the narrative moving across a grid based on four contrasting pairs: dangerous/safe, weak/powerful, gentle/aggressive, and bad/good.
By following this path, researchers can observe how the underlying meaning of the text changes from one section of the story to another.
Why Counting Word Frequency Changes the Results
Another important innovation involved distinguishing between words themselves and how often people actually use them.
In linguistics, researchers describe individual words as categories called "types," while each appearance of a word in text is known as a "token."
(For example, as a category "apple" is a type and every time the word "apple" is used in a sentence is a token.)
This distinction matters because a word that appears millions of times contributes much more to everyday communication than one that is rarely used.
Earlier research often gave each word equal importance, regardless of its frequency. The Vermont team instead incorporated how often words appear in real communication, allowing patterns to emerge that might otherwise remain hidden.
This approach was particularly important for identifying the widespread preference for safety-related language.
The ten-member research team was led by Peter Dodds and Chris Danforth, professors in UVM's College of Engineering and Mathematical Sciences. Their collaborators included researchers from the Santa Fe Institute, the Complexity Science Hub in Austria, Howard Hughes Medical Center, the University of California, Berkeley, the University of Adelaide, and MassMutual Data Science.
Rethinking What Human Language Reveals About Us
Understanding this hidden safety bias could have consequences for how researchers study communication across society.
If words consistently reflect a preference for safety, that tendency may influence how stories are told, how information spreads, and how people interpret events and experiences.
The findings could eventually inform research into political communication, mental health messaging, and AI systems designed to interact with people.
More broadly, the study challenges the idea that human language can be understood primarily through emotions such as happiness, fear, and excitement.
Instead, the researchers propose that meaning has a deeper structure connected to power, danger, and order. Their findings suggest that language may reflect the challenges humans face when navigating uncertain environments, maintaining relationships, and identifying threats.
By revealing this previously overlooked structure, the team offers a new way to understand what words communicate and why certain kinds of meaning dominate everyday conversation. Human language, their research suggests, may be more closely connected to our fundamental need for safety than scientists have traditionally recognized.
Story Source:

Journal Reference:
- Peter Sheridan Dodds, Thayer Alshaabi, Mikaela Irene Fudolig, Julia Witte Zimmerman, Juniper Lovato, Shawn Beaulieu, Joshua R. Minot, Michael V. Arnold, Andrew J. Reagan, Christopher M. Danforth. Ousiometrics: The essence of meaning aligns with a power-danger-structure framework instead of valence-arousal-dominance. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (19) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adr4039

Formosa Club calls on Europe and Taiwan to learn from each other
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

12:52:05 UTC
21:52:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – At its annual meet in Taipei Saturday, the Formosa Club called on Taiwan and the EU to learn from each other in facing down the threat of authoritarianism.
The group unites members of the European Parliament and legislators from European countries known for their support of Taiwan. Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) and German CDU Member of the European Parliament Michael Gahler addressed Saturday’s opening ceremony, per Liberty Times.
Taiwan’s advantage is that it knows China, so Europe should listen and learn, Gahler said. Lin said that Taiwan was willing to share its experience in countering hackers, disinformation, and hybrid warfare, standing together with Europe on the front line to defend democracy.
Gahler called on Europe to pay more attention to Taiwan and to voice its opinions in a clearer way. The two sides should also exchange information, including Taiwan’s understanding of China’s actions and motives, he said.
Lin also recommended Taiwan as a partner for reliable supply chains, as the war in Ukraine showed that overreliance on one economy was dangerous. Gahler responded by saying Europe had begun taking measures to reduce its reliance on China, even though it had started late.
The Formosa Club’s annual meeting will be attended by 52 lawmakers from 19 European countries and from the European Parliament, Liberty Times reported.

NASA’s asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:50:06 UTC
21:50:06 KST

NASA’s asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Tiny samples from asteroid Bennu are rewriting scientists' understanding of how our Solar System formed. New evidence suggests that Bennu was born where material from the inner and outer Solar System mixed, with Jupiter playing a surprising role in shaping its formation.
- Share:
Samples collected from asteroid Bennu by NASA are revealing surprising new details about how our Solar System formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago. A new chemical analysis challenges earlier theories about the asteroid's birthplace and suggests that Jupiter played an important role in shaping the materials from which Bennu and other ancient objects formed.
Bennu completes one orbit around the Sun every 1.2 years and makes a relatively close approach to Earth about every six years, coming within roughly 300,000 kilometers (186,000 miles). NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission traveled to the asteroid, collected material from its surface, and successfully delivered the samples to Earth in 2023.
On September 23, 2023, a capsule carrying approximately 120 grams of asteroid material landed in the Utah desert. Scientists around the world subsequently received small portions of the precious cargo for detailed study.
Among them was Maria Schönbächler, Professor of Isotope Geochemistry at ETH Zurich, whose laboratory received half a gram of Bennu material. Her team immediately began examining the samples for clues about the asteroid's history.
The research, now published in Science Advances, has uncovered a distinctive chemical signature that not only helps identify Bennu's origins but also provides new evidence about the processes that shaped the early Solar System.
Bennu's Chemical Fingerprint Reveals Its Cosmic Relatives
To investigate Bennu's origins, the ETH Zurich researchers examined isotopes of three elements: iron, titanium, and chromium.
Isotopes are different forms of the same chemical element that contain varying numbers of neutrons, giving them slightly different masses. By measuring the relative amounts of these isotopes, scientists can identify a material's chemical fingerprint. These patterns provide clues about where an asteroid's ingredients originated and, in some cases, when they formed.
The analysis revealed that iron and titanium are distributed remarkably evenly throughout Bennu's material. It also uncovered a close chemical relationship between Bennu, the asteroid Ryugu, and a rare group of primitive meteorites known as CI meteorites.
CI meteorites are carbon-rich remnants of the early Solar System that have undergone relatively little alteration over billions of years. They are exceptionally uncommon among meteorites recovered on Earth.
Bennu, Ryugu, and CI meteorites share strikingly similar isotopic fingerprints, suggesting that their original materials came from the same reservoir of ancient cosmic dust. Their chemical signatures also differ substantially from those of other known asteroids, meteorite groups, and planets.
These similarities offer an important clue about where these objects formed and what conditions existed during the Solar System's earliest stages.
Scientists Discover Bennu's Unexpected Birthplace
For years, researchers generally believed that primitive asteroids like Bennu originated in the outer Solar System, perhaps in the same distant regions where comets formed. They also suspected that Bennu's original material came together relatively late in the Solar System's development.
The new findings challenge both assumptions.
Instead, the researchers propose that the material that became Bennu, Ryugu, and CI meteorites accumulated near a boundary known as the water-ice line.
This boundary marks the region in the disk surrounding the young Sun where temperatures were low enough for water vapor to freeze into ice. Around 4.5 billion years ago, it may have been a particularly important meeting place for material traveling from different parts of the developing Solar System.
Dust originating in both the inner and outer regions mixed near this boundary. Water ice helped the smallest particles stick together, allowing them to gradually accumulate into larger bodies.
"Bennu is a hybrid: the material does not clearly match either the inner or the outer Solar System," says Schönbächler.
Its unusual chemical composition suggests that Bennu formed from a combination of materials originating in both regions rather than from a single, isolated source.
Jupiter May Have Played a Crucial Role in Bennu's Formation
The researchers also developed a scenario explaining how this mixing could have occurred, with Jupiter emerging as a key player.
Jupiter began forming extraordinarily early in Solar System history, within approximately one million years of the Sun's birth. At that time, the young Sun was surrounded by a rotating disk of gas, dust, and ice.
Within this disk, countless small particles gradually collided and stuck together, building larger objects through a process called accretion. Over time, some of these growing bodies became asteroids and planets.
As Jupiter rapidly increased in mass, its immense gravitational influence began reshaping the distribution of material throughout the disk.
The researchers suggest that the growing gas giant acted somewhat like a structural barrier, preventing most larger particles from crossing its orbital region while still allowing finer dust to move around it.
This fine material, originating from different parts of the disk, could then mix extensively near the water-ice line.
According to the proposed scenario, the parent bodies of Bennu and Ryugu, along with the objects that produced CI meteorites, formed from this thoroughly mixed material.
Jupiter may therefore have helped determine not only where these ancient asteroids formed but also which ingredients became incorporated into them.
Ancient Dust and Ice Reveal the Ingredients That Built Earth
The proposed formation scenario could also explain two of Bennu's most intriguing characteristics: its abundance of water-bearing material and its chemical resemblance to the Sun.
Near the water-ice boundary, ice could evaporate as temperatures changed, releasing water vapor that later condensed again in cooler regions. This process would have helped concentrate water in the material from which Bennu formed.
Meanwhile, Jupiter's influence may have limited the movement of larger particles, leaving the asteroid's parent material dominated by fine dust.
Because these tiny particles could circulate and mix efficiently throughout the disk, they preserved a chemical composition that closely resembles the overall elemental mixture found in the Sun.
The process is somewhat similar to the way fine household dust spreads and settles across many different surfaces rather than remaining in one location.
This extensive mixing could explain why Bennu's material retains such a representative sample of the ingredients present during the Solar System's earliest history.
"Bennu may offer our best glimpse of the original mix of chemical elements from which the terrestrial planets were ultimately built," as Schönbächler states.
Bennu is considered an exceptionally primitive asteroid because its material formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago and has experienced relatively little chemical alteration since then.
That makes its samples particularly valuable for reconstructing the conditions that existed before Earth and the other rocky planets finished forming.
By studying the asteroid's chemistry, scientists can better understand how the Solar System developed and which processes determined the composition of its planets.
Bennu's water-bearing minerals and organic compounds also make it important for investigating how early Earth obtained some of the chemical ingredients necessary for life.
Although these findings do not establish exactly how those materials reached our planet, they provide valuable evidence about where such ingredients originated and how they were distributed throughout the young Solar System.
A New Mission to Mars' Moon Could Reveal More
Despite the new discoveries, several questions remain unanswered.
"We are now wondering whether other asteroids have the same isotopic signature as Bennu and Ryugu," Schönbächler goes on to state.
Researchers also want to determine more precisely how Jupiter influenced the movement of dust and whether its gravitational effects were responsible for favoring the accumulation of particularly fine particles.
Additional asteroid samples could help scientists test the proposed formation scenario and establish whether Bennu's chemical signature is shared by other ancient bodies.
With the Bennu analysis now complete, Schönbächler is looking ahead to another opportunity to examine material from the early Solar System.
Japan's space agency, JAXA, is preparing a sample-return mission to Phobos, one of Mars' two moons. The mission is scheduled to launch at the end of October 2026, with the goal of collecting material from the Martian moon and bringing it back to Earth.
"It would be exciting to also obtain this material to analyse it in my laboratory," she says.
Schönbächler plans to apply to JAXA for access to the samples. However, the scientific community will need to be patient. The capsule carrying material from Phobos is not expected to return to Earth until 2031.
Those future samples could provide another important piece of the puzzle, helping researchers determine how different regions of the early Solar System exchanged material and ultimately produced the planets, moons, and asteroids we observe today.

Journal Reference:
- Maria Schönbächler, Mattias Ek, Manuela A. Fehr, Katarzyna M. Liszewska, Lara A. E. Meyer, Miriam Rüfenacht, James M. J. Ball, Paul Frossard, Jan Render, Quinn R. Shollenberger, Greg A. Brennecka, Thomas S. Kruijer, Josh Wimpenny, Martin Bizzarro, Jessica J. Barnes, Ann N. Nguyen. Nucleosynthetic constraints on the origin of Bennu and CI-like asteroids. Malaysia data center boom to strain electricity supply
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
20:39:40 CST
21:39:40 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's data-center expansion is expected to put increasing pressure on electricity supply, particularly in Johor, where power demand from new facilities could account for 18 percent of Peninsular Malaysia's electricity supply by 2031, according to BMI Country Risk and Industry Research.
BMI said in a recent note that it forecasts Johor's new data center capacity will require about 30 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity annually by 2031, up from a level equivalent to 6 percent of Peninsular Malaysia's electricity supply in 2026.
The additional demand would exceed 90 percent of the net increase in electricity generation expected across the peninsula over the same period.
The tight supply outlook reflects the peninsula's limited access to Sarawak's hydropower resources, while grid infrastructure development struggles to keep pace with data center construction.
BMI expects Malaysia's thermal power capacity to increase by a net 3 gigawatts (GW) between 2029 and 2031, from 33.3 GW in 2028 to 36.3 GW in 2031. Gas-fired electricity generation is forecast to rise by 13.6 TWh to 106.7 TWh.
However, it said grid connections could pose a bigger bottleneck than generation capacity, as local substations and transmission infrastructure become increasingly constrained in key data center hubs.
Although utility firm Tenaga Nasional Bhd plans to invest 43 billion ringgit in grid upgrades, major projects typically take five to 10 years to complete.
Malaysia has also tightened approval requirements for new data centers, requiring operators to demonstrate access to their own power and water supplies before connecting to the grid, according to BMI. ■

Feature: Kuala Lumpur shrouded in haze as iconic Petronas Twin Towers fade from view
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
20:39:36 CST
21:39:36 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Many tourists visiting Malaysia recently have shared photos of haze-shrouded Kuala Lumpur on social media, lamenting that the city's famous skyline seems to have "disappeared." Local residents have also complained of throat irritation, allergies and other health problems caused by the haze.
"I don't think the haze has ever been this bad since I was in primary school," said Azariah, a Malaysian girl born in the 1990s.
Haze has continued to plague Malaysia since August. According to real-time rankings of the world's most polluted major cities published by Swiss air quality tracker IQAir, Kuala Lumpur's air quality index (AQI) surged to 244 on the afternoon of Oct. 15, making it the most polluted major city in the world at the time. As of the morning of Oct. 23, the index remained at 172, a level classified as "unhealthy."
The haze has significantly disrupted daily life. Schools in some areas have been forced to close due to deteriorating air quality. The combination of persistent high temperatures and haze has also left some poultry farmers facing slower poultry growth and declining output, forcing them to invest more in ventilation and cooling facilities.
Malaysia's environmental authorities said the current haze episode has multiple causes, including open burning, the El Nino phenomenon and prevailing weather conditions, as well as transboundary haze from ongoing forest fires in various parts of Indonesia.
According to data from Nusantara Atlas, a deforestation monitoring platform, more than 1.9 million hectares of land in Indonesia had been burned by fires as of the end of September this year. Large amounts of smoke generated by forest and peatland fires have been carried across national borders by monsoon winds and atmospheric circulation, drifting into Malaysia and other neighboring countries.
Malaysia's meteorological authorities have forecast that a shift in wind direction next week could gradually ease the haze, while the northeast monsoon, expected to arrive in November, may also help improve air quality. However, persistent hot and dry conditions could keep the risks of forest fires and transboundary haze elevated across the region.
Against the backdrop of global warming, which is contributing to more frequent periods of extreme heat and drought, reducing the risk of forest and land fires, strengthening cross-border pollution monitoring and tackling pollution at its source have become shared challenges for countries in the region.
Malaysia's Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Arthur Joseph Kurup said the transboundary haze problem must be addressed through collective action and closer regional cooperation. He called on ASEAN member states to fulfill their respective responsibilities, strengthen data sharing, law enforcement cooperation and fire prevention efforts, and translate regional commitments into concrete action.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto recently approved the acceptance of firefighting assistance offered by Singapore and Malaysia. Scientists propose a way to detect dangerous “mirror life” before it exists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:39:16 UTC
21:39:16 KST

Scientists propose a way to detect dangerous “mirror life” before it exists
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- https://www.strath.ac.uk/
- Summary:
- Scientists have proposed a way to detect “mirror life,” a hypothetical form of life that could pose serious risks to humans, animals, and ecosystems if artificially created. Using special fluorescent molecules and a type of polarized light also used in 3D movie technology, researchers believe they could distinguish ordinary organisms from their mirror-image counterparts.
- Share:
Scientists have proposed what they believe is the first way to detect "mirror life," a hypothetical form of life built from molecules that are reversed versions of those found in living organisms on Earth.
Researchers from the University of Strathclyde and Durham University have developed a proposed detection technique that uses molecules capable of emitting light with distinct left and right-handed properties. By analyzing these light signals, scientists may eventually be able to distinguish conventional organisms from their mirror-image counterparts.
Although mirror life does not currently exist, some experts consider its potential creation a serious biological safety concern. These artificial organisms could behave in unpredictable ways when interacting with Earth's ecosystems and might evade certain natural defenses that protect people, animals, and plants.
The likelihood of mirror life emerging is considered low, but its possible consequences could be severe enough to justify developing detection methods in advance.
Why Mirror Life Could Pose a Biological Threat
Concerns about mirror life have prompted scientists to recommend restrictions on research intended to produce organisms capable of reproducing using mirror-image biological molecules.
The potential dangers have also attracted attention from governments and international organizations, including the UK Government Office for Science and the United Nations Secretary General's Scientific Advisory Board.
The underlying science involves a property of molecules known as chirality, often described as molecular "handedness." Just as a person's left and right hands are mirror images that cannot be perfectly aligned, some molecules can exist in two forms that have identical chemical components but different three-dimensional arrangements.
These subtle structural differences can have major biological consequences. Two mirror-image versions of a molecule contain the same atoms connected in the same order, yet the human body may respond to them very differently. For example, one form of a medication could successfully treat a disease, while its mirror-image counterpart might be ineffective or even harmful.
Scientists are concerned that organisms assembled from reversed biological building blocks could interact with existing life in unexpected ways.
Importantly, the researchers emphasize that mirror life remains entirely hypothetical. Their proposed detection method is intended as a precaution, not a response to an existing biological threat.
How Light Could Reveal Mirror-Image Life
The proposed approach relies on a phenomenon called circularly polarized luminescence (CPL), which can reveal the molecular handedness, or chirality, of certain substances and biological structures.
Light can exhibit different polarization patterns, including forms that rotate in opposite directions. By studying these patterns, researchers can obtain information about the three-dimensional arrangement of molecules.
The underlying concept has a surprisingly familiar application: the polarized light technology used in modern 3D movie glasses to create the illusion of depth.
The research, published in Royal Society Open Science under the title 'Circularly Polarized Luminescence (CPL) as a Contingency Assay for "Mirror Life" Bio-Hazards', was led by Dr. Lewis MacKenzie of the University of Strathclyde's Department of Pure and Applied Chemistry, working with Professor Robert Pal of Durham University.
Dr. MacKenzie said: "We don't expect mirror life to appear tomorrow, but if it did arise, the consequences could be severe, and it makes sense to develop detection methods before they are needed. Professor Pal and I had been working on CPL technologies before recent concerns became prominent, and guarding against mirror life was a clear fit for our research."
A Molecular Fingerprint for Detecting Mirror Life
To identify a possible mirror organism, the researchers suggest using specialized fluorescent probes that attach to particular structures inside cells.
Once bound to their targets, these probes would generate characteristic CPL signals. Scientists could analyze the resulting patterns to determine whether a biological sample contains the molecular handedness associated with ordinary terrestrial life or its reversed equivalent.
In effect, the light signals could serve as a molecular fingerprint, revealing differences that might otherwise be difficult to identify.
However, relying on a single fluorescent probe could produce misleading results. To improve reliability and reduce the risk of false readings, the team proposes combining several probes designed to recognize different cellular structures.
By examining multiple signals together, researchers hope to develop a more dependable way to distinguish conventional organisms from hypothetical mirror life.
Testing the Technology Without Creating Mirror Organisms
One important advantage of the proposed technique is that scientists could begin investigating and refining it using ordinary biological samples. There would be no need to manufacture mirror organisms simply to explore whether the underlying detection principles work.
The researchers also believe the method could eventually be incorporated into several types of scientific equipment, potentially allowing mirror-life screening in different environments.
Professor Pal has already demonstrated laboratory-scale CPL detection technologies involving microscopes, cameras, and biological cell plate readers, which are instruments commonly used to examine large numbers of cell samples.
However, the complete detection method specifically designed to identify mirror life has not yet been experimentally demonstrated. Further research will be necessary to determine whether the proposed approach can reliably distinguish between different forms of molecular handedness in biological samples.
Professor Pal added: "CPL detection relies on the same fundamental concept that allows modern 3D cinema glasses to create a stereoscopic image.
"This CPL detection approach can be adapted to many types of systems for analysis of cells, including biological plate readers, microscopes, and cameras. This means our mirror life assay approach could be generalized to many environments depending on end user needs."
Story Source:
Materials provided by https://www.strath.ac.uk/. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lewis E. MacKenzie, Dominic J. Black, Robert Pal. Circularly polarized luminescence as a contingency assay for ‘mirror life’ bio-hazards. Royal Society Open Science, 2026; 13 (10) DOI: 10.1098/rsos.260921

Astronomers uncover a mysterious magnetic web above the Sun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:23:38 UTC
21:23:38 KST

Astronomers uncover a mysterious magnetic web above the Sun
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- National Institutes of Natural Sciences
- Summary:
- The Sun’s seemingly peaceful regions are hiding a surprisingly complex magnetic world. Using a balloon-borne telescope high above Earth, scientists discovered delicate, thread-like magnetic structures woven through the solar atmosphere, apparently shaped by twisting motions on the Sun’s surface. They also mapped magnetic fields inside towering jets of solar material, revealing how those fields change with height.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered a surprisingly complex network of magnetic structures hidden above regions of the Sun that appear relatively calm. Using the Sunrise-III solar observatory, which traveled high into Earth's stratosphere aboard a balloon in 2024, an international research team led by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan (NAOJ) discovered intricate, thread-like magnetic features that had previously been difficult to observe.
The findings reveal that even the Sun's seemingly quiet regions contain elaborate magnetic structures. They also offer new clues to how energy travels upward through the solar atmosphere and contributes to its heating.
A Hidden Web of Magnetic Threads Above the Sun
Sunrise-III detected numerous thin, elongated magnetic structures woven into a larger network of magnetic fields above a quiet region of the Sun. This network, known as the magnetic canopy, extends through the chromosphere, a layer of the solar atmosphere located above the Sun's visible surface.
The canopy develops as magnetic fields concentrated at the solar surface (photosphere) spread outward and arch upward into the chromosphere (chromosphere). Rather than forming a relatively smooth, uniformly expanding structure, however, the new observations reveal that the canopy contains many narrow, thread-like features.
To investigate how these structures form, researchers used computer simulations that successfully reproduced the patterns recorded by Sunrise-III. The results suggest that movements on the solar surface twist magnetic field lines, creating the intricate structures observed higher in the atmosphere.
The observatory also examined another quiet region near the solar limb (visible edge of the Sun). There, it measured magnetic fields within spicules, narrow jets of solar material that extend upward from the surface. These observations revealed how the distribution of magnetic fields changes with increasing height above the Sun's visible edge.
Why the Sun's Quiet Regions Are Difficult to Study
Although the Sun is constantly active, much of its surface lacks prominent features such as sunspots. Scientists describe these comparatively inactive areas as "quiet." They cover most of the Sun, making them especially important for understanding how our star behaves.
However, quiet does not mean magnetically inactive. These regions contain magnetic fields that are generally weaker than those found in more active areas of the Sun. Their subtle structures are difficult to measure, especially with telescopes on the ground, where turbulence in Earth's atmosphere can blur fine details.
Sunrise-III was designed to overcome this obstacle by carrying a powerful solar telescope far above most of the atmosphere.
A Balloon-Borne Telescope Reveals New Solar Details
Sunrise-III is an international research project built around a 1-meter telescope carried by a high-altitude balloon. During its 2024 mission, the observatory floated approximately 35 kilometers (about 22 miles) above Earth in the stratosphere, where atmospheric interference is greatly reduced.
This elevated vantage point allowed the telescope to capture exceptionally detailed measurements of the Sun's magnetic fields.
The balloon's gondola carried three scientific instruments developed through contributions from different countries. One of these was SCIP (Sunrise Chromospheric Infrared spectroPolarimeter), a near-infrared instrument developed under NAOJ's leadership.
SCIP is designed to measure magnetic fields continuously across different layers of the solar atmosphere, from the photosphere to the chromosphere. This capability allowed researchers to examine how magnetic structures extend and change with altitude rather than studying only a single layer.
New Clues to How the Sun's Atmosphere Is Heated
By observing from the stratosphere, Sunrise-III provided researchers with an unusually detailed picture of magnetic fields above the Sun's quiet regions. Its measurements revealed that the chromosphere contains far more intricate magnetic structures than a simple expanding canopy would suggest.
Understanding these structures could help scientists investigate how energy generated by motions near the solar surface is transferred into higher layers of the atmosphere.
The discovery offers an important step toward explaining how magnetic activity contributes to heating the Sun's atmosphere, including in regions that appear calm when viewed from afar.
